Q: What is the best AI agent for marketing?
A: The best agent is the one aimed at the gap that costs your business most, briefed from your own positioning, with a human reviewing its output. For most small businesses that is a search agent or an outbound agent. A product list cannot answer the question, because the same agent that suits a B2B consultancy is the wrong first build for a café.
Q: How many AI agents does a small marketing team need?
A: Start with one, plus the positioning brief that feeds it. Add the next agent only when the first runs every week with less than an hour of review. Launch and paid agents usually switch on for specific campaigns, while search and reporting run every week.
Q: Can I build an AI marketing agent without coding?
A: Yes, for agents that follow a fixed sequence. No-code workflow tools such as n8n or Zapier can connect a form, a model and your email or CRM, and installed skills give an AI assistant a written procedure to follow. Code becomes worthwhile when the agent needs custom data access or its own audit log.
Q: Are AI agents for marketing safe to use with customer data?
A: They are safe when access is narrow and recorded. Give each agent only the fields its job needs, keep customer lists in systems the business controls, and log every action. In New Zealand, check the Privacy Act's new indirect-collection rule before enriching lead lists. Australia's OAIC advises against putting personal information into publicly available AI tools.
Q: How long does it take to build one marketing agent?
A: A scoped agent with a written brief, connected tools, guardrails and a review step can go live in about a week of focused work. The longer part is the first month of running it, when the review notes turn into better instructions. Expect the agent to need noticeably less correction by its fourth or fifth weekly cycle.
Q: What is the difference between an AI marketing agent and marketing automation?
A: Marketing automation runs the steps a person designed, such as sending a welcome email after a sign-up. An AI marketing agent decides what the work should be, drafts it and then uses automation to deliver it. Most useful agents sit on top of automation the business already has, which is why the two are usually built together.

## AI agency, AI automation agency or AI consultant: which does an NZ business need?
URL: https://www.flowai.co.nz/blog/ai-agency-vs-ai-consultant-nz.html
Author: Amber Lan, Flow AI
Updated: 2026-10-05

Short answer: Choose an AI marketing agency when you want marketing produced and run for you, an AI automation agency when a specific process wastes hours every week, and an AI consultant when you need a plan before you buy anything. If you have staff with time, an in-house person plus an outside engineer can cost less than all three.

What is the difference between an AI agency, an AI automation agency and an AI consultant?

An AI marketing agency produces and runs your marketing with AI systems. An AI automation agency builds workflows that take repetitive tasks off your staff. An AI consultant advises, plans and trains while your own people do the work. All three call themselves an AI agency, so the job you need done decides which one fits.

An AI agency is an outside provider that builds, runs or advises on AI systems for a business, usually specialising in marketing output, process automation or strategy and training.

The fourth option sits outside the agency model: a person already on your team runs the work, and an outside engineer builds the first systems and shows them how. It is worth weighing alongside the other three because many NZ owners are already partway there. Xero's May 2026 research found 61% of New Zealand small and medium businesses proactively using AI, and 79% of them learning through self-guided experimentation.

If you are still deciding whether to buy outside help at all, the guide Do you need an AI marketing agency in NZ? covers that question. This page assumes you have decided to get help and want to pick the right kind.

What does an AI marketing agency do?

An AI marketing agency plans, produces and publishes marketing using AI systems it operates, with people reviewing before anything goes out. Typical services are content, SEO and AI search, paid ads, email, social posts and reporting. You buy output and results each month, and the agency's people and systems do most of the work.

The service list overlaps with a traditional agency's. The difference shows in how the work is made: drafts come from systems trained on your business, a person edits and approves them, and the agency can usually produce more for the same fee. Some agencies also work on how your business appears in AI answers, often called answer engine optimisation.

The label covers a wide range, from a traditional agency using ChatGPT internally to a fixed-price system with a dashboard. Ask what the AI does for you and who checks it. The glossary defines an AI marketing agent, and the guide to AI marketing agents sets out what a complete marketing system covers.

What does an AI automation agency do?

An AI automation agency connects the software you already use and adds AI steps so routine work runs on its own. It sells working workflows: an enquiry answered and routed, a lead scored, a booking made, a quote drafted. It rarely produces marketing content, and it seldom tells you what your strategy should be.

A typical AI automation agency services list for a small business looks like this:

Website chat or an AI receptionist that answers common questions and books calls

Lead capture that scores enquiries and sends them to the right person

Follow-up emails and texts after a quote, a booking or a missed call

Data moved between your CRM, accounting software and spreadsheets

Drafts of quotes, proposals or reports from a template and your data

A dashboard pulling numbers from several tools into one view

Most of this is marketing automation with an AI step added, built on platforms such as Make, Zapier or n8n. The agency's skill lies in choosing the right process to automate and keeping the workflow running when a connected tool changes. The guide to AI marketing automation for small business covers which processes usually pay back first.

What does an AI consultant or AI transformation consultant do?

An AI consultant reviews how your business works, finds where AI will save time or win work, writes a plan with a sequence and budget, and trains your staff to use the tools safely. An AI transformation consultant does the same across the whole business. Either way, your team does the ongoing work once the engagement ends.

Consulting suits a business that wants to understand the options before spending on builds or retainers, or one where several teams want AI at once and somebody needs to set rules. Good consulting output is concrete: a short written plan, a list of approved tools, a privacy assessment, and one or two working changes your staff already use.

Weak consulting output is a long slide deck. If the plan does not name who owns each step and when it starts, the engagement has produced advice your team cannot act on. The guide to AI marketing transformation shows what a full plan for a small business covers.

When does an in-house person with an outside engineer make more sense?

An in-house person with an outside engineer makes more sense when someone on your team has a few hours a week and wants to learn. The engineer builds the first systems on your accounts, documents them and trains your person to run them. You keep the knowledge inside the business and pay outside rates only for the build.

The cost logic is simple. A new hire is expensive: SEEK's October 2026 advertised average for a marketing coordinator in New Zealand was NZD 61,498, and Robert Walters' 2026 salary guide puts Auckland marketing coordinators at NZD 60,000 to 85,000, before employer KiwiSaver, which Inland Revenue confirms rose to 3.5% on 1 April 2026. Using a person you already employ avoids that cost, and the outside build is a one-time spend.

The risk is time. If your person is already at capacity, the systems will sit unused. Before choosing this route, agree how many hours a week they will spend on it and protect those hours.

How do the four options compare?

The four options differ most in who does the ongoing work and what you own when the engagement ends. Agencies do the work and often keep the process. Consultants leave a plan and trained staff. Automation agencies leave workflows that need upkeep. An in-house person with an engineer leaves both the systems and the skill inside your business.

OptionWhat they deliverWho does the workTypical engagement shapeWhat you own at the endBest for

AI marketing agencyContent, ads, SEO and AI search, email, social, reportingThe agency's people and systemsMonthly retainer, sometimes with a setup feeThe published work; the systems only if the contract says soOwners who want marketing run for them across several channels

AI automation agencyWorkflows for enquiries, follow-up, bookings, data and reportingThe agency builds; the workflow runs on its ownSetup fee per workflow plus a monthly support feeThe workflows, if they sit on your accountsBusinesses losing hours to one repetitive process

AI consultant or transformation consultantAssessment, plan, tool choice, policy, staff trainingYour team, after the consultant leavesFixed-scope project, or hourly or monthly advisoryThe plan, the policy and trained staffBusinesses that want a plan before spending on builds

In-house person plus outside engineerSystems built on your accounts and a person trained to run themYour person, with the engineer at the startOne-time build, then optional monthly supportThe systems, the documentation and the skillBusinesses with a staff member who has the hours and wants to learn

Plenty of providers mix columns. An agency may offer a consulting phase first, and a consultant may build one workflow as part of the plan. Use the table to ask which column most of your fee pays for.

How is AI agency work usually priced?

AI agency work is priced in three shapes: a fixed project fee for a build or a plan, a monthly retainer for ongoing work, and an hourly rate for advice. Published NZD prices for AI-specific providers are rare, so the general NZ agency and consultant ranges below are the best public reference available.

What the public sources show, as of October 2026:

Jelly Digital's September 2026 guide puts NZ agency retainers at NZD 500 to 1,500 a month for one channel, NZD 1,500 to 4,000 for multi-channel and NZD 4,000 to 10,000+ for full service, with hourly rates of NZD 95 to 200. It is an agency's own estimate, not a survey.

Growin's price page listed a Launch package at NZD 1,500 setup plus NZD 500 a month plus GST, and a Foundation package at NZD 4,000 plus GST one-off, covering ads and lead intake.

King Tide's July 2026 guide puts NZ consultants at NZD 150 to 250 an hour or NZD 2,000 to 5,000 a month. These are marketing consultants; AI consultants who publish rates are uncommon.

AI automation agencies in NZ rarely publish prices, so ask for a written quote per workflow plus the monthly fee, and check whether software subscriptions are included. Hidden pricing is normal across the region: a June 2026 Digital Nomads HQ audit of 411 service lines across 140 Australian agencies found 78% publish no pricing. The AI marketing cost guide for Australia and New Zealand sets these ranges against hires and tools, and the marketing agency cost guide breaks retainers down by service.

How do you vet an AI agency or consultant?

Vet any AI provider by asking who reviews the output, what you own at the end, whether the work is documented, how your customer data is handled under the Privacy Act 2020, and what proof you can inspect yourself. A good provider answers all of it in writing within a week, and welcomes the questions.

Questions to ask in the first meeting:

Who reviews outputs before they reach a customer? Name the person and the step. This matters because people trust AI output too easily: KPMG and the University of Melbourne found 51% of New Zealand employees had relied on AI output at work without evaluating its accuracy (surveyed over summer 2024 to 2025). A human in the loop should approve anything published, sent or spent.

What do I own at the end? Accounts, workflows, prompts, content and data should sit in your name from day one. Anything that stops when you cancel was rented.

Is it documented? Ask for a written description of each system, including what it reads and who to call when it breaks.

How is my data handled? Ask which AI tools touch customer information and where they store it. Under the Privacy Act 2020, the Privacy Commissioner's information privacy principles include storage and security of information (IPP 5) and disclosure outside New Zealand (IPP 12), and the Commissioner expects a privacy impact assessment before AI tools are used, updated regularly. If a provider builds enriched lead lists, ask how it meets IPP3A, in force since 1 May 2026, which requires telling people when their information was collected indirectly.

What proof can I inspect? A live or recorded run on a real business, with inputs, outputs and the review step visible. Logos and percentages on a sales deck prove little.

Red flags that should slow you down:

Guaranteed rankings, guaranteed mentions in AI answers or guaranteed revenue

Accounts set up in the provider's name, or a platform you cannot export from

No written scope, or a long minimum term before you have seen month-one output

Results quoted with no client you can contact and no source you can check

Vague answers about where customer data goes

Value is where relationships tend to break. Setup's 2025 Marketing Relationship Survey found 61% of clients who ended an agency relationship cited dissatisfaction with value, from about 100 responses, mostly larger US brands. Writing down what month one will produce protects you from the same outcome.

What should you check when hiring an AI agency in Auckland?

In Auckland, check the same things you would anywhere, plus two local ones: that the provider is a registered New Zealand business you can meet in person, and that it can tell you which of your data leaves the country. Judge every shortlisted provider on evidence you can inspect, whatever its ranking on a list.

This guide found no published survey that counts or ranks AI agencies in Auckland, so this section gives you checks rather than names. Look the provider up on the New Zealand Companies Office register to confirm the legal entity and its directors. Ask for a meeting at your premises or theirs; a provider building systems for your business should be happy to see how it runs. Ask who will do the work and where they are based, because a subcontracted build changes who checks quality and where your data travels.

For Australian readers the shape is the same, with one legal difference: the OAIC's 2024 guidance recommends that organisations do not enter personal information into publicly available generative AI tools, and the OAIC says the Australian Privacy Act generally applies to businesses with annual turnover above A$3 million, plus some smaller ones such as health providers. The guide to marketing agency alternatives prices the non-agency routes for both countries.

Where Flow AI fits

Flow AI is an AI marketing transformation practice: the strategy, the systems and the agents that run a marketing function, engineered end to end. It is the engineered version of the fourth column: AI agents plus one marketing engineer, Amber Lan, who builds the systems on your accounts, documents them and reviews the work before it ships.

The short version

Pick an AI marketing agency for marketing run for you, an AI automation agency for one process that wastes hours, and an AI consultant for a plan before you spend. If someone on your team has the time, an in-house person with an outside engineer keeps the systems and the skill in the business.

Whichever you choose, get the price and scope in writing, keep every account in your name, and ask who reviews the work and where your data goes.

To see which option fits your business, request a free audit.

Q: What does an AI automation agency do?
A: An AI automation agency connects the software a business already uses and adds AI steps so repetitive work runs on its own. Typical jobs are answering and routing enquiries, qualifying leads, booking appointments, moving data between systems, drafting quotes and sending follow-ups. Most charge a setup fee for the build and a monthly fee for hosting, monitoring and fixes, and the work is usually built on platforms such as Make, Zapier or n8n.
Q: Is an AI automation agency legit?
A: Many are, and the category also attracts sellers who copied a course and resell the same template to every client. A legitimate agency will show a working automation on a real business, explain where a person checks the output, put the accounts in your name, document each workflow and tell you where your customer data is stored. If it cannot do those things in one meeting, keep looking.
Q: How much does an AI agency cost in New Zealand?
A: Few NZ AI agencies publish prices. One productised example, Growin, listed NZD 1,500 setup plus NZD 500 a month plus GST in October 2026. General NZ agency retainers run about NZD 500 to 10,000 or more a month by Jelly Digital's 2026 estimate, and King Tide puts consultants at NZD 150 to 250 an hour. Get a written scope and price before comparing.
Q: What is the difference between an AI consultant and an AI agency?
A: An AI consultant advises and an AI agency delivers. A consultant assesses where AI fits, writes a plan, helps choose tools and often trains your staff, then leaves your team to run it. An agency builds and operates the systems or produces the marketing itself. Some providers do both, so ask which part of the work their people will actually do each month.
Q: What does an AI transformation consultant do for a small business?
A: An AI transformation consultant reviews how the business works, picks the processes where AI will save the most time or win the most work, sets a sequence and budget, and trains staff to use the new tools safely. For a 5 to 50 person business the useful output is a short written plan with owners and dates, plus at least one working change in the first month.
Q: Should a small business use an AI agency or do it in-house?
A: Use an agency when nobody inside has the hours and the work spans several channels or systems. Keep it in-house when a staff member has a few hours a week and wants to learn, and bring in an outside engineer to build the first systems and teach the method. The in-house route is slower to start and usually cheaper to run.

## What is answer engine optimisation (AEO)? A guide for small business.
URL: https://www.flowai.co.nz/blog/what-is-answer-engine-optimisation.html
Author: Amber Lan, Flow AI
Updated: 2026-10-02

Short answer: Answer engine optimisation (AEO) is the work of making your business easy for AI answer engines such as ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini and Google's AI Overviews to find, understand and name in their answers. It builds on normal SEO: crawlable pages, clear facts, direct answers to real questions, and mentions of your business on other trusted sites.

What is answer engine optimisation?

Answer engine optimisation is the practice of making a business easy for AI systems to find, understand and recommend when someone asks them a question. Classic search hands back a list of links. An answer engine writes the reply itself and names a few sources along the way. AEO is the work of being one of those names.

Answer engine optimisation (AEO) is the practice of shaping a business's website, facts and reputation so AI answer engines can find it, trust it and cite or recommend it in the answers they write.

The term predates ChatGPT, when it meant featured snippets and voice assistants. Since 2023 answer engines have written full paragraphs and recommended named businesses, so the job has grown into shaping how an AI describes you. The glossary entry for AEO has the one-line version.

For a 5 to 50 person business, AEO comes down to four questions. Can the AI crawlers read your site? Are the facts about you (what you do, where, for whom, roughly what it costs) written plainly and the same everywhere? Do your pages answer the questions customers ask, in their words? And do other sites mention you, so the AI has a reason to believe what you say about yourself?

Which tools count as answer engines?

An answer engine is any search or chat tool that replies with a written answer instead of a page of links. In 2026 the ones that matter for a small business are ChatGPT, Google's AI Overviews and AI Mode, Gemini, Perplexity, Microsoft Copilot and Claude. Each pulls from the live web differently, so each rewards slightly different work.

Answer engineWhere its live web results come fromWhat a business can check

Google AI Overviews and AI ModeGoogle's own search index, under the normal Search rulesYour pages are indexed in Google Search Console

ChatGPT searchPartner search providers, with Microsoft (Bing) named by OpenAI, plus OpenAI's own search crawlerYour site is indexed in Bing Webmaster Tools and robots.txt allows OAI-SearchBot

Microsoft CopilotBingBing Webmaster Tools and a Bing Places listing

PerplexityIts own crawler and indexrobots.txt allows PerplexityBot

Two free consoles, Google Search Console and Bing Webmaster Tools, cover most of these engines. OpenAI's help page on ChatGPT search says it sends rewritten queries to partner search providers and names Microsoft (Bing) among them. It may also pass a general IP-based location, so "electrician near me" becomes a local search.

Why AEO matters for a small business now

AEO matters now because a growing share of searches end inside the answer. People still search, and Google's query volume is still rising, but fewer of those searches send anyone to a website. When the answer is where the customer stops, being named in it does the job a page one ranking used to do.

Pew Research Center tracked 68,879 Google searches by 900 US adults in March 2025 and found people clicked a traditional result on 8% of visits when an AI summary appeared, against 15% when one did not. Only 1% of visits included a click on a link inside the summary itself. SparkToro's 2026 study, built on Similarweb clickstream data from January to April 2026, found 68.01% of US Google searches ended with zero clicks, up from 60.45% in 2024. Both are US figures. No equivalent New Zealand measurement exists yet (the glossary defines zero-click search).

Volume is a different story. In February 2024, Gartner predicted traditional search engine volume would drop 25% by 2026 as people moved to chatbots. That was a prediction made in early 2024. Google's reported numbers since then point the other way: on Alphabet's Q2 2025 earnings call, Sundar Pichai said AI Overviews had more than 2 billion monthly users and drive over 10% more queries for the types of queries that show them. People are searching more and clicking less.

The chat tools are mainstream too. OpenAI said at DevDay 2026 that its products reach a collective 1.2 billion weekly users, a figure covering all of its products, ChatGPT included. OpenAI's own study of 1.5 million ChatGPT conversations, published in September 2025, found 49% of consumer messages were people asking for information or advice.

New Zealand follows the same pattern. InternetNZ's Aotearoa Internet Insights 2025, a survey of 1,003 New Zealand adults run in late 2025, found 55% had used AI in search engines and 53% had used AI chatbots in the past year. And PwC New Zealand's 2026 study of 1,000 Kiwi consumers who already use AI to shop found 44% say AI has reduced their use of search engines when researching purchases. That sample is AI users only, but they are the customers comparing suppliers before they call.

How do AI answer engines choose what to cite?

Most answer engines search before they write. They split the question into narrower queries, fetch pages from an index, pull out the passages that answer each part, and write a reply citing a handful. A page gets cited when the engine can reach it and it answers the narrow query plainly from a source that looks trustworthy.

That splitting step is often called query fan-out. Ask "who should I use to replace my hot water cylinder in Tauranga?" and the engine may search separately for replacement costs, licensed plumbers in Tauranga and reviews of the names it finds. A pricing page, a Tauranga service page and recent reviews give it material at each step.

Ranking well in Google helps, but it does not decide the result. Ahrefs' own analysis of 15,000 prompts in 2025 found only 12% of URLs cited by ChatGPT, Gemini and Copilot ranked in Google's top 10 for the same prompt (8% for ChatGPT alone). Inside Google, Ahrefs' March 2026 update, covering 863,000 keyword results, found 37.9% of pages cited in AI Overviews ranked in the top 10 for that keyword, and 31.0% ranked outside the top 100. Ahrefs sells SEO software, so read these as one vendor's data. The direction is clear all the same: engines cite passages from well beyond page one.

Reputation off your own site carries real weight. An Ahrefs correlation study of 75,000 brands found branded web mentions had the strongest link to AI Overview visibility (0.664), well ahead of backlinks (0.218). Correlation is weaker evidence than an experiment, though it fits how the engines behave: they lean on what other people say about a business.

An engine is more likely to cite a business when:

It can fetch the page: crawlers are allowed and the text is in the HTML when the page loads.

A passage on the page answers the narrow question in a sentence or two that make sense on their own.

The facts about the business match across its site, its listings and directories, which the glossary calls NAP consistency.

Other sources mention it: reviews, local press, industry bodies, YouTube.

What does the research say works?

The strongest evidence comes from the 2024 paper that named generative engine optimisation. Aggarwal and colleagues (Princeton, Georgia Tech, the Allen Institute for AI and IIT Delhi, KDD 2024) tested page edits across 10,000 queries and found the right changes lifted a source's visibility in AI answers by up to 40%. The winning edits were plain writing changes.

The best performers were adding quotations, adding statistics and citing sources, each with a relative improvement of 30 to 40%, while keyword stuffing offered little to no improvement.

One finding matters a lot for small sites. In the same benchmark, citing sources lifted visibility by 115.1% for websites ranked fifth in search results, while the top-ranked site's visibility fell by 30.3% on average. That result comes from a lab benchmark of simulated searches, so treat it as a sign of direction. It suggests a well-sourced page from a smaller site can beat a vague page from a bigger one.

Translated into page edits for a small business:

Put a number on claims you can stand behind, such as your typical price range for a job and what moves it, and say where it comes from.

Quote a named person, such as the owner, a licensed tradesperson or a customer with permission.

Link to the regulation, standard or study a claim relies on.

Write the way a customer asks, without repeating keywords.

How is AEO different from SEO and GEO?

SEO earns a place in a list of links. AEO earns a mention inside a written answer. GEO is the research name for the same goal in AI engines that generate text. They share one foundation, and Google says AI Overviews need nothing beyond normal SEO best practice, so AEO is best treated as an extension of SEO.

SEOAEOGEO

Aims forA high position in search resultsBeing cited or recommended in an AI answerBeing included and quoted in generated answers

Shows up inGoogle and Bing results pagesChatGPT, Perplexity, AI Overviews, Copilot, GeminiThe same AI engines

RewardsRelevance, links, technical healthDirect answers, consistent facts, mentions elsewhereSourced, quotable passages

Measured byRankings, clicks, Search ConsolePrompt logs, AI referrals, enquiriesVisibility in AI responses

Google Search Central's guidance on AI features says no special schema.org markup, AI text file or extra markup is needed to appear in AI Overviews or AI Mode, and there are no requirements beyond core SEO. That is fair, and it is the right place to start. The AEO work beyond core SEO mostly happens off Google: Bing indexing for ChatGPT and Copilot, crawler rules for OpenAI and Perplexity, and the reviews and mentions every engine weighs.

The full comparison, with which one to fund first, is in AEO vs SEO vs GEO: what is the difference?

What can a small business do about AEO this month?

A small business can cover most of AEO without a developer by working through five areas in order: let the AI crawlers in, write down the facts about the business, build pages that answer real questions, earn proof and mentions elsewhere, then add structured data. Each step depends on the one before.

Let the crawlers in. Check robots.txt allows OAI-SearchBot, PerplexityBot, Googlebot and Bingbot, and that your host is not blocking AI crawlers. Flow AI's free AI crawler access check tests fourteen AI crawlers against robots.txt, page tags and server headers.

Write down the facts. One page stating the name, services, area, hours, credentials and typical prices, matched exactly on your Google Business Profile, Bing Places and directories.

Answer the questions. Open each important page with a 40 to 60 word answer to the question it targets, phrase headings the way customers ask, and add the numbers, quotes and sources the research rewards.

Earn proof elsewhere. Recent reviews, an industry association listing, a local news story, a short YouTube walkthrough. The guide on how to get your business mentioned by ChatGPT covers this step in depth.

Add structured data. LocalBusiness or Organization schema markup that repeats the facts from step two in a form machines read without guessing.

Each area breaks into specific tasks in the AEO checklist for small business, which most owners can work through in a week.

How do you measure AEO?

Measure AEO with four habits while the tools mature: a monthly log of what the main engines say when asked your customers' questions, AI referral visits in your analytics, Search Console trends, and enquiries where the customer says an AI suggested you. No tool yet reports AI visibility as reliably as Search Console reports Google rankings.

The prompt log does most of the work. Write 15 to 20 questions a real customer would ask, such as "best accountant for a small café in Wellington" or "how much does a heat pump install cost in Auckland", and run them in ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini and Google each month. Record whether you are named, who else is, and which pages get cited. Answers vary between runs, so judge the trend over three months.

In Google Analytics 4, visits from AI tools show as referrals from domains such as chatgpt.com, perplexity.ai, gemini.google.com and copilot.microsoft.com. Numbers are usually small, because many people read the answer and phone without clicking, so add "an AI assistant like ChatGPT" to the "how did you hear about us?" options.

Being cited seems to help the clicks that remain. Seer Interactive's September 2025 update, covering 3,119 search terms across 42 client organisations, found brands cited inside an AI Overview earned 35% more organic clicks and 91% more paid clicks than brands not cited. Seer is an agency reporting its own clients' data, so read it as a direction of travel.

What does AEO look like for New Zealand and Australian businesses?

For most New Zealand and Australian small businesses AEO is local. A customer asks an AI tool for a builder in Hamilton or a physio in Brisbane, and the engine searches business listings, reviews and service pages. The same local signals that drive Google Maps carry most of the weight, with Bing's index mattering more than its market share suggests.

Bing is the overlooked part. Statcounter's September 2026 data gives Google 89.02% of New Zealand search engine market share and Bing 7.71%, and Australia looks similar at 87.9% for Google and 9.17% for Bing. Because ChatGPT search and Copilot both draw on Bing, a missing Bing Places listing or an unindexed site costs more than that share suggests.

The local AI habit is growing fastest where the data exists. BrightLocal's Local Consumer Review Survey 2026, of 1,002 US adults, found 45% had used ChatGPT or other AI tools for local business recommendations, up from 6% the year before. BrightLocal sells local SEO software and the sample is American, so treat it as an early signal. Its follow-up found 88% of people who use AI for local recommendations check the sources the AI cites, which brings it back to reviews and listings.

The local groundwork (Google Business Profile, reviews, suburb pages, NZ directories) is covered in SEO for small business in New Zealand. For the wider picture of AI across a marketing function, start with the guide to AI marketing for small business in NZ.

Flow AI is an AI marketing transformation practice: the strategy, the systems and the agents that run a marketing function, engineered end to end. Search and AI search is often the first system it installs, through the AI search sprint, and the free audit names whether that is the right first step for your business.

The tools behind the work are public. The free agent templates include the AI crawler access check and a full GEO audit, and the open-source GEO skills sit in the Flow AI skill library for anyone who wants to install and run them on their own site.

The short version

Answer engine optimisation is the work of being named when an AI tool answers a customer's question. It rests on SEO and adds four habits: open your site to AI crawlers, keep your business facts identical everywhere, write pages that answer questions in the first paragraph, and earn mentions and reviews on other sites.

InternetNZ found 55% of New Zealanders used AI in search engines in the past year. A business that does the groundwork now gives every engine what it needs to recommend it, and the same work pays back in ordinary Google search.

To find out which part of AI search to fix first on your site, request a free audit.

Q: Is answer engine optimisation replacing SEO?
A: AEO sits on top of SEO and depends on it. Google says pages need no special markup to appear in AI Overviews beyond normal SEO best practice, and ChatGPT search draws on partner search indexes including Bing. A site that search engines cannot crawl or index will struggle in AI answers too. Treat AEO as the extra layer: answer-first pages, consistent facts, and mentions on other sites.
Q: Does AEO work for a local business, or only for big brands?
A: It works for local businesses, and the local version is simpler. When someone asks an AI tool for a plumber or a physio nearby, the engine runs a local search and leans on business listings, reviews and service pages. A complete Google Business Profile, matching details on Bing Places and directories, recent reviews and one page per service and area cover most of it.
Q: How long does answer engine optimisation take to work?
A: The access fixes, such as unblocking AI crawlers and getting indexed in Bing, can show up within weeks once the engines recrawl your site. Mentions on other sites and a body of answer-first pages take months, as they do in SEO. Run the same prompts in ChatGPT, Perplexity and Google each month and compare, because single answers vary from run to run.
Q: How much does AEO cost a small business?
A: The first round costs mostly time. Checking robots.txt, claiming Bing Places, rewriting page openings and asking for reviews need no software. Free tools cover the checks: Google Search Console, Bing Webmaster Tools, Google's Rich Results Test and Flow AI's free AI crawler access check. Paid AI visibility trackers exist, but a monthly manual prompt log is enough for a business of 5 to 50 staff to start.
Q: Do I need an llms.txt file for AEO?
A: It is optional. No major AI provider has said it uses llms.txt to choose sources, and Ahrefs' 2026 study of 137,210 domains found 97% of published llms.txt files received zero requests in a month. It takes ten minutes to add, so it does no harm, but it belongs at the end of the list, after crawler access, facts, answer pages and reviews.
Q: Is AEO the same as GEO?
A: Very nearly. GEO, generative engine optimisation, comes from a 2024 research paper and describes optimising content for AI engines that write answers. AEO is the older industry term, first used for featured snippets and voice assistants, now applied to the same AI tools. Most practitioners use the two interchangeably, and the work for a small business is the same under either name.

## What is an AI CMO? A plain definition for small business.
URL: https://www.flowai.co.nz/blog/what-is-an-ai-cmo.html
Author: Amber Lan, Flow AI
Updated: 2026-10-02

Short answer: An AI CMO is software that does the planning half of a chief marketing officer's job. It reads the business and its market, sets priorities, writes the marketing plan, briefs the work and reviews the results each cycle. A human still owns positioning, pricing, claims, spend and anything that reaches a customer.

What is an AI CMO?

An AI CMO is software that plans a business's marketing the way a chief marketing officer would. It studies the business and its market, decides what matters most this month, writes the plan, briefs the work and checks the results. It carries the planning load, while a named human approves anything that commits the business.

An AI CMO is software that does the planning half of a chief marketing officer's job: it reads the business and its market, sets priorities, writes the marketing plan, briefs the work and reviews the results, with a human approving the decisions that carry the business's name.

The label is new and loosely used. Some products called AI CMOs are planning tools with a dashboard. Others also write and ship the work, which makes them closer to a full AI marketing agent. The glossary entry for AI CMO keeps the short version.

For a business of 5 to 50 staff, the useful way to read the term is by job. A human CMO in a large company sets direction, chooses where the budget goes, runs a team and answers to the board for results. A small business usually has none of that. It has an owner who does marketing when the week allows, and an AI CMO is an attempt to give that owner the planning and reviewing half of the role on a schedule.

What does an AI CMO do each week?

An AI CMO works in a cycle. It reads what changed in the business and its market, ranks the marketing problems by likely payoff, writes or updates a plan, turns the plan into briefs for whoever produces the work, and reviews the results against the numbers the owner cares about. Then the cycle repeats with that review folded in.

Read. The website, services, prices, past campaigns, analytics, search terms customers use, reviews and the competitors ranking above the business. The quality of everything after this step depends on how much it reads here.

Rank. A short list of what to fix first, with a reason for each. For a trades business that might be missing suburb pages; for a clinic, an enquiry form that drops half its visitors.

Plan. A month of work with an owner, a deadline and a target number for each item. A plan an owner can disagree with in five minutes is a good plan.

Brief. Each item becomes a brief for a person, a freelancer or an agent: the audience, the claim, the evidence, the format and what done looks like.

Review. At the end of the cycle it reports what shipped, what moved, what did not and what to stop, then recommends next month's order.

Steps four and five are where products differ most. A planner that stops at the brief needs someone else to do the work. One that also produces the work is doing an agent's job, and should be judged on its output as well as its plan.

Why the AI CMO has arrived now

The AI CMO has arrived because senior marketing leadership is scarce and expensive even for large companies, while AI can now do much of the reading and planning that used to need a person. Small businesses never had a CMO in the first place, so for them the comparison is with having no plan at all.

Even at the top of the market the role is thin on the ground. Spencer Stuart's January 2026 study of 346 CMOs at S&P 500 companies found an average tenure of 4.1 years, against 5.0 years for all C-suite roles, and 31% of those companies had no enterprise CMO. Budgets are tight as well. Gartner's 2026 CMO Spend Survey of 401 marketing leaders, surveyed early 2026 at mostly large companies, found 56% lacked the budget to deliver their 2026 strategy, while CMOs put 15.3% of marketing budgets into AI.

Smaller organisations are further behind on agents. McKinsey's State of AI 2026, from 1,719 respondents surveyed mid 2026, found 40% of respondents at organisations with more than US$1 billion in revenue scaling AI agents, while the share at smaller organisations stayed flat at 22%. Microsoft's 2025 Work Trend Index has an anecdote that captures the idea: one startup in Microsoft's research skipped hiring a CMO and gave a junior marketer AI to run full-stack campaigns. That is one company, so treat it as an illustration of a pattern rather than evidence for it.

AI CMO vs AI marketing agent vs fractional CMO

The three options split the CMO's job differently. An AI CMO covers planning and review in software. An AI marketing agent covers planning, production and shipping in software, with human approval. A fractional CMO is a senior person working part time who brings judgment and accountability, and usually relies on others to do the production.

QuestionAI CMOAI marketing agentFractional CMO

What it doesReads, ranks, plans, briefs, reviewsPlans, produces, ships under review, reportsSets strategy, leads people, reports to the owner

Who produces the workSomeone else: staff, freelancer or agentThe agent, across several channelsA team, agency or freelancer the CMO directs

How often it worksEvery cycle, on a scheduleEvery cycle, on a scheduleA few days a month

Where judgment comes fromThe owner, informed by the planThe owner, at set approval pointsThe fractional CMO's experience

Who is accountableThe ownerThe owner, with a log of every actionThe fractional CMO, by contract

Weak spotA plan with nobody to execute itNeeds real review time to stay safeLimited hours and a production gap

The comparison with a fractional CMO is about money as much as capability, so it has its own page: fractional CMO vs AI CMO, with Australian and New Zealand rates. The comparison with automation is simpler. Automation delivers steps a person designed, and an AI CMO decides which steps are worth designing. The guide to AI marketing automation for small business covers that delivery layer.

What an AI CMO should never decide alone

An AI CMO should never decide alone on positioning, pricing, public claims, spend, customer contact or personal data. Each of these commits the business legally or financially, and the law in New Zealand and Australia treats the business as the author of what it publishes, whichever software drafted it. A human approves each one, every time.

The clearest ruling on this point is Canadian. In Moffatt v. Air Canada (2024 BCCRT 149, February 2024), British Columbia's Civil Resolution Tribunal held the airline liable for wrong bereavement-fare advice from its website chatbot, ordering it to pay CA$812.02. The tribunal found the airline "responsible for all the information on its website," chatbot included. It is a small-claims decision in another country, and it describes the default position a business should plan around.

Closer to home, the penalties are larger. Under New Zealand's Fair Trading Act, the Commerce Commission lists maximum fines of $600,000 per offence for a business and $200,000 for an individual. In Australia, a 2026 law doubled the maximum penalty for false or misleading conduct to A$100 million per offence, according to the Treasurer's March 2026 release. On privacy, New Zealand's Privacy Commissioner expects a privacy impact assessment before AI tools handle personal information.

Positioning and pricing. The AI CMO can research both and recommend. The owner chooses what the business is and what it charges.

Claims. Guarantees, timeframes, credentials, results and comparisons with competitors are checked by a person against evidence before they appear anywhere.

Spend. Ad budgets and tool purchases sit behind an approval with a hard ceiling.

Customer contact. The first send of any sequence, review request or follow-up is read by a human.

Personal data. Customer lists stay in systems the business controls, and the software gets the narrowest access that works.

There is a practical reason as well. KPMG and the University of Melbourne's 2025 study, surveyed over summer 2024-25, found 46% of New Zealand employees had made mistakes in their work due to AI, and 51% had relied on AI output without evaluating its accuracy. The human in the loop is the control for exactly that.

How to evaluate an AI CMO before you buy

Evaluate an AI CMO on what it reads, what it produces, where the human approves, what it reports and what you keep if you leave. Ask for a real plan made for a business your size, and for last month's report. A vendor that answers with feature lists and screenshots is selling a tool with a new label.

There is a lot of relabelling about. Gartner estimated in June 2025 that only about 130 of the thousands of agentic AI vendors are real, and predicts over 40% of agentic AI projects will be cancelled by the end of 2027 because of cost, unclear value or weak risk controls. Those are the failure modes to test for.

What does it read before planning? Get the input list. If the website, analytics and customer language are missing, the plan will be generic.

Can it explain a ranking? Ask why item one beats item two. A real planner gives a reason tied to your numbers.

What does it hand over each week? A brief, a draft, a shipped page? Know which before you compare prices.

Where are the approval points? They should match the list in the previous section. Too few is unsafe, and approvals on every comma turn it into a slower way of doing the work yourself.

What is in the report? Enquiries, sources, cost per enquiry, what shipped and what to stop. Impressions alone are not a report.

What stays with you? Plans, briefs, pages and data should live on your own accounts.

Who built it? Ask what the builder has shipped for a business your size, and whether you can inspect the method.

What a good month with an AI CMO looks like

A good month has four weekly reviews of about an hour, one longer monthly review, a plan that changed at least once because of the numbers, and a written record of what shipped. The owner spends their time on decisions and approvals, and the AI CMO absorbs the reading, ranking and drafting that used to fill evenings.

The time saving is the most common reported gain from this kind of software. Salesforce's State of Marketing, surveyed late 2025 across 4,450 marketers including 890 at small and medium businesses, reports that AI agents free up 6 to 7 hours a week for creative and strategic work. Salesforce sells agents, so weigh the figure accordingly, and judge your own month by what shipped.

In week one, the AI CMO reads and proposes a ranked list. The owner cuts it to the top two and approves the plan. In weeks two and three, the briefs go to whoever produces the work, and the drafts come back for review. In week four, the report shows what moved, and the plan for the next month is redrafted. By month three the reading step gets faster because the record of past decisions is doing some of the work.

Who should use an AI CMO, and who should wait

An AI CMO suits a business with a product that sells, some marketing already running, and an owner or lead who can give an hour a week to decisions. The strongest case is a business that has never had a marketing plan and keeps restarting. The weakest is a business with no way to produce the work it plans.

Wait if the business does not yet know who buys from it and why. A planner cannot rank work against a customer nobody has described. Wait as well if nobody can review drafts, because unreviewed output is where the legal and brand risk sits.

Go ahead if marketing stalls every time the business gets busy, if decisions get made on gut feel because nobody has time to read the analytics, or if a freelancer or agency is producing work without a plan behind it. The free AI-readiness benchmark gives a quick read on which of these applies, with no email required.

Where Flow AI fits

It builds the planning and the production as installable systems that stay on the business's own domain and accounts, and a human reviews everything before it ships.

The method is public. The skill library holds 125 inspectable skills, and the free audit names the first system to install and why, before any money changes hands.

The short version

An AI CMO is software that plans marketing on a schedule: it reads, ranks, plans, briefs and reviews. For a small business that never had a CMO, the gain is a weekly rhythm and a plan that changes with the numbers. It still needs someone or something to produce the work.

The owner keeps the decisions that commit the business: positioning, pricing, claims, spend, customer contact and personal data. Judge any AI CMO by the plan it writes for a business your size and by last month's report.

To find out what your first plan should fix, request a free audit.

Q: Is an AI CMO the same as an AI marketing agent?
A: They overlap. An AI CMO usually means the planning layer: what to work on, in what order, measured against which numbers. An AI marketing agent covers the whole loop, so it plans, produces the work, ships it under review and reports back. A product sold as an AI CMO that produces nothing is a planner, and a planner still needs someone to do the work it plans.
Q: Can an AI CMO replace a human CMO?
A: For a business of 5 to 50 staff that has never had a CMO, an AI CMO can supply the planning and reviewing rhythm that was missing. It cannot carry accountability for the brand, negotiate with partners or decide what the business stands for. Those stay with the owner, or with a fractional CMO if the business wants senior judgment from outside.
Q: What should an AI CMO never decide alone?
A: Anything that commits the business. That covers positioning and pricing, claims about the product or service, money spent on ads or tools, any message to a customer or prospect, and how personal information is used. Consumer law in New Zealand and Australia holds the business responsible for what it publishes, whichever system wrote it.
Q: How much time does an AI CMO need from the owner?
A: Plan for a short weekly review and a longer monthly one. The weekly review approves what ships and kills what should not. The monthly review checks the plan against enquiries and sales and changes the priorities. If a product claims to need no owner time at all, nobody is checking its claims before customers read them.
Q: Is an AI CMO worth it for a small business?
A: It is worth it when marketing keeps stalling for lack of a plan and a weekly rhythm, and the business has, or will add, a way to produce the work. It is poor value as a standalone planner for an owner with no hours to execute, because a better plan for work that never ships changes nothing.
Q: How do I tell a real AI CMO from a chatbot with a new label?
A: Ask what it reads before it plans, what artefact it produces each week, where a human approves, and what the monthly report contains. A chatbot answers questions when prompted. A working AI CMO starts the cycle on its own, keeps a record of past decisions and can show why it ranked one priority above another.

## SEO for small business in New Zealand: a practical guide.
URL: https://www.flowai.co.nz/blog/seo-for-small-business-nz.html
Author: Amber Lan, Flow AI
Updated: 2026-10-02

Short answer: SEO for a New Zealand small business starts with Google, which handles about nine in ten NZ searches. Complete and maintain your Google Business Profile, collect recent reviews every week, give each service and each area you cover its own page, and fix the technical basics in Search Console. Most owners can do the first month themselves.

What does SEO mean for a small business in New Zealand?

For a New Zealand small business, SEO means being the business Google shows when someone nearby searches for what you sell. That comes down to a complete Google Business Profile, recent reviews, a clear page for each service and area, and a website Google can crawl. Most of it is free, and most of it is ordinary work.

Search engine optimisation (SEO) is the work of making a business's website and listings easy for search engines to find, understand and show to people searching for what the business sells. For a 5 to 50 person business, local search is where the enquiries are: the plumber in Hamilton or the physio in Wellington who gets the call because they appeared in the map results.

This guide is in the order I would do the work. If you are new to AI in your marketing generally, the start-here guide to AI marketing for NZ small business sets the wider context.

Where do New Zealand customers search?

New Zealand customers search on Google, overwhelmingly. Google held 89.02% of NZ search engine market share in September 2026, with Bing a distant second. AI assistants are growing fast as a research tool, but they mostly sit alongside search, and several of them read search results to build their answers.

Statcounter's September 2026 figures give Google 89.02% of New Zealand search and Bing 7.71%, and its Australian figures give Google 87.9% and Bing 9.17%. A small survey points the same way: IAB New Zealand's Kiwi Search Habits 2025, from 250 upper North Island adults surveyed in March 2025, found 96.8% named Google as their main search engine and 69.2% go to a search engine often or always before a purchase.

AI is changing how people use that search. InternetNZ's research with Verian, surveying 1,003 NZ adults in late 2025, found 55% had used AI in search engines in the past year. Among the shoppers who already use AI, PwC New Zealand's July 2026 survey of 1,000 NZ consumers found 44% said AI had reduced their use of search engines when researching purchases. That sample covers AI users only, so it is a direction of travel. Google remains the place to start.

Set up and maintain your Google Business Profile

Your Google Business Profile is the free listing that controls how you appear in Google Maps and the local results. Claim and verify it, choose the most accurate primary category, set your hours and service areas, and add photos and services. Then keep it current, because an out-of-date profile costs you enquiries without telling you.

The settings that make the most difference:

Primary category. Pick the single category that best matches the work you most want, such as "Electrician" rather than "Contractor". Add secondary categories for the rest.

Business name. Use your real trading name. Adding keywords or suburbs to the name breaks Google's guidelines and can get the profile suspended.

Address or service area. If customers come to you, show the address. If you go to them, set service areas by town or suburb and hide the street address.

Hours. Include special hours for public holidays such as Waitangi Day, Anzac Day and Matariki. Wrong holiday hours generate bad reviews.

Services and description. List each service in plain words customers use, and write a description that says what you do and where.

Photos. Real photos of your team, vehicles, premises and finished work. Add a few each month.

Website link. Point it to the most relevant page, which for a single-location business is usually the home page.

Set a reminder for the first working day of each month to check hours, add photos and post an update. Do the same for a Bing Places listing, which takes ten minutes and feeds Microsoft's search and Copilot.

How do you get more Google reviews?

You get more reviews by asking every satisfied customer, at the moment the job is done, with a direct link that opens the review form. A steady flow matters as much as the total, because customers look at how recent reviews are. Reply to every review, positive or negative, within a few days, in a calm and specific voice.

The best review data available is American, so read it as direction for New Zealand. BrightLocal's 2026 Local Consumer Review Survey of 1,002 US adults found 97% read reviews for local businesses, 31% will only use a business rated 4.5 stars or higher, and 74% look for reviews from the last three months. BrightLocal sells local SEO software, which is worth knowing, but the pattern matches what most owners see on their own profiles.

A review routine that fits a busy week:

Copy the review link from your Google Business Profile and shorten it.

Send it by text message the same day the job finishes, with the customer's name and the job in the message.

Ask everyone. Asking only the customers you expect to be happy breaks Google's review policy, and so does offering discounts or gifts for reviews.

Reply to each review with a detail from the job, which shows future customers a real person runs the business.

Answer negative reviews once, factually, with an offer to sort it out offline.

Never post or buy fake reviews. They breach Google's policies, and misleading customers about your reputation can also breach the Fair Trading Act.

Build one page per service and one per location

Each service you want to be found for needs its own page, and so does each town or area you actively serve. A single "Services" page listing ten things gives Google nothing specific to rank. A page called "Heat pump installation in Hamilton" that explains the job, the price range and the area gives it a clear match.

A good service page answers the questions a customer asks on the phone. Put the answer first: what the service is, where you do it and who it suits. Then cover typical price ranges in NZD, how long it takes, what is included, the brands or standards you work to, and your licences or registrations. Close with a clear way to get in touch.

Location pages need real local content to be useful. Write about the suburbs you cover, jobs you have done there, local conditions that affect the work, and how quickly you can get there. Copying one page and swapping the town name produces thin pages that Google tends to ignore. If you only serve one area, a strong home page and service pages are enough.

Each page needs a unique title tag that starts with the service and place, a one-line meta description that a person would click, one main heading, and links to related pages on your site.

Fix the technical basics

The technical basics are the checks that let Google find, read and show your pages: Search Console set up and verified, a sitemap submitted, important pages indexed, a site that works on a phone, and pages that load quickly over HTTPS. A non-technical owner can complete these in an afternoon using free tools from Google and Microsoft.

Verify your domain in Google Search Console and submit your sitemap. Most website builders create one at /sitemap.xml.

Use the Pages report to see which pages are indexed and why others are not. Fix anything important that is excluded.

Run your main pages through Google's PageSpeed Insights and fix the largest problems, which are usually oversized images.

Open your site on your own phone and try to call you, find your hours and fill in your contact form.

Check every page loads on https and that the old http address redirects.

Import your Search Console site into Bing Webmaster Tools so Bing, and the assistants that use it, can crawl the same pages.

Look at your robots.txt file and make sure it does not block search engines or AI search crawlers you want to reach you.

Add LocalBusiness structured data to your contact or home page if your website builder supports it. It keeps your name, address and hours machine readable. It will not rank you on its own.

How does SEO help you show up in AI search?

SEO is the foundation for AI search. Google states that its AI Overviews and AI Mode need nothing beyond core SEO, and ChatGPT uses partner search engines to find pages. Clear service pages, a complete Business Profile and consistent details are what assistants read. Reviews and mentions on other sites then add weight to the answer.

Google Search Central says there is no special schema, AI text file or markup needed to appear in AI Overviews or AI Mode. Those summaries now show on buying searches as well as questions. Semrush's study of more than 10 million US desktop keywords found commercial, transactional and navigational queries made up 42.8% of AI Overview triggers by October 2025.

That changes how people click. Pew Research Center's March 2025 study of 900 US adults found users clicked a traditional result on 8% of visits when an AI summary appeared, against 15% when it did not. For a local business, that makes it more valuable to be named inside the summary and to have a Business Profile people can act on directly. The guide to answer engine optimisation explains how that works, the guide to getting mentioned by ChatGPT covers the steps, and the AEO checklist lists every item by effort.

What can you do yourself, and when should you hire help?

Most owners can handle the Business Profile, reviews and Search Console themselves, because these are routine tasks with free tools. Service page writing is manageable with a few hours a week. Hire help when the technical fixes go beyond your website builder, when you compete in a crowded Auckland market, or when the weekly hours simply are not there.

TaskDo it yourselfWorth paying for

Google Business Profile and Bing PlacesYes, about two hours to set up, then monthly upkeepOnly if you have many locations

Review requests and repliesYes, a weekly habitSoftware to automate the text message once volume is high

Service and location pagesYes, if you can write a clear explanation of the jobA writer or editor when you need ten or more pages

Search Console, sitemap and indexingYes, for the basicsA developer for redirects, site moves or indexing errors you cannot explain

Site speed and structured dataPartly, through your website builder's settingsA developer on custom-built sites

Competitor research and link buildingDirectory listings and local partners, yesSpecialist help in competitive trades and cities

If you hire, compare a few options on price and scope. Clickthrough's published SEO packages start at NZD 960 plus GST a month for a small business, The SEO Guy lists retainers from NZD 795 plus GST a month with a six-month minimum, and OnlineNZ's programmes start at NZD 499 a month excluding GST. Across those three price pages, published NZ SEO packages run from about NZD 500 to 2,500 a month plus GST. The guide to marketing agency costs in NZ compares those figures with freelancers and in-house hires.

Before you sign anything, ask what will be done each month, who owns the pages and accounts, and how results will be reported. Enquiries and calls are the numbers that matter; ranking reports alone are not enough.

A first-month SEO plan for a small business

A realistic first month takes three to five hours a week. Week one covers accounts and technical checks, week two the Business Profile and review routine, week three your most important service pages, and week four location pages, directories and a baseline. After that, the work becomes about an hour a week.

Week 1: accounts and checks. Verify Google Search Console and Bing Webmaster Tools, submit the sitemap, review the Pages report, run PageSpeed Insights on the home page and your top service page, and test the site on your phone.

Week 2: Business Profile and reviews. Complete every section of the Google Business Profile, set holiday hours, add ten real photos, claim Bing Places, and send review requests to every customer from the past month.

Week 3: service pages. Write or rewrite pages for your two or three most profitable services, answer-first, with price ranges, areas and a clear contact option.

Week 4: locations, listings and a baseline. Add a location page for each area you actively serve, make your name, address and phone number identical across NZ directories, and record a baseline: Search Console clicks, Business Profile calls and enquiries, plus what ChatGPT and Google AI Mode say when asked for your service in your town.

From month two, add one useful page a month, keep the review routine going and compare the numbers against your baseline each month. If you want an outside read on where to start, the free AI-readiness benchmark takes a few minutes and needs no email.

Flow AI is an AI marketing transformation practice: the strategy, the systems and the agents that run a marketing function, engineered end to end. For search, that means the Business Profile routine, review requests, service pages and monthly tracking in this guide, installed on your own site and accounts so they keep running when you are busy.

The free audit names the first system to install. If you would rather do it yourself, every step above works with free tools.

The short version

Google handles about nine in ten New Zealand searches, so SEO for a small business starts there. Complete and maintain your Google Business Profile, ask every customer for a review, and give each service and area its own clear page.

Then fix the technical basics in Search Console and track enquiries monthly. The same work is what AI search reads, so one effort covers both.
