Q: Can I do SEO for my small business myself?
A: Yes. The work that matters most for a local NZ business is free and needs no technical skill: completing your Google Business Profile, asking for reviews, writing one clear page per service and per area, and checking Google Search Console once a month. Budget three to five hours a week for the first month, then about an hour a week to keep it going.
Q: How long does SEO take to work in New Zealand?
A: Changes to your Google Business Profile and fixes to indexing problems can show up within a few weeks. New service and location pages usually take two to four months to settle in the results, longer in competitive trades in Auckland. Track enquiries and Search Console clicks monthly and judge the trend over a quarter, because week-to-week movement is mostly noise.
Q: How much does SEO cost for a small business in NZ?
A: Doing it yourself costs your time and nothing else, since Google Business Profile and Search Console are free. Published NZ agency packages from Clickthrough, The SEO Guy and OnlineNZ run from about NZD 500 to 2,500 a month plus GST. The marketing agency cost guide on this site breaks those prices down alongside freelancer and in-house options.
Q: Do I still need SEO now that people use ChatGPT?
A: Yes. Google still handles about 89% of New Zealand searches according to Statcounter's September 2026 data, and AI assistants lean on search results and search partners to find businesses. Google says its AI features need nothing beyond core SEO. Good SEO is the foundation that AI search builds on, with reviews and mentions on other sites adding weight.
Q: Do I need a .co.nz domain for SEO in New Zealand?
A: A .co.nz domain helps Google and customers see that you serve New Zealand, and it is the usual choice for a local business. A .com can still rank here if the site clearly states its NZ location, uses NZD prices and has a Google Business Profile. If you already have a .com that works, moving domains is rarely worth the disruption.
Q: What is the most important SEO task for a local business?
A: For most local NZ businesses, it is the Google Business Profile: the right primary category, accurate hours including public holidays, service areas, photos and a steady flow of reviews with replies. It controls how you appear in Google Maps and the local results, and it is free. Service pages on your own site come next.

## Outbound sales automation for small business: a practical guide for NZ and Australia.
URL: https://www.flowai.co.nz/blog/outbound-sales-automation.html
Author: Amber Lan, Flow AI
Updated: 2026-10-02

Short answer: Outbound sales automation for a small business means using software and AI to build a target list, research each account, draft short personal emails and send follow-ups on a schedule, while a person approves every first message and handles every reply. In New Zealand and Australia it must also meet spam law on consent, identification and unsubscribing.

What is outbound sales automation?

Outbound sales automation means letting software and AI find businesses that fit your offer, research them, and send short first-contact messages with follow-ups on a schedule. A person reviews what goes out and handles every reply. For a small business, the goal is a few good conversations a month from a short list.

Outbound sales automation is the use of software and AI to find prospective customers, research them, and send and follow up on first-contact messages on a schedule, with a person reviewing what goes out and handling the replies. The glossary entry gives the short definition, and cold email is its most common channel.

Inbound and outbound work as a pair. Inbound is people finding you through search and referrals; the guide to content marketing for NZ small business covers that half. Outbound is you reaching out first. Content gives your outbound emails something worth linking to, and outbound puts your content in front of the people you most want to read it. For the wider plan, the guide to AI marketing transformation for small business shows where outbound sits.

How well does cold email work for a small business?

Cold email works for small businesses that send a small number of relevant, personal messages to a well-chosen list. Published benchmarks range from about 3% replying per campaign to under 1% per email sent, depending on how they count. Small firms and founders are the most responsive group.

The two most quoted benchmarks measure different things, so always say which one you mean. Instantly's Cold Email Benchmark Report 2026, built from its own platform data across 2025, reports an average reply rate of 3.43% per campaign, with the top quarter at 5.5% or more and the top 10% at 10.7% or more. Belkins' 2026 study of 7.5 million cold emails sent for its clients in 2025 measured 0.45%, calculated as replies divided by every email sent. One is an average across campaigns on a software platform; the other counts every email in an agency's programmes. Both are vendor data, and both are mostly from outside New Zealand.

The Belkins data has good news for this audience. Belkins found businesses with 0 to 10 employees replied at 0.72%, the highest of any company size, and founders and owners replied at 0.57%, above C-level executives at 0.42%. If you sell to other small businesses, the people you are writing to are the ones most likely to answer.

How to build a target list

Build a short list of businesses that match your best existing customers, and write down why each one fits. Fifty to a hundred well-chosen accounts is plenty for a small business. Record where you found each contact's address and why your offer is relevant to their role, because New Zealand spam law depends on both.

  Describe your ideal customer. Look at your three best clients and note industry, size, location, the trigger that made them buy, and the job title of the person who signed.

  Find matching businesses. Industry association member lists, event exhibitor lists, local business directories, LinkedIn company search and your own lost quotes are good starting points for NZ and Australian firms.

  Find the right person. Pick one named person per business whose role your offer is relevant to. A generic info@ address is a weaker choice.

  Record the evidence. Note where the address was published and why your offer fits their job. If someone ever asks, this is your record of consent.

  Verify the address. Run addresses through an email verification tool before sending. Bounces damage your sending reputation quickly.

Automation helps with steps two and five. AI can scan a directory, match it against your description and draft a shortlist. You still choose who makes the list.

How to research and personalise each email

Give each email one specific, true reason for writing to that person now, such as a new branch, a job ad, a recent project or a post they wrote. AI can do the research and suggest the reason. Keep the email short, ask a low-pressure question, and check every fact before it goes out.

This is where AI saves the most time. An AI agent can read a company's website, recent news and public posts, then summarise the three facts most relevant to your offer and draft a first line. What it produces is a draft. It will sometimes pick a stale fact or misread a page, so the person sending checks it.

Short emails perform better. Instantly's 2026 benchmark found its elite performers write fewer than 80 words per first-touch email. A good first email for a small business has four parts: the specific reason you are writing, one sentence on what you do for businesses like theirs, an easy question ("worth a short chat, or not the right time?"), and your name, business and contact details.

Keep the ask soft. A small business in New Zealand or Australia often sells into a market where people know each other, so a polite email that is easy to decline protects your reputation as well as your reply rate.

How to set up a follow-up sequence

Set up a sequence of three to five short emails spaced several days apart, each adding something new, such as a useful article or a relevant example. Stop the sequence the moment someone replies. Most replies come from the first email, so put most of your effort there.

Instantly's 2026 benchmark found 58% of replies come from the first email and 42% from follow-ups, with the best sequences running four to seven touchpoints. Follow-ups are worth sending, and the first email does most of the work. A sequence I would start with:

  StepTimingWhat it says

  
    Email 1Day 1The specific reason, one line on what you do, a soft question

    Email 2Day 4A short reply in the same thread with one useful link, such as a guide you wrote

    Email 3Day 9A relevant example of the problem you solve, in two or three sentences

    Email 4Day 16A polite close: happy to leave it here, and how to reach you later

  

Write the sequence templates once, then let AI fill the personal lines for each account. The guide to AI marketing automation for small business covers the tools that run the schedule, and the AI marketing examples for small business include outbound alongside nine other marketing jobs.

What are the deliverability basics?

Deliverability is whether your emails reach the inbox. For a small business it comes down to a separate sending domain, correct authentication records, a gradual warm-up, verified addresses, low daily volumes, plain text emails and a working unsubscribe. Get these right before the first send, because a damaged domain takes weeks to recover.

  Use a separate sending domain. Register a second domain close to your main one and send outbound from it, so problems never touch the address your customers and suppliers email.

  Set up SPF, DKIM and DMARC. These DNS records tell inbox providers that you are allowed to send from the domain. Your email provider's help pages give the exact values.

  Warm up the domain. Start with a handful of emails a day and increase slowly over several weeks. Many sending tools include a warm-up feature.

  Keep volumes low. A small business programme rarely needs more than a few dozen new contacts a day per mailbox.

  Write plain text. Skip images, heavy formatting and multiple links in first emails.

  Watch bounces and complaints. Pause and fix the list if either rises.

What do NZ and Australian spam laws require?

Both countries require consent, clear identification of the sender, and a working unsubscribe that is honoured within five working days. New Zealand's law allows deemed consent for a conspicuously published business address when the message is relevant to the person's role. Australia's regulator guidance centres on express or inferred consent. In both, the sender must prove consent.

New Zealand's Unsolicited Electronic Messages Act 2007 says a person must not send an unsolicited commercial electronic message with a New Zealand link, and puts the onus of proving consent on the sender. The Department of Internal Affairs sums up the rules as three steps: consent, identify the business responsible, and honour unsubscribe requests within five working days. In Australia, ACMA's guidance on the Spam Act 2003 says you must first have consent, it is up to you to prove it, and you cannot send an electronic message to ask for consent.

  RuleNew Zealand (UEM Act 2007)Australia (Spam Act 2003, per ACMA)

  
    ConsentExpress, inferred or deemed. Deemed needs a conspicuously published address, relevance to the person's role, and no "no spam" statement.Express or inferred. ACMA's guidance does not describe published addresses as enough; check the Act or ACMA.

    ProofThe sender carries the onus of proofIt is up to the sender to prove consent

    IdentifyWho authorised the message and how to contact them, accurate for at least 30 daysYour business's legal name, or name and ABN, with contact details correct for 30 days

    UnsubscribeClear, free, same channel, working for at least 30 days, effective 5 working days after useHonoured within 5 working days, with no login or extra personal details required

    Maximum penalty$200,000 for an individual, $500,000 for an organisationInfringement notices and court penalties set by ACMA and the courts

  

The penalty figures come from section 45 of the New Zealand Act. Enforcement is real: ACMA's January to March 2026 enforcement report records Lululemon Athletica Australia paying a A$702,900 penalty for sending over 370,000 marketing emails with no way to unsubscribe. This is a summary for planning; check the Act or the regulator for your own situation.

Where should a human stay in the loop?

A person should approve the target list, read every first email before it is sent, handle every reply, and decide who gets removed. Software can find, research, draft, schedule and track. A small business's name travels further than a large company's, so the review step protects the asset that matters most.

This is the human in the loop principle applied to sales. It is a common gap: Australia's National AI Centre found only about half of current SME AI users check AI outputs before they affect customers, in its December 2025 to February 2026 pulse.

  AutomateKeep human

  
    Finding businesses that match your descriptionDeciding who goes on the list

    Verifying email addressesConfirming the address was published and the offer fits the role

    Researching each account and drafting the first lineReading and approving every first email

    Scheduling follow-ups and stopping on replyWriting every reply to an interested prospect

    Processing unsubscribesHandling complaints and questions about consent

    Logging activity in your CRMDeciding when a conversation becomes a proposal

  

LinkedIn deserves its own note. LinkedIn's User Agreement (section 8.2) prohibits bots or other unauthorised automated methods to add contacts or send messages. Use AI to research and draft, and send LinkedIn notes yourself. For finding where your buyers talk in public, Flow AI's free Reddit opportunity research skill maps relevant threads and the language people use, which also gives your emails better first lines.

What should you measure?

Measure meetings booked and the replies that lead to them first, then the bounce and complaint rates that protect your domain. Track reply rate per email sent, so you can compare with Belkins, or per campaign, to compare with Instantly. Open rates are unreliable because some mail apps load images automatically.

  MetricHow to calculateWhat to do with it

  
    Positive reply rateInterested replies divided by people contactedThe main health check for list and message

    Meetings bookedCount per monthThe number that pays for the programme

    Reply rate per email sentAll replies divided by all emails sentCompare with Belkins' 0.45% method

    Bounce rateBounced emails divided by emails sentIf it climbs, stop and re-verify the list

    Unsubscribes and complaintsCount per sendA rise means the list or message is off target

  

Review monthly. If a segment produces no positive replies after a hundred contacts, change the list before you change the copy. A starting set of outbound workflows is in Flow AI's free agent templates.

Where Flow AI fits

Flow AI is an AI marketing transformation practice: the strategy, the systems and the agents that run a marketing function, engineered end to end. For outbound, that means setting up the list, research, drafting and sequencing system on your own accounts, with the consent record and the human review step built in from the first send.

It starts with a free audit, which names the first system worth installing. If outbound is that system, a starter sprint installs it and the retainer keeps it running. The skills behind it are public in the Flow AI skill library, and the start-here guide to AI marketing for NZ small business shows how outbound connects to the rest.

The short version

Outbound sales automation for a small business is a short list, one true reason to write to each person, a short email with a soft ask and a few follow-ups. AI does the research and drafting, and the software keeps the schedule. You approve the first message, answer the replies and keep the consent record.

In New Zealand and Australia, the spam law rules come first. Get those right, along with the deliverability basics, measure replies with a stated method, and a few hours a week can produce a steady flow of good conversations.

To find out whether outbound is the right first system for your business, request a free audit.

Q: Is cold email legal in New Zealand?
A: Commercial email with a New Zealand link, such as one sent to a New Zealand business, needs consent under the Unsolicited Electronic Messages Act 2007. For business-to-business email, deemed consent can apply when the address is conspicuously published, the message is relevant to the person's role, and there is no statement saying they do not want messages. Every email must identify the sender and include a working unsubscribe. Check the Act for your own case.
Q: Is cold email legal in Australia?
A: The Spam Act 2003 requires consent before sending a commercial electronic message with an Australian link, and ACMA says the sender must be able to prove it. You cannot send a message asking for consent. Each message must identify your business and include an unsubscribe honoured within five working days. ACMA's guidance is strict, so read it before relying on a published address.
Q: What is a good cold email reply rate?
A: It depends on how it is measured. Instantly's 2026 benchmark reports a 3.43% average reply rate per campaign across its platform, with the top quarter at 5.5% or more. Belkins measured 0.45% per email sent across 7.5 million emails in 2025. Compare your numbers with the benchmark that uses the same method, and watch your own trend month to month.
Q: How many follow-up emails should I send?
A: Instantly's 2026 benchmark puts the best-performing sequences at four to seven touchpoints, with 58% of replies coming from the first email and 42% from follow-ups. For a small business, three to five emails spaced several days apart is a sensible range. Stop the sequence when someone replies, and remove anyone who asks you to stop straight away.
Q: Should I automate LinkedIn outreach?
A: Be careful. LinkedIn's User Agreement prohibits bots and unauthorised automated methods to add contacts or send messages, so tools that send connection requests for you put your account at risk. Use automation to research and draft, then send LinkedIn messages by hand. For a small business with a short list, writing and sending ten personal notes a week by hand is manageable.
Q: How much time does outbound take each week?
A: With a system in place, two to three hours a week covers a small programme: about an hour to add and research new accounts, an hour to review drafts, and the rest for replies. The first month takes longer while you define your ideal customer, set up the sending domain and write the templates. Replies to interested prospects always deserve your own time.

## How much does a marketing agency cost in NZ?
URL: https://www.flowai.co.nz/blog/marketing-agency-cost-nz.html
Author: Amber Lan, Flow AI
Updated: 2026-10-02

Short answer: Most New Zealand marketing agencies charge NZD 95 to 200 an hour. Monthly retainers run about NZD 500 to 1,500 for one channel, NZD 1,500 to 4,000 for several, and NZD 4,000 to 10,000 or more for full service, plus GST and ad spend. From NZD 1,000 a month, an agency has room to do one channel properly.

What does a marketing agency cost in New Zealand in 2026?

A New Zealand marketing agency in 2026 bills NZD 95 to 200 an hour, or a monthly retainer that grows with the number of channels it runs. One channel costs about NZD 500 to 1,500 a month, several channels NZD 1,500 to 4,000, and a full-service retainer NZD 4,000 to 10,000 or more, before GST and ad spend.

Those bands come from Jelly Digital's September 2026 NZ pricing guide, which puts agency hourly rates at NZD 95 to 200 and multi-channel retainers at NZD 1,500 to 4,000 a month. A second Auckland agency lands in a similar place: King Tide Marketing's July 2026 guide prices one channel done properly at NZD 1,000 to 2,000 a month and genuine multi-channel work from NZD 5,000. Both are agencies estimating their own market, so read them as a range and check them against the published price pages further down.

Very little of this is public. Digital Nomads HQ audited 411 service lines across 140 Australian agencies in June 2026 and found 78% published no pricing at all. Expect to ask for a quote, and expect it to arrive in a format that is hard to set beside the next one. That is why the last half of this guide is about comparing quotes. The wider guide to AI marketing costs in Australia and New Zealand puts agencies next to tools, freelancers and hires.

What does a marketing retainer buy?

A marketing retainer is a fixed monthly fee paid to an agency or freelancer for an agreed scope of ongoing work, such as SEO, social media or paid ads management. The fee buys a block of people's time. Divide it by the agency's hourly rate and you get the hours you can expect each month.

The arithmetic is worth doing before any meeting. At NZD 95 to 200 an hour, a NZD 1,500 retainer buys between about 7.5 and 16 hours a month. A NZD 4,000 retainer buys about 20 to 42 hours. Account management, meetings and reporting come out of those hours before anyone writes a post or adjusts a campaign.

A small retainer spread over many channels gets thin quickly. Ten hours a month split across three channels is about three hours each, enough to keep something running and rarely enough to build it. That is the logic behind King Tide's advice to put a modest budget into one channel and do it properly. The glossary has a short entry for marketing retainer if you need the term for a board paper or a quote comparison.

Marketing agency prices by service

Priced by service, New Zealand agencies charge about NZD 500 to 3,000 a month for SEO, NZD 500 to 2,000 for social media, and NZD 300 to 1,500 to manage Google Ads, or 10 to 20% of the ad spend. One-off work such as a website or a brand identity is quoted as a project, from about NZD 1,500.

ServiceTypical NZ price (excl. GST)Source

SEO, monthlyNZD 750 to 3,000 a monthJelly Digital, Sep 2026

SEO, published packagesNZD 499 to about 2,460+ a monthOnlineNZ, The SEO Guy, Clickthrough, as of October 2026

Social media managementNZD 500 to 2,000 a month (entry packages from NZD 149)Jelly Digital; OnlineNZ

Google Ads managementNZD 300 to 1,500 flat, or 10 to 20% of spend, plus the spendJelly Digital

Brand identityNZD 2,000 to 10,000+ one-offJelly Digital

Published price pages give the clearest picture, because the number is on the page. As of October 2026, Clickthrough lists SEO packages at NZD 960, NZD 1,460 and from NZD 2,460 a month plus GST, The SEO Guy lists retainers at NZD 795 a month on a six-month minimum and NZD 1,495 a month, and OnlineNZ lists SEO programmes from NZD 499 to 1,999 a month and social management from NZD 149 a month, on one month's notice.

The spread inside one service is wide because the work differs. Clickthrough's entry package covers 5 to 10 pages; a package four times the price should cover far more of the site, plus new content and technical fixes. Ask for the page count and the monthly deliverables in writing, then compare like with like.

What you get at each price tier

Each price tier buys a different shape of work. Under NZD 1,500 a month you get one channel kept running. NZD 1,500 to 4,000 buys one main channel built properly with support on a second. Above NZD 4,000, an agency can coordinate several channels and tie its reporting to enquiries and sales.

Monthly retainer (NZD, excl. GST)What it usually coversWhat it usually leaves outGood fit

Under 1,500One channel maintained: a small SEO package, a set number of social posts, or ads management on a modest budgetStrategy, new content at volume, any second channelA business with one obvious channel and someone in-house to supply material

1,500 to 4,000One primary channel built properly, plus support on a secondCoordinated multi-channel campaigns, brand workMost 5 to 20 person businesses with a working website

4,000 to 10,000+Several channels run together, regular content, campaign planning, monthly reportingAd spend and large creative projects, which are usually billed separatelyBusinesses with a sales team waiting on leads and the budget to feed it

The middle band is where King Tide's own guide puts "primary channel plus support" at NZD 2,000 to 4,000 a month. Before you sign at any tier, ask what the first 90 days produce. A sensible answer names deliverables, such as pages built and tracking installed, and one number that should move. Agencies rarely promise outcomes, and that is reasonable. What you can hold them to is the work and the reporting.

Which costs sit outside the agency retainer?

The retainer is rarely the whole bill. Ad spend is paid on top, often with a minimum. Setup or onboarding fees are common, quotes usually exclude GST, and software the agency uses may be passed on to you. Your own time counts too: someone in the business has to brief, approve and supply material every month.

The Australian audit puts numbers on this. Digital Nomads HQ found ads setup fees of AUD 499 to 1,999, onboarding fees from AUD 550, and 22% of agencies disclosing a minimum ad spend of AUD 500 to 15,000 or more a month. The same audit found 78% of listed prices exclude GST. In New Zealand, a business that is not GST registered should add 15% to any plus-GST price, because it cannot claim the GST back.

Ad spend, the money paid to Google or Meta. A fee of 10 to 20% of spend rises as spend rises, so ask for a cap.

Setup fees for account builds, tracking and audits. Ask whether they are one-off and what you own at the end.

Minimum terms. A six-month minimum appears on at least one published NZ price page, while others ask a month's notice.

Tools such as SEO software, schedulers and reporting dashboards. Some agencies include them and some pass them on.

Your hours for briefing, approving and finding photos. Put an hourly value on them and include it in the comparison.

How much should a small business spend on marketing?

New Zealand's government guidance leaves the number to you. The business.govt.nz guide lists four ways to set a budget: spend what your objectives need, take a share of sales, match competitors, or spend what feels affordable. For hiring outside help, an Auckland agency puts the sensible floor at NZD 1,000 to 1,500 a month.

The business.govt.nz marketing strategy page, last edited in August 2026, lists those four methods and recommends no percentage. You will see "5 to 10% of revenue" quoted as a rule on agency blogs. This guide could not find it at any primary source for New Zealand small business, so it is left out.

The floor comes from an agency being candid about its own market: King Tide Marketing advises that if you cannot put at least NZD 1,000 to 1,500 a month into marketing, you should not hire anyone. Below that, your own time with good tools, or a freelancer for one defined project, usually goes further. For context on what small firms spend, LocaliQ's December 2025 survey of more than 730 small businesses, mostly in the US and Canada, found 33% had monthly marketing budgets under USD 1,000. That is North American data, so treat it as a rough guide.

The objectives method suits most owners. Decide how many extra enquiries a month you want, estimate what each one is worth, and work back to a budget. That leads straight into the comparison below.

How to compare agency quotes on cost per enquiry

Cost per enquiry is total marketing spend in a period divided by the number of genuine enquiries it produced. It turns quotes with different scopes into one comparable number. Add the fee, ad spend, tools and a value for your own time, then divide by the enquiries you expect or have measured.

Total the monthly cost of each option: fee, ad spend, any setup fee spread over 12 months, tools, and your own hours at an hourly value you choose.

Agree what counts as an enquiry: a call, form or booking from a real prospect. Leave out spam and job seekers.

Ask each provider for a realistic enquiry estimate, or use your own past numbers for that channel.

Divide cost by enquiries, then compare the result with what an enquiry is worth to you: average job value multiplied by the share of enquiries you win.

After three months, recalculate with real numbers and keep whichever option wins.

Example option (invented numbers)Monthly costEnquiriesCost per enquiry

Agency A: NZD 2,500 retainer, NZD 1,500 ad spend, 3 hours of your time at NZD 100NZD 4,30020NZD 215

Agency B: NZD 1,200 retainer, NZD 1,500 ad spend, 8 hours of your time at NZD 100NZD 3,50012NZD 292

The numbers are made up to show the method. Here the cheaper retainer loses, because it needs more of the owner's time and produces fewer enquiries. Whether NZD 215 is good depends on your margins. If an average job is worth NZD 3,000 and you win one enquiry in four, each enquiry is worth about NZD 750, and both options pay for themselves. The glossary entry on cost per enquiry gives the definition in one line.

What to ask a marketing agency before you sign

Ask who will do the work, how many hours or deliverables the fee covers each month, what the minimum term and notice period are, and who owns the accounts and content if you leave. Those four answers tell you most of what a proposal leaves vague. Then ask how they report, and on which number.

Who works on my account each week, and how senior are they?

What exactly ships each month, in pages, posts, campaigns or hours?

Are the ad accounts, analytics and website set up in my business's name?

What are the setup fees, the minimum term and the notice period?

Is GST included, and are tools or ad spend marked up?

Which number will your monthly report lead with?

Can I speak to a current client of a similar size in New Zealand?

Red flags worth walking away from include a guaranteed ranking or a guaranteed number of leads, ad accounts held in the agency's name, reports full of impressions with no line for enquiries, a long lock-in with no exit for missed deliverables, and nobody able to tell you who does the work.

Survey data backs up asking hard questions early. Setup's 2025 Marketing Relationship Survey, a small sample of about 100 mostly US responses, found 61% of clients who ended an agency relationship cited dissatisfaction with value, up from 36% in 2024, and 44% said the agency did not understand their business. The same survey found clients who chose an agency through word of mouth were more often satisfied (82%) than those who found one through search (70%). Ask peers in your industry who they use.

A New Zealand marketing agency costs NZD 95 to 200 an hour, or a retainer of about NZD 500 to 1,500 a month for one channel, NZD 1,500 to 4,000 for several and NZD 4,000 to 10,000 or more for full service. Add GST, ad spend, setup fees and your own time to reach the real number.

Q: Is a cheap marketing agency worth it?
A: A cheap agency can be worth it when the scope is narrow and written down, for example a small SEO package covering a set number of pages, or ads management on a modest budget. It goes wrong when a low fee is spread across several channels, because the hours per channel become too small to build anything. Divide the fee by the hourly rate and check the hours make sense for the work promised.
Q: How long are marketing agency contracts in New Zealand?
A: Terms vary from month to month to six months or longer. Published NZ price pages show both ends: The SEO Guy's entry SEO retainer has a six-month minimum, while OnlineNZ asks for one month's notice. SEO usually carries longer minimums because results take months to show. Ask for the notice period in writing and an exit clause if agreed deliverables are missed.
Q: Do NZ marketing agency prices include GST?
A: Most do not. Agency quotes and published price pages in New Zealand are usually written as plus GST, which adds 15%. A GST-registered business can claim that back, so the plus-GST figure is its real cost. A business that is not registered pays the full amount, so add 15% before comparing a quote with a salary or a freelancer's rate.
Q: How much does an SEO agency cost in NZ?
A: Published New Zealand SEO packages ran from about NZD 499 to 2,460 or more a month plus GST as of October 2026, across OnlineNZ, The SEO Guy and Clickthrough. Jelly Digital's 2026 guide puts the typical range at NZD 750 to 3,000 a month. The difference between the ends is mostly the number of pages covered and whether new content and technical work are included.
Q: Should I pay an agency a percentage of my ad spend?
A: A percentage fee, often 10 to 20% of spend in New Zealand, is common for Google Ads management and fair at small budgets. The catch is that the fee rises every time spend rises, even when the work does not. Ask for a flat fee or a cap once your spend passes a level you agree, and make sure the ad account sits in your business's name.
Q: What is a good cost per enquiry for a small business?
A: A good cost per enquiry is one well below what an enquiry is worth to you. Work that out as your average job value multiplied by the share of enquiries you win. If an average job is worth NZD 3,000 and you win one in four, each enquiry is worth about NZD 750, so any marketing that brings enquiries in under that is paying for itself.

## Marketing agency alternatives for NZ small business.
URL: https://www.flowai.co.nz/blog/marketing-agency-alternatives-nz.html
Author: Amber Lan, Flow AI
Updated: 2026-10-02

Short answer: The main alternatives to a marketing agency in New Zealand are doing it yourself with AI tools, a freelancer at NZD 50 to 150 an hour, a fractional marketing manager from about NZD 1,200 a month, a specialist package, an AI-led service, or an in-house hire on NZD 55,000 to 150,000 a year.

What counts as a marketing agency alternative?

A marketing agency alternative is any way of getting your marketing done without a full-service agency retainer. In New Zealand the realistic options are your own time with AI tools, a freelancer, a fractional marketing manager or CMO, a specialist package, an AI-led service, or a hire. Each one buys a different mix of judgment and hours.

The reason owners look is usually cost. Jelly Digital's September 2026 NZ guide puts full-service retainers at NZD 4,000 to 10,000 or more a month, before GST and ad spend. For a business of 5 to 50 staff that is often more than the marketing needs, and the guide to what a marketing agency costs in NZ breaks that number down.

Most small businesses already use some outside help. LocaliQ's December 2025 survey of more than 730 small businesses, mostly in the US and Canada, found 60% work with at least one marketing partner. The question is which kind of partner, and how much of the work stays with you.

The alternatives side by side

The options range from DIY at the cost of your own hours to an in-house hire at NZD 55,000 to 150,000 a year. In between, freelancers, fractional managers, specialist packages and AI-led services each cost roughly NZD 500 to 6,000 a month in New Zealand, depending on scope and seniority.

OptionTypical NZ cost (excl. GST)What you getSuitsWatch for

DIY with AI toolsTool subscriptions plus your hoursWhatever you have time to doBudgets under NZD 1,000 a monthWork stops when you get busy

FreelancerNZD 50 to 150 an hour, or NZD 500 to 3,000 a monthOne or two skills done wellA clear, single jobBreadth, holidays, one point of failure

Fractional marketing managerFrom about NZD 1,200 a month; NZD 70 to 105 an hour at contract ratesA part-time owner for marketing who plans and doesSeveral channels, no full-time budgetDays per month cap the output

Fractional CMONZD 4,000 to 6,000 a month strategy only; NZD 6,000 to 10,000+ hands-onSenior direction for a teamBusinesses with doers who lack directionStrategy with nobody to execute it

Specialist packageSEO NZD 499 to about 2,460+ a month; social from NZD 149A fixed scope on one channelOne channel that clearly mattersScope limits, minimum terms

AI-led servicePublished examples: NZD 500 to 1,000 a month plus setupSystems and agents with human reviewSomeone in-house can review weeklyWhich parts a person checks

In-house hireNZD 55,000 to 150,000 salary, plus on-costsA full-time person in the businessMarketing every week across channelsRecruitment time, one person's skill set

The full-service agency is the benchmark the others are measured against, at NZD 4,000 to 10,000 or more a month. The sections below give the source for each range and what to ask before you commit.

Doing it yourself with AI tools

Doing your own marketing with AI tools costs the least in cash and the most in your time. It works when the owner or a staff member has a fixed few hours each week and one channel to focus on, such as a Google Business Profile or a monthly email. It tends to stall in the busy season.

The time is real. LocaliQ's same survey found 53% of small business respondents spend 1 to 10 hours a week on marketing. AI tools shorten the writing and design steps inside those hours, and they do less for the planning and the follow-through, which is where DIY marketing usually stops.

A few habits make DIY hold up. Pick one channel and one measure, block the same slot every week, and keep a written list of what you post and what came back. The free agent templates give you starting structures for common jobs, and the cost guide for AI marketing in Australia and New Zealand prices the tool stack. When a month passes with nothing shipped because you were serving customers, it is time to buy help.

Hiring a freelance marketer

A freelancer suits a business with one clear marketing job, such as a website rewrite, a Google Ads account or a content calendar. New Zealand freelancers charge about NZD 50 to 150 an hour or NZD 500 to 3,000 a month on retainer, which is usually below agency rates for the same hour.

Two Auckland agencies give overlapping ranges. King Tide Marketing's July 2026 guide puts NZ freelancers at NZD 60 to 150 an hour or NZD 500 to 3,000 a month, and consultants at NZD 150 to 250 an hour, while Jelly Digital puts freelancers at NZD 50 to 120 an hour. Experience and specialism explain most of the spread.

The limit is breadth. One person is rarely strong at SEO, paid ads, copy and design all at once, and a business that needs four skills can end up managing four freelancers. Ask for samples in your industry, a written scope with a fixed price or an hours cap, and what happens to the work when they go on holiday. The agency vs freelancer vs in-house comparison sets the freelancer against the other two models in detail.

A fractional marketing manager or fractional CMO

A fractional marketing manager is a marketer who runs your marketing for a set number of days or hours each month, planning and doing the work. A fractional CMO is more senior and mostly sets direction. Published NZ prices start near NZD 1,200 a month for the first and NZD 4,000 a month for the second.

As of October 2026, Flex Marketing in Auckland lists outsourced marketing and fractional senior marketing manager packages from NZD 1,200 plus GST a month. For an hourly benchmark, Robert Walters' 2026 salary guide puts Auckland contract rates for a marketing manager at NZD 70 to 105 an hour and a CMO at NZD 160 to 240. Those are placed contractors, so independent fractional rates can sit either side.

At the senior end, Kyttn prices a NZ fractional CMO at NZD 4,000 to 6,000 a month for strategy only and NZD 6,000 to 10,000 or more with execution, with a NZD 489 plus GST diagnostic, the same bands King Tide publishes. A fractional CMO pays off when you already have people to do the work. If nobody will execute the plan, a hands-on manager is the better buy. The fractional marketing manager guide goes deeper, and the glossary defines a fractional marketing manager in one line.

Specialist and productised packages

A specialist package buys one channel at a fixed monthly price, usually SEO, social media or Google Ads. Published New Zealand SEO packages ran from about NZD 499 to 2,460 or more a month plus GST as of October 2026. They suit a business that knows which channel brings its customers and wants that one done consistently.

These are the easiest option to compare because the price is on the page. OnlineNZ lists SEO programmes at NZD 499 to 1,999 a month and social management at NZD 149 to 349 a month, on one month's notice. Clickthrough lists SEO from NZD 960 a month for a small business site of 5 to 10 pages, and The SEO Guy lists an NZD 795 a month retainer with a six-month minimum.

The fixed scope is the strength and the limit. A package does what it lists, and anything outside it, such as a new landing page or a campaign for a slow month, is extra. Read the inclusions line by line, check the minimum term, and confirm the reporting shows enquiries as well as rankings.

An in-house marketing hire

An in-house hire gives you a person inside the business every week, which suits a company with steady work across several channels and someone to manage them. In New Zealand, salaries run from about NZD 55,000 for a coordinator to NZD 150,000 for an Auckland marketing manager, plus KiwiSaver, ACC levies and overheads.

The salary data spans employer adverts and recruiter placements. SEEK's October 2026 data shows an advertised average of NZD 106,322 for a marketing manager in the marketing and communications industry, across 386 openings, and NZD 61,498 for a marketing coordinator across 371 openings. Robert Walters puts Auckland marketing managers at NZD 120,000 to 150,000, and King Tide puts coordinators at NZD 55,000 to 70,000.

On top of salary, Inland Revenue lifted the default employer KiwiSaver contribution from 3% to 3.5% on 1 April 2026, rising to 4% on 1 April 2028. King Tide adds about 20% for tools, training and recruitment. A first hire is often a coordinator, which brings energy and hours but rarely strategy, so plan who will set direction.

AI-led marketing services

An AI-led marketing service installs software systems and AI agents that do the production work of marketing, with a person reviewing what goes out. Published New Zealand examples cost about NZD 500 to 1,000 a month plus a setup fee. They suit a business where someone can spend an hour or so a week approving work.

The category is new, and scopes vary widely. As of October 2026, Growin, a NZ AI marketing agency, lists a Launch package at NZD 1,500 setup plus NZD 500 a month and a Foundation package at NZD 4,000 one-off, plus GST, scoped around ads and lead intake. Flow AI publishes a NZD 997 starter sprint and a NZD 1,000 a month retainer, described further down.

Before you buy any of them, ask four things. Which work does software do and which does a person check? Who approves anything published under your business name? Do you own the accounts, content and data? How do you leave, and what do you keep? A service that shows its working before you pay is easier to judge than one that only describes outcomes. The definition of an AI marketing agent explains what the software side should do.

How to choose the right alternative

Choose by answering four questions: how many hours a week you or a staff member can give marketing, how many channels genuinely bring customers, whether anyone in-house can review work, and what monthly budget you can hold for six months. The answers usually point to one or two options from the table above.

Under NZD 1,000 a month and a few hours a week of your own: DIY with tools, plus a freelancer for one defined project.

One channel that clearly matters: a specialist package or a freelancer on that channel.

Several channels and nobody to own them: a fractional marketing manager or an AI-led service with a named reviewer.

A team that does the work but lacks direction: a fractional CMO.

Steady weekly work across channels and a budget for a salary: an in-house hire, often with a specialist package alongside.

Several channels at once, a sales team waiting on leads and NZD 4,000 or more a month: a full-service agency remains the right call.

Then compare your shortlist on cost per enquiry: the total monthly cost, including ad spend and a value for your own hours, divided by the genuine enquiries it produces. After three months, recalculate with real numbers and keep the option that wins.

The short version

The alternatives to a full-service agency in New Zealand are DIY with AI tools, a freelancer at NZD 50 to 150 an hour, a fractional manager from about NZD 1,200 a month, a fractional CMO from NZD 4,000, a specialist package from about NZD 500, an AI-led service, or a hire on NZD 55,000 to 150,000 a year.

Match the option to your hours, your channels and whether someone can review the work, then compare the shortlist on cost per enquiry. An agency is still the right buy for coordinated multi-channel growth with the budget behind it.

Q: What is the cheapest alternative to a marketing agency?
A: Doing it yourself with AI tools is the cheapest in cash, because you pay only for subscriptions. It is rarely the cheapest in total, since your hours have a cost and marketing tends to stop in your busiest months. For a business that cannot spend NZD 1,000 a month on outside help, it is still the right place to start, ideally with one channel and a fixed weekly slot.
Q: Is a freelancer cheaper than a marketing agency in NZ?
A: Usually, per hour. New Zealand freelancers charge about NZD 50 to 150 an hour against NZD 95 to 200 for agencies, according to Jelly Digital and King Tide Marketing. A freelancer covers one or two skills well, though, so a business needing several channels may end up hiring two or three freelancers and managing them itself, which narrows the gap.
Q: What does a fractional marketing manager cost in NZ?
A: Published NZ prices start from about NZD 1,200 plus GST a month for a part-time senior marketing manager, as of October 2026. Placed contractors in Auckland earn NZD 70 to 105 an hour at marketing manager level, per Robert Walters' 2026 guide. A fractional CMO, which is more senior and more strategic, runs NZD 4,000 to 10,000 or more a month.
Q: When is a full-service agency still the right choice?
A: An agency is the right choice when you need several channels running together every week, a sales team is waiting on leads, and the budget is there to fund NZD 4,000 or more a month plus ad spend. It is also a good fit when you need specialist work such as large media buying or a rebrand that no single freelancer or part-time marketer could cover.
Q: Are AI-led marketing services reliable?
A: They are a newer category, so judge each one on what it shows you. Ask which work is done by software and which by a person, who approves anything published under your name, whether you own the accounts and content, and how you leave. A service that can show its working before you pay is easier to assess than one that only describes outcomes.
Q: Can I switch from an agency to an alternative mid-contract?
A: Check your notice period first. Published NZ terms range from one month's notice to six-month minimums. Before you switch, make sure the ad accounts, analytics, website logins and content files are in your business's name, so the next provider starts from your history. Running the new option on one channel for a month before the agency's notice ends reduces the gap.

## How to get your business mentioned by ChatGPT.
URL: https://www.flowai.co.nz/blog/how-to-get-mentioned-by-chatgpt.html
Author: Amber Lan, Flow AI
Updated: 2026-10-02

Short answer: There is no form to submit your business to ChatGPT. ChatGPT, Perplexity, Google AI Mode and Copilot build answers from the open web and their search partners, so you get mentioned by being easy to find and confirm: crawlable pages that answer buyer questions, consistent business details, recent reviews, and mentions on sites the assistants already trust.

Can you submit your business to ChatGPT?

You cannot submit a business to ChatGPT, because no submission form, directory or paid listing exists. ChatGPT, Perplexity, Google AI Mode and Copilot assemble each answer from pages they can find on the open web and from their search partners. Your job is to make your business easy for those systems to find and confirm.

This matters more each quarter. OpenAI said at DevDay in September 2026 that its products reach a collective 1.2 billion weekly users, a figure that covers all of its products together. Closer to home, InternetNZ's Internet Insights research, surveying 1,003 New Zealand adults in late 2025, found 53% had used a text-based AI chatbot in the past year and 55% had used AI inside a search engine.

The useful question is what those assistants read when someone asks for a business like yours. The guide to answer engine optimisation covers the theory. This page is the practical version, in the order I would do it for a small business.

Where does ChatGPT get its information about businesses?

When ChatGPT searches the web, it rewrites the question into targeted queries, sends them to partner search providers including Microsoft Bing, and reads the pages that come back. It then writes an answer and cites some of those pages. Your website, your Google and Bing listings, directories, reviews and press mentions are all raw material for that answer.

OpenAI's help page on ChatGPT search says it sends rewritten queries to search partners, names Microsoft among them, and may pass a general location based on your IP address. That last detail means a "near me" prompt from Hamilton gets treated as a Hamilton search.

Ranking on Google helps, but it does not decide who gets named. Ahrefs' own analysis of 15,000 prompts in 2025 found only 12% of URLs cited by ChatGPT, Gemini and Copilot ranked in Google's top 10 for the same prompt, and 8% for ChatGPT alone, compared with 28.6% for Perplexity. Ahrefs sells SEO tools, so treat it as one vendor's measurement, but the direction is consistent across its studies: the assistants read widely, and what other sites say about you counts.

The strongest signal Ahrefs has found is being talked about. In its 2025 study of 75,000 brands, branded web mentions correlated with AI Overview visibility at 0.664, against 0.218 for backlinks, and 26% of brands had no AI Overview mentions at all. Correlation does not prove cause. It does tell you where to spend your hours.

Step 1: Check what ChatGPT, Perplexity, Google AI Mode and Copilot say about you

Start by asking the assistants the questions your customers ask, and write down what comes back. Fifteen minutes with eight prompts across four assistants gives you a baseline: whether you are named, whether the details are right, which competitors appear, and which websites the assistants cite. Every later step is measured against this list.

Write prompts the way a customer would type them, including the town or suburb. For a plumbing firm in Christchurch, that might look like this:

"Who is a good plumber in Christchurch for a blocked drain?"

"Recommend a plumber in Riccarton who does hot water cylinders."

"What do people say about [your business name]?"

"[Your business name] vs [main competitor]: which is better for a bathroom renovation?"

"Is [your business name] open on Saturdays, and where are they based?"

Then run each prompt in every assistant. They behave differently, so test all four.

AssistantHow to test fairlyWhat to record

ChatGPTUse a temporary chat so memory of past conversations does not colour the answer, and make sure web search is onNamed or not, accuracy of details, the cited links

PerplexityWorks without logging in and lists its sources above the answerWhich sites it cites, since these are the pages it trusts for your category

Google AI ModeUse the AI Mode tab on a Google search, and note any AI Overview on the normal results pageWhether your Google Business Profile or site is cited, and which competitors appear

Microsoft CopilotAsk at copilot.microsoft.com; answers lean on BingWhether your Bing listing details are current

Keep the results in a spreadsheet with the date. The column that teaches you the most is the list of cited sites. If every answer about electricians in your city cites the same two directories and one local news story, those are the pages you need to be on.

Step 2: Make sure the assistants can reach your website

An assistant can only cite pages its crawler is allowed to read. Check your robots.txt file for rules that block AI search crawlers, confirm your site appears in Bing as well as Google, and make sure your main pages load as plain text without needing a login or heavy script. These checks take under an hour.

OpenAI runs separate crawlers for separate jobs. OpenAI's crawler documentation says sites that opt out of OAI-SearchBot will not be shown in ChatGPT search answers, while GPTBot relates to model training and is controlled separately. Some website builders and security plugins block AI bots by default, so open yourdomain.co.nz/robots.txt and look for OAI-SearchBot, or a blanket rule that blocks every bot.

Bing matters more than its market share suggests. Statcounter's September 2026 data gives Bing 7.71% of New Zealand search, against 89.02% for Google, yet Bing feeds Copilot and is a named search partner for ChatGPT. Register the site in Bing Webmaster Tools, submit your sitemap, and claim a Bing Places listing. Most small businesses have never done either.

Step 3: Write pages an assistant can quote

Assistants quote pages that state facts plainly, near the top, in sentences that make sense on their own. Give each service its own page that says what you do, where, for whom, and roughly what it costs. Answer the questions customers ask on the phone in short sections, and add sources and specifics wherever you can.

The research backs specifics over polish. The GEO study by Aggarwal and colleagues, published at KDD 2024 and tested on 10,000 queries, found that methods such as adding statistics, quotations and cited sources lifted a source's visibility in generative engine answers by up to 40%. It is a lab benchmark, so read it as direction, but keyword stuffing did nothing in the same tests.

For a small business, the practical rewrite looks like this:

Open each service page with a two-sentence answer: the service, the area you cover, and who it suits.

State the facts an assistant will be asked for: suburbs served, hours, licences or registrations, price ranges, typical turnaround.

Add a short questions section using the exact questions from your inbox and phone calls.

Name real things: the brands you install, the council you deal with, the certification body you are registered with.

Add LocalBusiness structured data so your name, address and hours are machine readable. Google says no special markup is needed for its AI features beyond core SEO, so treat schema as housekeeping that keeps your details tidy.

The AEO checklist has the full list, ranked by effort.

Step 4: Earn mentions on sites the assistants already cite

Assistants name businesses that other websites talk about. Use the cited sources from Step 1 as your target list: the directories, local news sites, industry associations, comparison articles and video channels that keep appearing. Getting your business accurately listed or mentioned on those pages is the highest-return work in this guide for most local firms.

Video is worth a look. Ahrefs' later study of 75,000 brands found YouTube mentions had the strongest correlation with brand visibility across ChatGPT, AI Mode and AI Overviews, at about 0.737, and its March 2026 analysis found YouTube was the most-cited domain in AI Overviews, at 5.6% of all citations. A plumber filming two-minute answers to common questions on a phone is building exactly that kind of footprint.

Places to look for an NZ business, depending on your trade:

Your industry or trade association's member directory, with a full profile.

Local directories such as NZ Business Directory, Yellow and Neighbourly, plus any marketplace like Builderscrack that shows up in your test answers.

Local news and community sites, through sponsorships, events or a useful comment on a local story.

Supplier and partner pages that list approved installers or stockists.

"Best of" roundups for your city that the assistants already cite. Ask to be considered, with facts the writer can check.

Accuracy beats volume here. One current listing on a site the assistants read is worth more than twenty on directories nobody visits.

Step 5: Keep your business details identical everywhere

Assistants cross-check facts across sources, and conflicting details make them hesitant to name you. Use one exact version of your business name, address, phone number and hours on your website, Google Business Profile, Bing Places, Facebook and every directory. Update all of them the same week whenever something changes, such as a move or new hours.

This is called NAP consistency, and it is how an assistant decides that the "Smith Electrical" in a directory and the "Smith Electrical Ltd" on your site are the same entity. Search your own business name in each assistant and fix any outdated details at the source page. Old addresses and closed branches are the errors to look for first.

Keep a simple master record (a single document with the exact details) and copy from it every time. If you trade under a name that differs from the company register, say so on your About page in one plain sentence.

Step 6: Build a steady flow of recent reviews

People who get a business recommendation from an AI assistant tend to check it against reviews, and the assistants read those reviews too. A steady flow of recent, specific reviews on Google and the platforms your industry uses gives both the assistant and the customer something to confirm. Ask every happy customer, every week.

The local data here is American, so treat it as direction for New Zealand. BrightLocal's 2026 Local Consumer Review Survey of 1,002 US adults found 45% had used ChatGPT or other AI tools for local business recommendations, up from 6% a year earlier, and 74% look for reviews written in the last three months. Its follow-up on 455 of those AI users found 88% check the sources the AI cites, with ChatGPT used by 31% and Google AI Mode by 23% for local recommendations.

So the recommendation is only half the job. When the customer clicks through, they need to land on a profile with recent reviews that mention the job they want done. Ask for reviews by text message straight after the work is finished, include the direct link, and reply to every review, good or bad, within a few days.

How long does it take, and how do you track progress?

Technical fixes such as unblocking a crawler or claiming a Bing listing can show up within weeks. Anything that depends on other sites mentioning you takes months. Track it by re-running your Step 1 prompts on the first working day of each month and logging whether you are named, what is said and which sources are cited.

Four things to watch in that monthly log:

Mention rate: of your prompts, how many name you in each assistant.

Accuracy: whether the hours, location and services quoted are right.

Cited sources: whether your own pages and new listings start appearing as citations.

Referral visits: in Google Analytics, check traffic from chatgpt.com, perplexity.ai and copilot.microsoft.com.

Answers vary between runs, so look for a trend across two or three months before deciding anything works. If you want to see how this differs from classic search work, the comparison of AEO, SEO and GEO lays out what each one measures, and the guide to SEO for small business in NZ covers the Google side.

Where Flow AI fits

Flow AI is an AI marketing transformation practice: the strategy, the systems and the agents that run a marketing function, engineered end to end. For AI search, that means the test prompts, listing fixes, page rewrites and monthly tracking above, installed as a system on your own site and accounts. The AI search sprint describes exactly what gets installed.

It starts with a free audit that names the first system to install, which for many local businesses is this one. You can also do every step here yourself: nothing in this guide needs a paid tool.

The short version

ChatGPT has no sign-up form. It and the other assistants search the web and name the businesses they can confirm. Check what they say about you today, let their crawlers in, write pages that state plain facts, and get listed accurately on the sites they already cite.

Then keep your details identical everywhere, collect recent reviews every week, and re-run your prompts monthly. Most of this is an afternoon of setup and a small weekly habit.

To find out which of these steps your business needs first, request a free audit.

Q: Can I pay to get my business mentioned by ChatGPT?
A: There is no paid listing that puts your business into ChatGPT's answers. ChatGPT search draws on the open web and on partner search providers, so the paths in are the same ones that work for search: pages it can crawl, consistent business details, reviews and mentions on other sites. Anyone selling a guaranteed ChatGPT placement is selling something OpenAI does not offer.
Q: Does getting mentioned by ChatGPT work for a local NZ business?
A: Yes, and local businesses have an advantage because the questions are specific. OpenAI's help page says ChatGPT search may use a general location from your IP address, so a prompt like "electrician near me" becomes a local search. A Tauranga electrician with a clear suburb page, a complete Google Business Profile and recent reviews is competing with a handful of local firms for that answer.
Q: How long does it take to get mentioned by ChatGPT?
A: Expect weeks for fixes that change what search engines can read, such as unblocking a crawler or publishing a clear service page, and months for anything that depends on other sites mentioning you. There is no fixed timetable from OpenAI. Run the same set of test prompts once a month and record the result, so you can see movement instead of guessing at it.
Q: Is getting mentioned by ChatGPT different from SEO?
A: It overlaps heavily with SEO and adds a few things. Google says its AI features need nothing beyond core SEO, and ChatGPT search uses partner search providers, so crawlable, useful pages still come first. What changes is the weighting: Ahrefs found branded web mentions correlated with AI visibility far more strongly than backlinks, so being talked about elsewhere counts for more.
Q: Why does ChatGPT say something wrong about my business?
A: Usually because the web says something wrong or inconsistent about it: an old address in a directory, a closed branch still listed, or a service page that never states what you do. Fix the source pages first, starting with your own site and Google Business Profile, then the directories. Re-test a few weeks later, because assistants answer from what they can find and confirm.
Q: Should I block AI crawlers like GPTBot from my website?
A: That is a business choice, and OpenAI treats its two crawlers separately. GPTBot relates to model training. OAI-SearchBot is the crawler for ChatGPT search, and OpenAI says sites that opt out of it will not be shown in ChatGPT search answers. A business that wants to be recommended should at least allow OAI-SearchBot in its robots.txt file.

## What is a fractional marketing manager, and does your NZ business need one?
URL: https://www.flowai.co.nz/blog/fractional-marketing-manager-nz.html
Author: Amber Lan, Flow AI
Updated: 2026-10-02

Short answer: A fractional marketing manager is an experienced marketer who works for your business part time, usually one or two days a week, owning the plan and the results without a full-time salary. Robert Walters' 2026 guide puts Auckland contract marketing managers at NZD 70 to 105 an hour, roughly NZD 2,450 to 3,700 a month for one day a week.

What is a fractional marketing manager?

A fractional marketing manager is an experienced marketer who works for several businesses at once and gives each one a fixed share of the week. They own the marketing plan, manage the people and tools doing the work, and report results, the way a manager would, while being paid for a day or two a week instead of a salary.

A fractional marketing manager is an experienced marketer who works for several businesses at once, giving each a fixed share of their week, and owns that business's marketing plan and results as a manager would, without being a full-time employee.

The word fractional is the whole idea. The business buys a fraction of a senior person, usually through a monthly agreement, and that person treats the business as one of a small portfolio of clients. The difference from a consultant is ownership: a consultant hands over advice, while a fractional manager stays and is answerable for whether the plan happens.

The glossary entry for fractional marketing manager gives the short definition. This guide covers what the role costs in New Zealand in 2026 and how to decide whether it fits.

Fractional marketing manager, director or CMO: what is the difference?

The three titles describe seniority and focus more than contract type. A fractional CMO works on positioning and budget with the owner. A fractional marketing manager runs the plan week to week and manages the suppliers. A fractional marketing director sits between the two, and New Zealand providers use all three titles loosely.

The rates follow the seniority. In the Robert Walters Salary Guide 2026, Auckland contract rates run NZD 70 to 105 an hour for a marketing manager, NZD 120 to 140 for a head of marketing and NZD 160 to 240 for a chief marketing officer. Those figures are for contractors placed through a recruiter, drawn from a survey of more than 5,500 professionals across Australia and New Zealand, so independent fractional marketers set their own prices around them.

Because the titles blur, compare people on what they will do in a normal week. A useful question: "On a Tuesday when you are working for us, what are you doing?" A fractional CMO answers with pricing, positioning and the board report. A fractional manager answers with briefs, supplier check-ins, campaign reviews and the monthly numbers. The fractional CMO glossary entry and the guide to fractional CMO vs AI CMO cover the senior end in more depth.

What does a fractional marketing manager do each month?

In a typical month a fractional marketing manager sets or updates the plan, briefs whoever produces the work, checks it before it goes out, manages the budget and reports what happened. Most small business engagements are one or two days a week, roughly 35 to 70 hours a month, often fixed to the same weekday.

A realistic month for a 15 person service business, at one day a week, looks like this:

Week one. Review last month's enquiries and their sources, agree the month's priorities with the owner, write the briefs.

Week two. Check drafts from the freelancer or agency, fix the website pages that are losing enquiries, review the ad account.

Week three. Approve and schedule the work, handle the supplier who missed a deadline, prepare the next campaign.

Week four. Write the monthly report: what shipped, what it cost, which channel produced enquiries, what to stop.

Notice how little of that is production. At eight hours a week, most of the time goes on deciding and checking. That is the value of the role, and it means the business still needs someone, or something, to make the work.

What does a fractional marketing manager cost in NZ?

Based on 2026 NZ rates, a fractional marketing manager costs roughly NZD 2,450 to 3,700 a month for one day a week, and about double that for two days. Some packaged services start lower, from about NZD 1,200 a month, and fractional CMO engagements start around NZD 4,000 a month.

The monthly figures below are arithmetic on published hourly rates, at about 35 hours a month per weekly day. Packaged prices are quoted as published, GST exclusive.

OptionPublished rateRoughly per monthSource

Contract marketing manager, one day a weekNZD 70 to 105 an hour (Auckland)NZD 2,450 to 3,700Robert Walters 2026

Contract marketing manager, two days a weekNZD 70 to 105 an hour (Auckland)NZD 4,900 to 7,350Robert Walters 2026

The sources: Flex Marketing's outsourced marketing page lists packages from NZD 1,200 plus GST a month, a "from" price only. King Tide's April 2026 guide puts a NZ fractional CMO at NZD 4,000 to 6,000 a month for strategy only and NZD 6,000 to 10,000 hands-on, and Kyttn's fractional CMO page publishes the same bands, with a NZD 489 plus GST diagnostic. The Maestro marketplace quotes NZD 6,000 to 12,000 a month for fractional CMOs at NZ businesses turning over NZD 3 million to 20 million.

For Australian readers, Cemoh's live consultant rate guide showed marketing manager consultants at AUD 855 a day or AUD 112 an hour as of 2 October 2026, excluding GST and including super and leave.

Production is extra in every row. The manager's fee buys direction and checking; the writing, design and ads are a separate line. The full cost guide for Australia and New Zealand prices that production side.

How does it compare with an agency, a freelancer or a full-time hire?

A fractional marketing manager sits between a freelancer and a full-time hire on cost, and is the only one of the four whose main job is owning the plan. An agency and a freelancer mostly produce. A full-time manager plans and produces but costs more than NZD 100,000 a year before tools.

OptionTypical NZ costOwns the planMakes the workBest when

Fractional marketing managerAbout NZD 2,450 to 7,350 a month for one or two days a weekYesA little; directs othersSpend is going out and nobody senior owns it

Agency retainerNZD 1,000 to 10,000 a monthSometimesYesYou know which channels to run and want them done

FreelancerNZD 50 to 150 an hourRarelyYes, one skillOne clear job, such as writing or ads

Full-time marketing managerNZD 106,000 to 150,000 a year base, plus on-costsYesYesMarketing is a full week of work, every week

The agency range is from King Tide's July 2026 NZ hiring guide, which puts agencies at NZD 1,000 to 10,000 a month and freelancers at NZD 60 to 150 an hour, and Jelly Digital's September 2026 price guide, which puts NZ freelancers at NZD 50 to 120 an hour. Both are agency estimates rather than surveys.

For the hire, SEEK's October 2026 data shows an advertised average of NZD 106,322 for marketing managers across 386 openings, and Robert Walters puts Auckland marketing managers at NZD 120,000 to 150,000 base. On top of salary, Inland Revenue confirms the employer KiwiSaver contribution rose to 3.5% on 1 April 2026, plus employer superannuation contribution tax, and King Tide adds about 20% for tools, training and recruitment. A NZD 106,000 salary becomes roughly NZD 110,000 with KiwiSaver alone, or around NZD 9,200 a month, before laptops and software. The agency vs freelancer vs in-house guide works through that comparison in full.

Which businesses get the most from a fractional marketing manager?

A fractional marketing manager suits a business that already sells a proven offer, already spends money on marketing and has nobody senior watching that spend. The typical case is a growing service business of 10 to 50 staff where the owner is still approving ads between client jobs.

Signs the timing is right:

Two or more suppliers (an agency, a freelancer, a web developer) and nobody coordinating them.

Monthly marketing spend that nobody can tie to enquiries.

A marketing coordinator or junior who needs direction and review more than extra tasks.

A growth target for the next year that needs a written plan behind it.

A full-time hire that feels a year early.

That last one matters. A fractional manager is often the best way to find out what the full-time job is. After six months the business knows how many hours marketing really takes, which channels work, and what kind of person to hire.

Who does the work when the manager is part time?

The production still has to come from somewhere: freelancers, an agency, an in-house coordinator, AI systems or the owner. A fractional manager at one day a week has time to plan, brief, check and report, and very little time left for writing and design. Budget for production separately.

A frequent mistake is hiring a fractional manager and expecting a department. Another is pairing a manager with a production setup too small to execute the plan. A sensible split is to work out what the plan needs each month (four articles, weekly social posts, one email, an ad account) and price that production before signing the manager.

There are now four realistic production options to pair with a fractional manager. A freelancer per skill keeps cost tied to output. An agency retainer gives one contact for several channels. A junior hire gives continuity. AI systems with human review can produce first drafts, pages and reports at a volume a small budget cannot buy in hours, which leaves the manager's day for judgment. The guide to marketing agency alternatives in NZ compares those production options side by side.

When is a leaner setup the better first step?

A leaner setup is the better first step when the business is still proving its offer, has little or no marketing spend yet, or needs production more than direction. In those cases the money goes further on a clear plan and a small production system, with a fractional manager added once there is spend to manage.

A fractional manager's value comes from directing existing activity. With nothing running yet, much of their first few months goes on setting up basics that a written plan and a few systems can cover more cheaply. King Tide's guide sets an honest floor: below NZD 1,000 to 1,500 a month for marketing, it advises against hiring anyone.

Leaner first steps that keep a fractional manager on the table for later:

A free, written audit of what to fix first, so the first spend goes on the biggest gap.

Fixing the website and Google Business Profile, which every later channel depends on.

One channel run well for three months, with enquiries tracked from day one.

A short paid diagnostic from a fractional marketer, which many offer, before any monthly commitment.

The free AI-readiness benchmark is a quick way to see which of these gaps is biggest, with no email needed.

How to hire a fractional marketing manager well

Hire a fractional marketing manager on evidence of results for businesses your size, a clear weekly scope, and an agreed report. Ask how many clients they hold at once, what they did for a similar business, and what the first 90 days produce. Avoid long lock-ins until the first quarter has shown results.

How many clients do you hold right now? Ask which weekday is yours and what happens when another client has a busy month.

What did you change for a business like ours? Ask for a real plan or report, with the client's permission, and look for numbers tied to enquiries.

What will exist after 90 days? A written plan, a tracking setup, a supplier list and a monthly report are reasonable answers.

Who does the production, and who pays for it? Get this in writing before the start date.

What do we keep if we stop? Plans, accounts, reports and logins should belong to the business.

What is the notice period? Packaged services often run month to month, while Maestro describes fractional CMO engagements of 6 to 12 months.

It covers the production and reporting side that a fractional manager directs, with Amber Lan building and reviewing the systems herself. It can sit under a fractional manager or come before one.

The short version

A fractional marketing manager is a senior marketer you share by the day. In New Zealand in 2026 that is roughly NZD 2,450 to 3,700 a month for one day a week on Robert Walters' Auckland contract rates, with fractional CMOs from about NZD 4,000. The role buys direction and checking; production is a separate budget.

It pays off when there is spend to direct and nobody senior directing it. Before that, a written plan and a small production system usually go further, with the fractional manager added when the work outgrows the owner.
