Q: What is the best AI marketing example for a small business to start with?
A: Start with positioning: an AI system drafts a one-page file of what the business claims, who it serves and the proof behind each claim, and the owner approves every line. It produces nothing customers see, yet every other example reads from it. After that, most small businesses add search or content, because both depend on the positioning file and both keep working between busy weeks.
Q: Do these AI marketing examples need expensive software?
A: No. Each example runs on tools most small businesses already pay for or can get cheaply: a general AI assistant, the website, Google Business Profile, an email account, a scheduler and a spreadsheet or CRM. The expensive part is the setup: writing the instructions, connecting the data and agreeing who approves what. Once that exists, the weekly running cost is mostly a person's review time.
Q: How much time does a person need to spend reviewing AI marketing work?
A: Plan for a few hours a week when two or three examples are running, mostly in short sittings. Review is fastest when the AI system works from a written positioning file and a tone guide, because the reader checks facts rather than rewriting. Outbound emails and review replies take the most attention, since both reach a named person, so batch them into one daily or weekly slot.
Q: Are the businesses in these examples real Flow AI clients?
A: No. The plumbing firm, the accounting practice and the other businesses on this page are illustrations, invented to show how each marketing job works at small business scale. None of them is a client and no example claims a result. The statistics quoted alongside them come from named surveys and reports, each linked to the original source so you can check the sample and the date.
Q: Can AI reply to Google reviews for my business?
A: AI can draft the reply, and a person should post it. A good system reads the review, uses its specifics, matches the business's tone and flags complaints for the owner. BrightLocal's 2026 survey found 89% of US consumers expect owners to respond and half are put off by templated replies, so a draft that is reviewed and personalised beats both silence and an automatic stock answer.
Q: Is it legal to use AI for cold email in New Zealand?
A: Using AI to research and draft is legal; the message itself must follow the Unsolicited Electronic Messages Act whoever wrote it. That means a consent basis (for cold business email, usually a published business address and a message relevant to the person's role), accurate sender details and a free unsubscribe honoured within five working days. Check the Act or the Department of Internal Affairs guidance for your own case.

## AI marketing automation for small business: what to set up first.
URL: https://www.flowai.co.nz/blog/ai-marketing-automation-small-business.html
Author: Amber Lan, Flow AI
Updated: 2026-10-02

Short answer: AI marketing automation is software that runs marketing steps on triggers, such as a welcome email after a sign-up, with AI writing, sorting and personalising the content inside each step. A small business should start with six: a welcome sequence, enquiry follow-up, quote follow-up, review requests, abandoned bookings or carts, and re-engagement.

What is AI marketing automation?

AI marketing automation is software that runs marketing steps on triggers, with AI working inside each step. The trigger is something a contact does, such as signing up, booking or going quiet. The step is a message or a task. AI drafts the message, sorts the contact, picks the version or summarises the reply.

AI marketing automation is software that runs marketing steps a person has designed, triggered by what a contact does, with AI drafting, sorting and personalising the content inside each step.

The two halves are worth keeping apart. Marketing automation is older than the current AI tools and handles delivery: it sends the email three days after the quote. AI handles the content and the judgment calls inside the step: what the email says, whether this enquiry is a tyre-kicker, which of two subject lines this person sees. An AI marketing agent goes one level up again and decides which automations should exist at all.

For a business of 5 to 50 staff, the practical question is narrower than the vendor pages suggest. It is which handful of automated steps pay for themselves, and how few tools can run them.

What does marketing automation do on its own?

On its own, marketing automation sends the right message at the right moment without anyone remembering to. It watches for triggers, waits, checks conditions and sends. It does this every time, at two in the morning and during the busiest week of the year, which is where most of its value comes from.

The platform data on automated email is consistent. Klaviyo's 2026 benchmarks, from more than 183,000 customers, show automated flows generating nearly 41% of email revenue from 5.3% of sends, with revenue per recipient nearly 18 times higher than campaigns. Omnisend's January 2026 study of 150,000 brands found automated emails produced 30% of email revenue from 2% of sends. Both are global ecommerce platforms with no New Zealand or Australian split, so read them as evidence about how automated messages behave, and expect a service business to see smaller absolute numbers.

What automation cannot do on its own is decide what to say. Every branch needs a message written by someone, and a rule built by someone. That writing load is why so many small businesses set up one welcome email years ago and never touched it again.

What does AI add to marketing automation?

AI adds the writing and the sorting that used to make automation too much work for a small team. It drafts each message in a sequence from a brief, classifies incoming enquiries, varies copy for different customer types and summarises what came back. The rules stay simple, and the content inside them improves.

Small businesses here are already using AI for the writing half. Constant Contact's June 2026 report on Australian and New Zealand small businesses states: "In Australia and New Zealand, marketing adoption of AI tools has skyrocketed to 88.7%, officially making local small businesses the highest adopters of AI globally." That figure counts any use of AI tools in marketing, and the report does not publish the ANZ sample size. Among AI users, the top uses were writing emails, subject lines or social captions (45.1%), analysing marketing trend data (37%) and generating visual content (35.2%).

In practice, AI is useful in four places inside an automation:

Drafting the sequence. Give it the offer, the customer and the objection, and it writes five emails in your voice for you to edit.

Sorting enquiries. It reads a form submission and tags it by service, urgency or fit, so the right follow-up runs.

Varying the message. A returning customer and a first-time enquirer get different wording from the same trigger.

Summarising replies. It reads what came back and tells the owner which threads need a human today.

The six automations a small business should run first

Run these six first: a welcome sequence, enquiry follow-up, quote follow-up, review requests, abandoned bookings or carts, and a re-engagement message. Each one fires on something a customer did, each one replaces a task people forget, and together they cover the path from first contact to repeat business.

Enquiry follow-up. An instant acknowledgement when the form is submitted, an alert to whoever handles it, and a second message if nobody has replied within a working day. Start here.

Welcome sequence. Three to five emails over two weeks for new subscribers or customers: who you are, what you do best, the proof, and one clear next step.

Quote follow-up. A reminder a few days after a quote goes out, and a second one before it expires. A quote nobody chases is easy to lose to a competitor who does.

Review requests. A short message after the job or delivery asking for a Google review, with the link. Reviews feed both local search and AI answers about the business.

Abandoned booking or cart. A reminder to anyone who started a booking or checkout and stopped. Omnisend's 2026 ecommerce report found welcome and abandoned cart emails made up 76% of all automation-related orders on its platform.

Re-engagement. A message to customers who have not bought or booked in a set period, timed to the business's natural cycle, whether that is a service interval or a seasonal job.

Social scheduling is often on lists like this. It is useful, and it is publishing rather than automation in the triggered sense, so it sits outside the first six. Outbound prospecting is also separate, with its own rules, covered in the guide to outbound sales automation.

Four ways to run marketing automation, compared

A small business can run automation four ways: do it yourself on an email or CRM platform, use an all-in-one platform, pay a freelancer or agency to build and maintain it, or use an AI agent that builds and runs it under review. They differ mainly in who writes the messages and who notices when something breaks.

ApproachWho writes the messagesWho maintains itBest forWatch for

DIY on an email or CRM platformThe owner, with an AI writing toolThe ownerOne or two sequences, an owner with some eveningsSequences written once and never updated

All-in-one platformThe owner, with built-in AI and templatesThe owner, inside one vendorBusinesses that want CRM, forms and email in one loginPaying for modules nobody uses; hard to leave

Freelancer or agency buildThe freelancer or agencyThe builder, while they are paidA defined set of flows with a clear briefWorkflows nobody inside the business understands

AI agent, human approvedThe agent drafts, the owner approvesThe agent, with a log of changesBusinesses that want the six running and improving without the build workUnreviewed sends; weak access controls

The choice often comes down to time. Constant Contact found 67.3% of ANZ small businesses had increased the time they spend on marketing, and 22% find marketing takes too much time to manage. Automation that the owner has to build and maintain adds to that time before it saves any.

Keep the stack to three tools

Cap the stack at three tools: one system that holds contacts and sends messages, one form or booking tool that feeds it, and one AI writing tool for drafts. Every extra tool adds a login, a monthly fee and an integration that can fail without anyone noticing, and a failed integration usually means an unsubscribe that did not sync.

Small businesses tend to buy tools faster than they wire them up. A business with a separate CRM, email platform, SMS tool, form builder, scheduling app and review tool has six places where a contact record can disagree with itself. Pick the contact system first, because it holds consent and history. Then add only what it cannot do.

The check is simple. If a customer unsubscribes, does every tool that can message them know within minutes? If the answer involves a spreadsheet, the stack is too big.

NZ and Australian rules for automated marketing

Automated marketing in New Zealand and Australia sits under spam law, privacy law and consumer law. Spam law requires consent, accurate sender details and a working unsubscribe. Privacy law governs how personal information is collected and handed to AI tools. Consumer law holds the business responsible for every claim, whoever or whatever wrote it.

In New Zealand, the Unsolicited Electronic Messages Act applies to every commercial email and text. Consumer Protection's guidance says messages need consent, accurate business contact details and a free unsubscribe that works within five business days, and businesses can be fined up to $500,000. In Australia, the Spam Act 2003 sets the same three rules in sections 16 to 18: no unsolicited commercial messages, accurate sender information and a functional unsubscribe facility.

Privacy rules are tightening. New Zealand's new IPP3A, in force since 1 May 2026, requires businesses that collect personal information indirectly to take reasonable steps to tell the person, which matters for bought or enriched lists. The Privacy Commissioner expects a privacy impact assessment before AI tools handle personal information, and advises against it when in doubt. In Australia, the OAIC recommends against entering personal information into publicly available generative AI tools, and from 10 December 2026, businesses covered by the Privacy Act that use automated decision-making affecting people must describe it in their privacy policies. The Privacy Act mainly covers businesses with turnover above A$3 million, so many small firms sit outside it, though the guidance is still sound practice.

Customers care about this. The Privacy Commissioner's 2026 survey of 1,245 New Zealanders found 82% want more say in how their information is collected and used. A checklist for the six automations:

Record consent at the point of sign-up, with the date and the source.

Put the business name, contact details and an unsubscribe link in every template.

Sync unsubscribes across every tool automatically.

Draft in AI tools with placeholders; merge names and details inside your own platform.

Check every claim in a template against evidence before it goes live, because Fair Trading Act fines reach $600,000 per offence for a business.

This is general information. For a specific situation, take advice from a lawyer.

Where the human stays in the loop

A human reads the first send of every new automation, approves every claim and offer in the templates, and reviews the results monthly. After that the automation runs unattended between reviews. The review takes little time, and it is the difference between a sequence that improves and one that keeps repeating an old mistake.

Small businesses are right to be careful. In the same Constant Contact report, 29.9% of ANZ small businesses worried customers may sense a loss of personal touch from AI, 27.6% said customers had raised data privacy and oversight concerns, and 36% already practise full transparency about their automation. Telling customers a reminder is automated costs nothing and builds trust.

The review also catches errors. KPMG and the University of Melbourne found 51% of New Zealand employees had relied on AI output at work without evaluating its accuracy. In an automated sequence, one unchecked error goes to every contact who hits that trigger, for months.

How to tell whether your automation is working

Judge each automation on one number tied to its job. Enquiry follow-up is measured by response time and enquiries that become quotes. Quote follow-up by quotes accepted. Review requests by reviews received. Welcome and re-engagement sequences by bookings or orders from those contacts. Open rates alone say little about revenue.

Set a baseline before switching anything on: how many enquiries a month, how many become quotes, how many quotes are accepted, how many reviews arrive. Then compare monthly. Some automations show their effect in the first few weeks because they fire on events that happen daily. Others, like re-engagement, need a full customer cycle before the numbers mean much. As a rule of thumb, the enquiry and quote follow-ups show a difference first, because they touch the contacts closest to buying.

When a number does not move, look at the message before the rule. A follow-up that arrives at the right time with the wrong offer is a writing problem, and that is the part AI helps with most. The free agent templates include starting points for these sequences.

Where Flow AI fits

Flow AI is an AI marketing transformation practice: the strategy, the systems and the agents that run a marketing function, engineered end to end. For automation, that means the six sequences above built on the business's own accounts, drafted by agents, approved by a person and reviewed against the numbers each month.

The short version

Marketing automation sends the right message when a customer does something. AI writes and sorts the content inside each step, which removes the writing load that stopped most small businesses from automating. Start with enquiry follow-up, then add the other five, on no more than three tools.

Record consent, sync unsubscribes, keep personal data out of public AI tools and have a person read every first send. The guide to the AI CMO covers the planning layer that decides what to automate next.

To find out which automation your business should run first, request a free audit.

Q: What should a small business automate first?
A: Start with the enquiry follow-up: an instant acknowledgement when someone fills in the form, then a reminder to the team and a second message if nobody has replied within a day. It touches the people most likely to buy, it needs no list to have been built first, and any business that takes enquiries can set it up in an afternoon on tools it may already pay for.
Q: What is the difference between marketing automation and AI marketing automation?
A: Marketing automation runs steps a person designed: if a contact does this, send that. AI marketing automation adds AI inside those steps, so it can draft the message, sort an enquiry by type, pick which version a contact sees or summarise replies. The rules still decide when something happens. The AI changes what the message says and how it is routed.
Q: Do I need consent to send automated marketing emails in New Zealand?
A: Yes. Under the Unsolicited Electronic Messages Act, commercial emails and texts need the recipient's consent, accurate details about the business and a free unsubscribe that works within five business days. Consumer Protection notes fines of up to $500,000. Automation makes compliance easier if consent is recorded at sign-up and unsubscribes sync to every tool automatically.
Q: Is free-tier marketing automation enough to start?
A: Often, yes. Many email and CRM platforms include basic triggers and sequences on their entry plans, which covers a welcome sequence, enquiry follow-up and review requests. Pay for more when a real limit gets in the way, such as contact numbers, branching or SMS. Buying the advanced plan before the first sequence is live is the commonest way small businesses overspend.
Q: Can I put customer data into ChatGPT to write automated emails?
A: Be careful. Australia's privacy regulator recommends against entering personal information into publicly available generative AI tools, and New Zealand's Privacy Commissioner expects a privacy impact assessment before AI tools handle personal information. Write templates with placeholders in the AI tool, then let your email platform merge in names and details inside a system you control.
Q: How many marketing tools does a small business need for automation?
A: Usually three: one place that holds contacts and sends email, one booking or form tool that feeds it, and one AI writing tool for drafts. Many businesses manage with two. Each extra tool adds a login, an integration that can break and a place where an unsubscribe can fail to sync, which is a legal problem as well as a tidy-desk problem.

## Marketing agency vs freelancer vs in-house hire: which suits your NZ business?
URL: https://www.flowai.co.nz/blog/agency-vs-freelancer-vs-in-house.html
Author: Amber Lan, Flow AI
Updated: 2026-10-02

Short answer: A freelancer is usually cheapest for New Zealand small businesses at NZD 50 to 150 an hour. An agency retainer costs NZD 1,500 to 10,000 a month for more than one channel, and an in-house marketer costs about NZD 76,000 to 167,000 a year once KiwiSaver and overheads are added. Ongoing workload decides which fits.

Agency, freelancer or in-house: which costs least?

A freelancer costs the least per hour in New Zealand, at NZD 50 to 150. An agency costs more per hour, at NZD 95 to 200, but brings a team. An in-house marketer costs the most in total, about NZD 76,000 to 167,000 a year all in, and gives you a full working week.

The hourly figures come from two Auckland agencies' 2026 guides. Jelly Digital puts NZ agency rates at NZD 95 to 200 an hour and freelancers at NZD 50 to 120, and King Tide Marketing puts freelancers at NZD 60 to 150 an hour and consultants at NZD 150 to 250. The in-house figure is calculated below from SEEK and Robert Walters salary data.

Price per hour only matters once you know how many hours of marketing the business needs. Ten hours a month is a freelancer's job. Forty hours a week is a hire. Everything in between is where agencies, fractional marketers and the newer AI-led options compete. For the agency side in detail, see the guide to marketing agency cost in NZ, and for tools and AI options as well, the AI marketing cost guide for Australia and New Zealand.

The three models side by side

The three models trade cost against breadth and control. A freelancer is flexible and cheap for one skill. An agency covers several skills at a higher rate and is easy to end. An in-house hire knows your business best and costs the most to start and to stop. This table sets them out on the same lines.

FreelancerAgencyIn-house hire

Typical NZ cost (excl. GST)NZD 50 to 150 an hour, or NZD 500 to 3,000 a monthNZD 95 to 200 an hour; retainers NZD 500 to 10,000+ a monthAbout NZD 76,000 to 167,000 a year all in

Skills coveredOne or twoSeveral, across a teamOne person's skill set, plus whatever you buy in

Hours you getWhat you pay forWhat the retainer covers, after account managementAbout a full working week

Ramp-upDays to a few weeksA few weeks of onboardingWeeks to recruit, then months to learn the business

Control day to dayMedium: you brief directlyLower: you brief an account managerHigh: they work inside the business

Cover for holidays and illnessUsually noneBuilt inNone unless you plan it

Ending itPer the agreed noticeNotice period or minimum term, often one to six monthsA fair employment process

Best forA clear, defined jobSeveral channels needing coordinationSteady weekly work and someone to manage it

What does an in-house marketer cost in NZ?

An in-house marketer in New Zealand costs the salary plus about a fifth again. On SEEK's advertised averages, a marketing coordinator comes to about NZD 76,000 a year all in and a marketing manager about NZD 131,500. At Robert Walters' Auckland average for a manager, the all-in cost is about NZD 167,000 a year.

The inputs are sourced. SEEK's October 2026 data puts the advertised average for a marketing coordinator at NZD 61,498 across 371 openings and a marketing manager at NZD 106,322 across 386 openings, both in the marketing and communications industry. Robert Walters' 2026 salary guide puts Auckland marketing managers at NZD 120,000 to 150,000, averaging NZD 135,000. Recruiter-placed roles skew to larger employers, which is why that figure runs above SEEK.

On-costs come next. Inland Revenue raised the default employer KiwiSaver contribution from 3% to 3.5% on 1 April 2026, rising to 4% on 1 April 2028. ACC's 2026/27 Levy Guidebook sets the Work levy for advertising services at NZD 0.11 per NZD 100 of liable earnings, plus a flat Working Safer levy of NZD 0.08; your own rate follows your business's industry classification. King Tide adds about 20% for tools, training and recruitment.

Cost line (NZD a year)Coordinator (SEEK avg)Manager (SEEK avg)Manager (Robert Walters Auckland avg)

Base salary61,498106,322135,000

Employer KiwiSaver at 3.5%2,1523,7214,725

ACC Work and Working Safer levies at NZD 0.19 per 100 (advertising services rate)117202257

Approximate all-in cost76,100131,500167,000

Per monthAbout 6,300About 11,000About 13,900

The 20% allowance is an agency's estimate, so adjust it to your own software and recruitment costs. Paid leave and the months a new hire spends learning the business also reduce output in year one. A coordinator brings hours and energy, and usually needs someone senior to set direction.

What are you paying for with an agency?

With an agency you pay for a team's skills across several channels, cover when people are away, and an arrangement you can end on notice. You also pay for account management and agency overheads, so the hours that reach your marketing are fewer than the retainer suggests. Retainers run NZD 500 to 10,000 or more a month.

Jelly Digital's bands are NZD 500 to 1,500 a month for one channel, NZD 1,500 to 4,000 for several and NZD 4,000 to 10,000 or more for full service. At NZD 95 to 200 an hour, a NZD 2,500 retainer buys roughly 12 to 26 hours a month, and meetings and reporting come out of that.

The common failure is a mismatch between the agency and the business. Setup's 2025 Marketing Relationship Survey, a small sample of about 100 mostly US responses, found 61% of clients who ended an agency relationship cited dissatisfaction with delivery and 44% said the agency did not understand their business. Before signing, ask who works on your account, what ships each month, and whether the ad accounts and analytics sit in your name.

What is a freelance marketer, and what do they charge?

A freelance marketer is a self-employed marketing specialist who works for several clients on a project, hourly or monthly retainer basis, usually in one or two skills such as copywriting, SEO or paid ads. In New Zealand they charge about NZD 50 to 150 an hour, or NZD 500 to 3,000 a month on retainer.

The two NZ sources overlap: Jelly Digital's NZD 50 to 120 an hour and King Tide's NZD 60 to 150. Senior consultants who mainly advise sit higher, at NZD 150 to 250 an hour. For comparison, Robert Walters' guide puts Auckland contract rates for a marketing manager at NZD 70 to 105 an hour and a marketing coordinator at NZD 50 to 70. Those are recruiter-placed contractors, a useful sense check on what an experienced independent should cost.

Freelancers work best on a defined job with an end point or a fixed monthly output: a website rewrite, a Google Ads account, a content calendar. Ask for work samples in your industry, a written scope with a fixed price or an hours cap, and a plan for when they are away. Freelance marketing in NZ also suits owners who want to brief the person doing the work directly, with no account manager in between.

How to compare the three on cost per enquiry

Compare the three models on cost per enquiry: the total monthly cost, including ad spend and the hours you spend managing, divided by the genuine enquiries produced. It puts an hourly freelancer, a monthly retainer and an annual salary on one scale, and it shows when a cheaper option is costing you more.

Example (invented numbers)Monthly costEnquiriesCost per enquiry

Freelancer: NZD 1,500 retainer, NZD 1,000 ad spend, 5 hours of your time at NZD 100NZD 3,00012NZD 250

Agency: NZD 3,000 retainer, NZD 1,000 ad spend, 3 hours of your timeNZD 4,30020NZD 215

In-house coordinator: about NZD 6,300 all in, NZD 1,000 ad spend, 4 hours of your timeNZD 7,70025NZD 308

The numbers are made up to show the method. In this example the agency wins on enquiries alone, while the in-house coordinator also covers work an enquiry count misses, such as sales material and events. Set what counts as an enquiry before you start, then recalculate after three months with real numbers. The glossary defines cost per enquiry in one line.

Which model suits which situation?

Match the model to the work. A defined job with an end point suits a freelancer. Several channels that need coordinating suit an agency. Steady weekly work, enough to fill a full-time role, suits a hire once someone can manage that person. Budget sets the floor, and below about NZD 1,000 a month outside help rarely has room to work.

Nobody owns marketing and the budget is under NZD 1,000 a month: do it yourself with tools, and buy a freelancer for one defined project. King Tide advises not hiring anyone below NZD 1,000 to 1,500 a month.

One channel brings most customers: a freelancer or a specialist agency package on that channel.

Several channels matter and nobody has time to run them: an agency retainer of NZD 1,500 to 4,000, or a fractional marketing manager.

Marketing work fills most of a week, every week: an in-house coordinator, with a specialist freelancer or agency for the technical channels.

A growth push across channels with a sales team waiting on leads: a full-service agency, or an in-house manager directing specialists.

The part-time senior option sits between rows three and four, and the fractional marketing manager guide covers it in depth. The guide to marketing agency alternatives lists every option with prices.

Can you combine an agency, a freelancer and an in-house hire?

Many small businesses end up with a mix, and it often works well. The usual pattern is one in-house person who owns the calendar and knows the customers, plus an agency or freelancer for a technical channel such as SEO or paid ads. The in-house person briefs and checks the outside help.

A hybrid works when roles are written down. Decide who owns the plan, who owns each channel, and who reports the monthly numbers. Keep every account in your business's name so a change of supplier costs weeks, and your history stays put. The trap is paying two parties to do the same job, so check overlaps whenever you add one.

The short version

A freelancer is cheapest for one defined job at NZD 50 to 150 an hour. An agency covers several channels for NZD 1,500 to 10,000 a month. An in-house marketer costs about NZD 76,000 to 167,000 a year once KiwiSaver at 3.5%, ACC levies and overheads are added.

Choose by workload and by who will manage the work, keep your accounts in your own name, and compare every option on cost per enquiry after three months.

For help choosing between them for your business, request a free audit.

Q: How much does a freelance marketer charge in NZ?
A: New Zealand freelance marketers charge about NZD 50 to 150 an hour, according to 2026 guides from Jelly Digital (NZD 50 to 120) and King Tide Marketing (NZD 60 to 150). Monthly retainers run NZD 500 to 3,000. Senior consultants charge NZD 150 to 250 an hour. Rates rise with specialism, so a paid ads specialist usually costs more than a generalist social media freelancer.
Q: Is it cheaper to hire a marketer or use an agency?
A: For one or two channels, an agency or freelancer is usually cheaper. A marketing coordinator on SEEK's advertised average costs about NZD 6,300 a month once KiwiSaver, ACC levies and a 20% allowance for tools and recruitment are added, and a manager about NZD 11,000. A hire becomes the cheaper option when there is enough steady work to fill a full-time role.
Q: What is the difference between a freelancer and an agency?
A: A freelancer is one person with one or two skills, usually at a lower hourly rate. An agency is a team, so it covers more skills and keeps working when one person is away, but you pay for account management and overheads. Freelancers suit a defined job. Agencies suit work across several channels that needs coordinating.
Q: Can I combine an agency, a freelancer and an in-house hire?
A: Yes, and many small businesses do. A common pattern is a junior in-house marketer who owns the calendar and day-to-day content, with an agency or specialist freelancer for one technical channel such as SEO or paid ads. The in-house person briefs and checks the outside help, which keeps the knowledge of the business in the business.
Q: What if I choose the wrong model?
A: Freelancers and agencies are easier to change than an employee: published NZ agency terms run from one month's notice to six-month minimums, while ending employment takes a fair process. Keep ad accounts, analytics and content in your business's name from day one, so switching costs you weeks rather than your history. Review every model on cost per enquiry after three months.
Q: What does KiwiSaver add to the cost of a marketing hire?
A: From 1 April 2026 the default employer KiwiSaver contribution is 3.5% of gross pay, up from 3%, and it rises to 4% on 1 April 2028, according to Inland Revenue. On a NZD 106,322 marketing manager salary, 3.5% is about NZD 3,700 a year. ACC levies for an office-type business add a few hundred dollars more.

## AEO vs SEO vs GEO: what is the difference?
URL: https://www.flowai.co.nz/blog/aeo-vs-seo-vs-geo.html
Author: Amber Lan, Flow AI
Updated: 2026-10-02

Short answer: SEO gets your pages ranked in search results. AEO gets your business quoted or recommended inside the answers AI tools write. GEO is the research term for the same goal in generative AI engines such as ChatGPT and Perplexity. In practice AEO and GEO overlap almost completely, and both rest on good SEO.

The short answer: SEO, AEO and GEO side by side

SEO, AEO and GEO are three names for getting found when someone searches. SEO aims for a high position in a list of links. AEO aims for a mention inside the answer an AI tool writes. GEO is the academic name for that same AI goal. The table sets them side by side.

SEOAEOGEO

Full nameSearch engine optimisationAnswer engine optimisationGenerative engine optimisation

Aims forA high position in search results, and the clickBeing cited or recommended in an AI answerBeing included and quoted in an AI-generated answer

Shows up inGoogle and Bing results pages, Google MapsChatGPT, Perplexity, Google AI Overviews and AI Mode, Copilot, GeminiThe same AI engines

What it rewardsRelevant pages, links, technical health, local signalsDirect answers, consistent business facts, reviews and mentions elsewherePassages with statistics, quotations and cited sources

Main free toolsGoogle Search Console, Bing Webmaster ToolsThe same, plus a monthly prompt log and robots.txt checksThe same as AEO

How it is measuredRankings, impressions, clicks, enquiriesHow often you are named, AI referral visits, enquiries that mention AIVisibility in AI responses

Where the term comes fromThe web industry, since the late 1990sThe SEO industry, first for featured snippets and voiceA 2023 research paper, published at KDD 2024

The rest of this page explains each column, where the three overlap, and how to decide what to do first. For the deeper guide to the AI side, read what is answer engine optimisation.

What is SEO, and what does it still do?

Search engine optimisation is the work of helping search engines crawl, understand and rank your pages so people click through to your site. It still does two jobs nothing else replaces: it sends the clicks that remain, and it puts your pages into the indexes that most AI engines search before they answer.

Google still dominates search here. Statcounter's September 2026 figures give Google 89.02% of New Zealand search engine market share, with Bing at 7.71%. In a smaller survey, IAB New Zealand's March 2025 poll of 250 upper North Island adults found 96.8% named Google as their main search engine and 69.2% go to a search engine often or always before a purchase. The sample is small and regional, but it matches what owners see in their own analytics.

What has changed is the click. Pew Research Center's March 2025 study of 68,879 Google searches by 900 US adults found people clicked a traditional result on 8% of visits when an AI summary appeared, and 15% when one did not. Clicks fall without AI summaries too: Seer Interactive's data from 42 client organisations showed organic click-through fell 41% between June 2024 and September 2025 even on queries with no AI Overview. SEO still earns visibility. It earns fewer visits per ranking than it used to.

The glossary entry for search engine optimisation has the short definition, and SEO for small business in New Zealand covers the local playbook.

What is AEO?

Answer engine optimisation is the work of making your business easy for AI answer engines to find, trust and name. Where SEO chases a position, AEO chases a sentence: "for a heat pump install in Hamilton, people often recommend..." followed by your business. The engines build that sentence from pages, listings, reviews and mentions across the web.

AEO began as a term for featured snippets and voice assistants, the boxes and spoken replies that gave one answer to a question. It now covers ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, Copilot and Google's AI Overviews and AI Mode. The work splits into two halves. On your own site, it means pages that answer questions directly, facts stated plainly, and structured data. Off your site, it means Bing indexing, AI crawler access, reviews, directories and other people mentioning you.

The off-site half is where AEO and SEO part ways most. An Ahrefs correlation study of 75,000 brands found branded web mentions had the strongest link to AI Overview visibility (0.664), against 0.218 for backlinks, the classic SEO signal. Ahrefs sells SEO tools and correlation is weaker evidence than an experiment, but it points the same way as the research on GEO.

What is GEO, and where did the term come from?

Generative engine optimisation is the practice of adapting content so generative AI engines include, quote and cite it in their answers. The term comes from a research paper by Aggarwal and colleagues, first posted in November 2023 and accepted at KDD 2024, which built a benchmark to test which page edits made AI engines cite a source more often.

Generative engine optimisation (GEO) is the practice of adapting web content so generative AI engines, such as ChatGPT, Perplexity and Google's AI Overviews, are more likely to include, quote and cite it in the answers they write.

The paper gives GEO its evidence base. The researchers, from Princeton, Georgia Tech, the Allen Institute for AI and IIT Delhi, tested 10,000 queries across 25 domains and found GEO methods boosted a source's visibility in generative engine responses by up to 40%. Adding quotations, adding statistics and citing sources performed best, each improving visibility by 30 to 40%, while keyword stuffing offered little to no improvement.

The result most useful to a small business: citing sources lifted visibility by 115.1% for sites ranked fifth in search results, while the top-ranked site's visibility fell by 30.3% on average. That comes from a lab benchmark of simulated searches, so read it as a sign of direction. It suggests a smaller site with well-sourced pages can be quoted ahead of a bigger one. The glossary entry for GEO has the one-line version.

Is GEO just another name for AEO?

For practical purposes, yes. AEO came from the SEO industry and GEO from academic research, and both now describe getting cited in answers written by AI. Some writers use GEO for chat tools and AEO for Google's answer boxes, but the industry has settled on no firm line, and the work for a small business is identical under either label.

A few other acronyms circulate. AIO stands for either AI Overviews or "AI optimisation". LLMO means large language model optimisation. Vendors coin new ones regularly, often to name a product. A useful test for any acronym in a proposal: ask which engines it targets and how results will be measured. If the answers match AEO, it is AEO.

This page uses AEO as the umbrella term and GEO when referring to the research, which is how most practitioners write about it.

Where do SEO, AEO and GEO overlap?

They overlap on almost everything a small business does first. Crawlable pages, a clear page for each service, honest answers to real questions, matching business details and steady reviews count towards all three. Google says AI Overviews need nothing beyond core SEO, so for Google's own AI the overlap is close to total.

Google is direct about this. Google Search Central's guidance on AI features says there is no special schema.org structured data, AI text file or markup needed to appear in AI Overviews or AI Mode, and no requirements beyond core SEO. That is a fair statement for Google's products, and owners should take it at face value: good SEO is the entry ticket to AI Overviews.

The engines outside Google draw on other indexes, and the overlap thins there. Ahrefs' 2025 analysis of 15,000 prompts found only 12% of URLs cited by ChatGPT, Gemini and Copilot ranked in Google's top 10 for the same prompt, and 28.6% for Perplexity. Even inside Google, Ahrefs' March 2026 update found 37.9% of pages cited in AI Overviews ranked in the top 10 for that keyword. A page one ranking helps, and plenty of cited pages sit well below it.

Which tasks serve which discipline?

Most tasks serve all three disciplines at once, and a handful serve only one. Sorting the work this way stops a business paying twice for the same job under different names. The table below lists the common tasks for a 5 to 50 person business and marks where each one pays off.

TaskSEOAEO and GEO

Get indexed in Google Search ConsoleYesYes: feeds AI Overviews, AI Mode and Gemini

Get indexed in Bing Webmaster ToolsSmall share of searchesYes: feeds ChatGPT search and Copilot

Allow OAI-SearchBot and PerplexityBot in robots.txtNo effectYes

One page per service and areaYesYes

Open each page with a 40 to 60 word answerHelps featured snippetsYes: gives engines a passage to quote

Add statistics, quotes and sources to pagesHelps trustYes: the best-tested GEO methods

Google Business Profile and Bing PlacesYes: local results and MapsYes: local AI recommendations

Reviews and mentions on other sitesYesYes: strongest correlation with AI visibility

Backlink buildingYesWeaker link than brand mentions

LocalBusiness and Organization schemaRich resultsOptional for Google AI; makes facts machine-readable

The tasks that sit only on the AI side are short: Bing indexing, AI crawler rules and the prompt log. They take an afternoon between them. Flow AI's free AI crawler access check covers the crawler rules, and the AEO checklist lists every task in order.

Which should a small business prioritise first?

Most small businesses should fix the SEO basics first, then add the AEO tasks that happen off Google, then refine pages with GEO methods. The right mix depends on how customers buy. A local trade lives on Google Maps and reviews. A consultancy whose buyers research for weeks gains more from pages that AI tools can quote.

Type of businessThe first 10 hoursThe next 10 hours

Local service (trades, clinics, salons, hospitality)Google Business Profile, Bing Places, matching details on NZ directories, a review request routineOne page per service and suburb, each opening with a direct answer

Considered purchase or B2B service (accountants, consultants, builders of new homes)Pages answering pricing, comparison and "who is this for" questions, with sources and numbersMentions on industry bodies, podcasts and partner sites; a monthly prompt log

Online shopProduct pages with full specifications and prices, indexed in Google and BingBuying guides that answer comparison questions; reviews on product pages

New business with no rankingsIndexing in both consoles, a clear About page, AI crawler accessDirectory listings and a first set of reviews

Buying-intent searches are where AI answers increasingly appear. Semrush's study of more than 10 million US desktop keywords found commercial, transactional and navigational queries made up 42.8% of AI Overview triggers by October 2025, when in January informational queries had made up 91.3% of them. For a business that sells, that is the reason to start now. InternetNZ's late 2025 survey of 1,003 New Zealand adults found 55% had used AI in search engines in the past year, so the habit is already local.

The tools are public. The free agent templates include the AI crawler check and a full GEO audit, and the open-source GEO skills are in the skill library for anyone who prefers to run them in-house.

The short version

SEO ranks your pages. AEO gets your business named in AI answers. GEO is the research term for that same AI goal, and the two are used interchangeably. Most of the work is shared, and Google says its AI Overviews need nothing beyond core SEO.

The extra AI work is small and mostly off Google: Bing indexing, AI crawler access, reviews and mentions, and a monthly check of what the engines say. Do the shared basics first, then add those.

To see which of the three needs attention first on your site, request a free audit.

Q: Do I need to choose between SEO, AEO and GEO?
A: No choice is needed, because most of the work counts for all three. Indexable pages, clear answers to customer questions, consistent business details and reviews help you rank in Google and get named by ChatGPT. The only real decision is order. For most small businesses, fix the SEO basics first, then add the AEO work that happens off Google, such as Bing indexing and AI crawler access.
Q: Is GEO just a rebrand of AEO?
A: Close to it. AEO is the older industry term, first used for featured snippets and voice assistants. GEO comes from a 2024 research paper by Aggarwal and colleagues that tested how to get content cited by AI engines that write answers. The two now describe the same goal, and practitioners use them interchangeably. Pick one term inside your business and use it consistently.
Q: Will Google AI Overviews replace SEO?
A: AI Overviews run on Google's search index, and Google says the requirements to appear in them are the same as core SEO. So SEO feeds AI Overviews directly. What is shrinking is the click: Pew Research found Google users clicked a traditional result on 8% of visits with an AI summary, against 15% without one. Ranking still matters, and being cited in the summary matters more than it did.
Q: What is AIO, and how does it differ from AEO?
A: AIO is used two ways: as short for AI Overviews, Google's AI summaries, and as short for AI optimisation, another name for the same work as AEO and GEO. Vendors coin new acronyms often, and few of them describe new work. If a proposal uses AIO, ask which engines it targets and how results will be measured. The answers matter more than the label.
Q: Can I do AEO without doing SEO?
A: Only partly. Reviews, directory listings and mentions on other sites help in AI answers whether or not your own site ranks. But AI engines fetch pages from search indexes, so if Google and Bing cannot crawl and index your site, the engines have less of your own material to quote. A site with the basic SEO done gives every AEO task a firmer base.
Q: Which is cheaper for a small business, SEO or AEO?
A: The first round of each costs mostly owner time. Many AEO tasks, such as allowing AI crawlers, claiming Bing Places and rewriting page openings as direct answers, take an afternoon each with free tools. Ongoing SEO costs more because pages and links take months to build. Because the work overlaps, doing both together usually costs less than treating them as separate projects.

## The AEO checklist for small business (2026).
URL: https://www.flowai.co.nz/blog/aeo-checklist.html
Author: Amber Lan, Flow AI
Updated: 2026-10-02

Short answer: An AEO checklist for a small business covers six areas: open your site to AI crawlers, publish consistent facts about the business, write pages that answer customer questions directly, earn reviews and mentions elsewhere, add accurate structured data, and track what AI engines say about you. Most owners can work through it in a week.

How to use this checklist

Work through the six groups in order, one or two a day, and tick each item off when it is done. The order matters: AI engines cannot quote a site they cannot read, and they trust facts that match across the web. The first two groups take about a day between them, and the rest fill the week.

The checklist is written for a 5 to 50 person business with a website, a Google Business Profile or the intention of one, and nobody on staff who writes code. Where a task needs a developer, it says so. If the terms are new, start with what answer engine optimisation is, and if you are unsure how AEO relates to the SEO you already do, read AEO vs SEO vs GEO.

DayGroupItemsRough time

MondayAccess for AI crawlers1 to 42 to 3 hours

TuesdayFacts about the business5 to 83 to 4 hours

Wednesday and ThursdayPages that answer9 to 13A day and a half

Friday morningProof and mentions14 to 162 hours to set up, then monthly

Friday afternoonStructured data and measurement17 to 203 hours

The times are estimates for a site of ten to thirty pages. A larger site takes longer on the page work, and nothing else changes.

Access for AI crawlers (items 1 to 4)

Access comes first because every later item depends on it. An AI engine answers from pages it has fetched, either through its own crawler or through a search index such as Google's or Bing's. If robots.txt, a firewall or JavaScript rendering stops those crawlers, nothing else on this list can help.

1. Allow the AI search crawlers in robots.txt

Open yourdomain.co.nz/robots.txt and look for rules that block OAI-SearchBot and ChatGPT-User (ChatGPT), PerplexityBot (Perplexity), Claude-SearchBot and Claude-User (Claude), Googlebot and Bingbot. A line such as "User-agent: * Disallow: /" blocks all of them. Training crawlers (GPTBot, ClaudeBot, Google-Extended) are a separate choice, and blocking them does not stop the search crawlers when each is named on its own line. Flow AI's free AI crawler access check tests fourteen AI crawlers at once.

2. Check your host and security settings

Some hosts, CDNs and security plugins offer settings that block AI bots, and on some plans these are switched on by default. Look in your Cloudflare, Wix, Squarespace or WordPress security settings for anything labelled AI bots, AI crawlers or bot fight mode. Also ask your web person whether any page sends a "noindex" meta tag or an X-Robots-Tag header by mistake.

3. Make sure your text is in the HTML

Many AI crawlers do not run JavaScript, so text that appears only after scripts load may never be seen. A quick test: open a page, choose View Page Source in your browser, and search for a sentence from the page. If it is missing from the source, ask your developer about server-side rendering for your main pages.

4. Get indexed in Google and Bing

Verify your site in Google Search Console and Bing Webmaster Tools, submit your sitemap to both, and check that your main pages show as indexed. Bing Webmaster Tools can import a verified site straight from Search Console in a few clicks. Bing matters more than its share suggests: OpenAI's help page on ChatGPT search says it sends queries to partner search providers and names Microsoft (Bing) among them, even though Statcounter puts Bing at 7.71% of New Zealand search in September 2026.

Facts about the business (items 5 to 8)

AI engines describe a business by assembling facts from its site, its listings and other people's pages. When those facts agree, the engine can state them with confidence. When the address, services or hours differ between sites, it may describe you wrongly or leave you out. This group makes every source say the same thing.

5. Write a one-page fact sheet

List the facts an AI would need to recommend you: legal and trading name, what you do in one sentence, services, service area by suburb or city, hours, typical price ranges, licences and memberships, year founded, and the owner's name. Put the same facts on your About page in plain sentences. This document becomes the source of truth for items 6 to 8 and 17.

6. Match your name, address and phone everywhere

Search your business name and check every listing against the fact sheet: same spelling, same address format, same phone number. The glossary calls this NAP consistency. Fix old addresses from past premises first, since those cause the most confusion.

7. Complete Google Business Profile and Bing Places

Fill every field in your Google Business Profile: categories, services with descriptions, hours, holiday hours, photos and the business description. Then claim Bing Places for Business, which can import from Google. ChatGPT treats "near me" prompts as local searches, and these listings are what local searches read.

8. Claim the directories your customers use

In New Zealand that usually means Yellow, Finda and NZ Business Directory, plus trade sites such as NoCowboys and Builderscrack where they fit. In Australia, Yellow Pages, True Local and hipages. Add your industry association's member directory. Five accurate listings beat twenty half-finished ones. The local groundwork is covered in more depth in SEO for small business in New Zealand.

Pages that answer (items 9 to 13)

AI engines quote passages, so pages need sentences that answer a question on their own. This group turns your most important pages into answers: a direct opening, headings phrased as customer questions, facts with sources, and pages for the questions buyers ask before they call. It is the longest group and the one that keeps paying back.

9. Open each important page with a direct answer

Start your home page, service pages and pricing page with a 40 to 60 word paragraph that answers the page's main question completely. "We install heat pumps across Hamilton and Waikato, usually within a week of quoting..." gives an engine a sentence it can lift. Put the welcome message and the history lower down.

10. Phrase headings as the questions customers ask

Collect real questions from your inbox, phone calls, quote requests and Google's "People also ask" boxes. Turn the most common into H2 headings ("How long does a bathroom renovation take?") and answer each in the first sentence below it. Customers' own words are the best keywords you have.

11. Add numbers, quotes and sources

The research behind GEO tested this directly. Aggarwal and colleagues' KDD 2024 paper found adding quotations, adding statistics and citing sources each improved visibility in AI answers by 30 to 40%, while keyword stuffing offered little to no improvement. On your pages, that means real price ranges, timeframes, a quote from a named person, and links to the standards or regulations you work to.

12. Publish the pages buyers ask AI about

Write a page for each question buyers ask before they choose: what it costs and what changes the price, how you compare with the alternatives, who the service suits and who it does not, and one page per service per area. These are buying questions, and Semrush's study of more than 10 million US keywords found commercial, transactional and navigational queries made up 42.8% of AI Overview triggers by October 2025.

13. Date your pages and keep them current

Show a "last updated" date on guides and pricing pages, and refresh the figures when they change. Set a calendar reminder to review your top five pages every six months. Out-of-date prices on your own site can end up repeated in AI answers.

Proof and mentions (items 14 to 16)

AI engines weigh what other people say about a business alongside what it says about itself. Reviews, local press, association listings and videos give an engine independent evidence. This group sets up the habits that build that evidence month by month, since none of it can be finished in a single day.

14. Ask for reviews every month and reply to them

Recency matters to customers and to the engines that read reviews. BrightLocal's Local Consumer Review Survey 2026, of 1,002 US adults, found 74% look for reviews written in the last three months, and 31% will only use a business rated 4.5 stars or higher. Send a review link with every finished job and reply to every review, good or bad. BrightLocal sells local SEO software and the sample is American, but the habit holds anywhere.

15. Earn mentions on other sites

Aim for one new mention a month: a local news story, a supplier's case study, a podcast, a "best of" roundup, an industry association feature. An Ahrefs study of 75,000 brands found branded web mentions had the strongest correlation with AI Overview visibility (0.664), well ahead of backlinks (0.218). Ahrefs sells SEO tools and this is a correlation, but it is the clearest signal available. The guide on how to get your business mentioned by ChatGPT goes deeper on this item.

16. Put two or three short videos on YouTube

Film answers to your most common questions on a phone, two to four minutes each, with your business name and area in the title and description. Ahrefs' March 2026 analysis of 4 million AI Overview URLs found YouTube was the most cited domain, at 5.6% of all citations. A short video also gives customers a reason to trust you before they call.

Structured data (items 17 and 18)

Structured data restates your business facts in a format machines read without guessing. Google says it is not required to appear in AI Overviews, and it is fair to take that at face value. It still earns rich results in Google search and removes doubt about names, addresses and services, so it is worth an afternoon.

17. Add LocalBusiness or Organization schema

Add one block of schema markup to your home page with the facts from item 5: name, address, phone, hours, area served, and "sameAs" links to your Google Business Profile, Facebook, LinkedIn and directory listings. Most website builders and SEO plugins have a form for this. Test it with Google's Rich Results Test and the Schema.org validator. Google's guidance on AI features is clear that no special schema is needed for AI Overviews or AI Mode, so treat this as tidy housekeeping.

18. Mark up FAQs, products and articles only where they match the page

Add FAQPage markup to pages with a real question and answer section, Product markup to product pages, and Article markup to guides. Google now shows FAQ rich results for only a small set of authoritative sites, so add FAQ markup to make the questions and answers explicit, and expect no visual change in results. Markup that describes content the page does not show breaks Google's guidelines.

Measurement (items 19 and 20)

Measure AEO with simple habits while the tools mature. No dashboard yet reports AI visibility as reliably as Search Console reports Google rankings, so a monthly prompt log and a few analytics settings give the clearest picture. Judge the trend over three months, because AI answers vary from one run to the next.

19. Run a monthly prompt log

Write 15 to 20 questions a customer would ask, such as "best physio for running injuries in Christchurch" or "how much does a kitchen renovation cost in Auckland". Run them each month in ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini and Google, and log whether you are named, who else is, and which pages are cited. Use a fresh chat each time so earlier conversations do not colour the answer.

20. Track AI referrals and ask customers

In Google Analytics 4, build a report for referrals from chatgpt.com, perplexity.ai, gemini.google.com and copilot.microsoft.com. Add "an AI assistant like ChatGPT" to the "how did you hear about us?" question on forms and in phone scripts. BrightLocal's 2026 research found 88% of people who use AI for local recommendations check the sources it cites, so many AI-influenced customers will arrive through your listings, and only asking reveals them.

Is llms.txt worth adding?

An llms.txt file is an optional extra, and it belongs after the twenty items above. It is a plain text file at the root of your site that lists your most useful pages for AI systems. It takes ten minutes to write, but no major AI provider has said it uses llms.txt to choose what to cite.

The usage data is thin. Ahrefs' June 2026 study of 137,210 domains found 28% publish a valid llms.txt file, yet 97% of those files received zero requests in a month, and AI retrieval bots made only 1.1% of the requests that did arrive. Ahrefs' sample skews to sites with analytics installed, so it is not a random sample of the web. Flow AI publishes one because it costs nothing to maintain. Add one if you like, and expect nothing from it yet. The glossary entry for llms.txt explains the format.

Where Flow AI fits

Flow AI is an AI marketing transformation practice: the strategy, the systems and the agents that run a marketing function, engineered end to end. The free audit works through this checklist on your site and names the first system to install, which for many businesses is the AI search sprint.
