The short version

Open your site to AI crawlers and get indexed in Google and Bing. Make your business facts match everywhere. Rewrite your main pages so each opens with a direct answer and backs its claims with numbers and sources. Then build reviews and mentions every month, add accurate schema, and log what the engines say.

The first two groups take a day and protect everything else. The rest compound, and every item helps in ordinary Google search too. For the full background, read the guide to answer engine optimisation.

To have the checklist run on your site and the first fix named, request a free audit.

Q: Do I need to do all 20 items to see results?
A: No. The first four, covering crawler access and indexing in Google and Bing, matter most, because an engine that cannot read your site cannot quote it. After that, the Google Business Profile, a fact sheet and answer-first openings on your top five pages give the biggest return for the time. The rest compound over months, so spread them out rather than skipping them.
Q: How is an AEO checklist different from an SEO checklist?
A: About two thirds of the tasks are the same, because AI engines search indexes built by search engines. The AEO-only tasks are allowing AI search crawlers such as OAI-SearchBot and PerplexityBot, getting indexed in Bing for ChatGPT and Copilot, writing passages that make sense when quoted alone, and logging what AI engines say about you each month. An SEO checklist rarely covers those.
Q: Should I block GPTBot and other AI training crawlers?
A: That is a separate decision from AEO. Training crawlers such as GPTBot and Google-Extended collect content to train models, while search crawlers such as OAI-SearchBot fetch pages to answer questions live. Many businesses allow the search crawlers and make their own choice on training. Blocking a training crawler does not stop the matching search crawler, as long as robots.txt names them separately.
Q: Does schema markup help with AI search?
A: Google says no special schema is needed to appear in AI Overviews or AI Mode. Schema still earns rich results in Google and states your business facts in a form any machine can read without guessing, so it is worth adding for your organisation, location and products. Keep it accurate and matched to what the page says, because wrong schema does more harm than none.
Q: How often should I repeat the AEO checklist?
A: Run the access checks every quarter and after any website rebuild, host change or new security plugin, because those are the moments crawlers get blocked by accident. Repeat the prompt log monthly. Review the fact sheet whenever prices, hours or services change, and refresh your most important pages at least twice a year so the dates and figures stay current.
Q: Is there a free tool to check AI crawler access?
A: Yes. Flow AI's free AI crawler access check tests fourteen AI crawlers against your robots.txt, page tags and server headers and gives the fix for any that are blocked. You can also read your robots.txt directly at yourdomain.co.nz/robots.txt, and check indexing in Google Search Console and Bing Webmaster Tools, both free.

## What is an AI marketing agent? A definition for small business.
URL: https://www.flowai.co.nz/blog/what-is-an-ai-marketing-agent.html
Author: Amber Lan, Flow AI
Updated: 2026-09-10

Short answer: An AI marketing agent is software that reads your business, decides what marketing to do next, produces the work across several channels and ships it under a human's review. A tool waits to be prompted one task at a time. An agent holds a goal, chooses its next task and reports what changed.

Why the term needs a small business definition

    An AI marketing agent is software that runs marketing work rather than assisting with it. The term needs a small business definition because the existing ones do not have one in mind: they describe a capability layer for a team that already has marketers, budgets and a CRM, which is not the reader who most needs the answer.

    The pattern in the existing pages is clear. IBM frames agentic AI for CMOs and enterprise decision makers. Zapier frames it as something a marketing team builds itself. Creatio's glossary entry sits inside a CRM platform's vocabulary. All three are accurate, and none answers what a plumbing company with eleven staff is asking: does this thing do the marketing, or just help somebody do it faster.

    So this page defines the category from the buyer's side. The guide to AI marketing for small business covers the wider context, and the cost guide for Australia and New Zealand covers the money.

    What is an AI marketing agent?

    An AI marketing agent is software that plans and produces marketing work across several channels and then ships it under human review. Unlike a tool that waits to be prompted, an agent holds a goal, chooses its own next task, uses the business's own systems to do it, and reports what it did and what changed.

    An AI marketing agent is software that reads your business, decides what marketing to do next, produces the work across several channels, and ships it under a human's review, instead of waiting for a person to prompt it one task at a time.

    Three properties separate an agent from everything else with AI in the name. It is goal-held: given an outcome, such as more enquiries from local search, not a task list. It is connected: it reads and writes to the real website, inbox, CRM and analytics. And it is persistent: it keeps a record of the business and its own past work, so the second month builds on the first.

    What it is not is an autonomous marketing department. The word agent now covers chatbots, prompt libraries and single-task scripts, and a business that buys a prompt library expecting a department gets neither. The test: if a person starts the work each week it is a tool, and if the work starts on its own and a person reviews it, it is an agent.

    Why AI marketing agents matter now

    Agents matter now because small business AI use has crossed from experiment to normal while agent-shaped AI is still rare. Around half of small firms in Australia and New Zealand already use AI in some form, but very few use anything that runs work on its own, which is where the advantage sits.

    The adoption numbers are no longer arguable. MYOB's April 2026 Business Monitor, surveying more than 1,000 Australian SMEs, found 40% currently using AI and those businesses growing 2.8 times faster than the ones that are not. In New Zealand, Xero's May 2026 research puts 61% of small and medium businesses proactively using AI, with 79% of them learning through self-guided experimentation. The trend is not local: the U.S. Chamber of Commerce recorded 58% of small businesses on generative AI, up from 40%.

    The second number is the interesting one. Salesforce's tenth State of Marketing report, from 4,450 marketers including 890 in the SMB segment, found only 13% of marketers using agentic AI, while 80% of SMB marketers expect AI agents to improve their marketing return.

    Depth matters more than presence. Deloitte Access Economics, from a survey of 1,000 Australian SMBs, associates moving from basic to intermediate AI use with roughly 45% higher profitability, and intermediate to fully enabled with a further 111%. Self-guided experimentation is the basic tier, and an agent is one route out of it.

    How an AI marketing agent works

    An AI marketing agent works as a repeating five-step loop: it reads the business, plans the month, executes across departments, reports what happened, and waits for a human review before anything reaches a customer. The loop repeats with that review folded back in, which is what makes the second month better than the first.

    
      It reads the business. The website, services, prices, customer list, analytics, the search terms people already use, and the competitors ranking above it. Most tools skip this, which is why generic AI output reads as generic.

      It plans. From that reading it writes a plan: which marketing job is most broken, what to do first, and what the result should look like. A plan is testable, and an owner can disagree with it in five minutes.

      It executes across departments. The approved plan becomes work in several lanes at once: pages and schema for search, articles for content, posts for social, sequences for outbound, tests for conversion.

      It reports. Each cycle ends with what shipped, what moved, what did not, and what it recommends next. Reporting is the only way an owner can hold software accountable, and its absence means the product is not an agent.

      A human reviews. Nothing goes out under the business's name unreviewed. The review is small, usually under an hour a week, and it is where judgment enters: what to claim, what to promise, what to kill.

    
    One example. A trades business wants more local enquiries. The agent reads the site, finds no service pages for three of the six suburbs it covers, drafts them from the existing pricing and guarantees, and adds the local schema and tracking.

    The ten marketing jobs an AI marketing agent covers

    A complete AI marketing agent covers ten marketing jobs: positioning, search and AI search, content, social, outbound, growth and conversion, launch, community, paid and data, and measurement. Most products sold as agents cover one or two well. The number of jobs covered is the fastest way to tell a feature from a department.

    
      Marketing jobWhat the agent does in it

      
        PositioningWrites down what the business claims and who it is for, so every lane says the same thing.

        Search and AI searchBuilds the pages, structure and schema that make a business findable in Google and quotable in AI answers.

        ContentProduces the guides and service pages that carry the positioning and earn the search demand.

        SocialTurns each piece of content into platform-native posts on a schedule.

        OutboundBuilds target lists, researches each account, and drafts sequences that reference something real.

        Growth and conversionFixes the path from visit to enquiry: forms, offers, page speed, follow-up timing, and the tests behind them.

        LaunchSequences a new service or price change across channels so it lands as one moment.

        CommunityFinds the forums and threads where the business's customers ask questions, and answers them.

        Paid and dataSets up tracking that survives, reads what the spend returned, and says where the next dollar goes.

        MeasurementReports enquiries, sources and cost per enquiry each cycle, and names what to stop.

      
    
    Nobody needs all ten in month one, and the order matters more than the count: positioning before content, content before social, tracking before paid. Flow AI's installable departments follow that order, with search and AI search the usual first install.

    AI marketing agent vs marketing automation vs ChatGPT vs an agency

    The four options differ on one axis: who decides and who executes. General AI tools have a human deciding and a human executing with help. Marketing automation has a human deciding and software executing rules. An agency has humans doing both. An agent proposes the decisions and executes the work, with a human approving.

    
      CriterionAI marketing agentMarketing automationGeneral AI toolsMarketing agency

      
        Who decidesThe agent proposes, a human approvesA human writes every rule firstThe human, every timeThe agency proposes, the client approves

        Who executesThe agent, several channels at onceThe platform, only what the rules coverThe human, assistedAgency staff, often junior

        What it knows about your businessA durable record: services, prices, customers, past workContact behaviour, not contextWhatever is pasted in the chatWhat the last meeting covered

        What it costs to startOne department installed, then a monthly runA subscription plus every workflow builtA cheap seat plus the owner's hoursA setup fee plus a retainer

        What you keepPages, systems, plan and record, on your own accountsWorkflows, inside that vendorOnly what you savedDeliverables, rarely the process

        Who answers if nothing shipsThe report shows it, the reviewer answersNobody: rules never noticeThe owner, entirelyThe account manager

      
    
    The comparison people get wrong most often is agent against automation. Marketing automation is a delivery layer: it sends the email, moves the contact, waits three days. It has no opinion about whether the email should exist. An agent supplies that opinion and the content, then uses automation to deliver them.

    The comparison people underrate is agent against general AI tools. A general model can write a better paragraph than most agencies. What it cannot do is remember the business next Tuesday, notice that nothing shipped in July, or open the analytics unasked. Continuity was always the constraint.

    What an AI marketing agent must never do without a human

    An AI marketing agent must never publish claims, contact customers, spend money, change prices or delete work without a named human approving it. Autonomy is valuable in production and dangerous at the boundary where work meets a customer, a regulator or a bank account. That boundary is a design decision, not a setting.

    
      Make a claim about the business. Guarantees, credentials, timeframes, licences and pricing are the business's word, not the software's. Consumer law in Australia and New Zealand does not care that a machine wrote the warranty.

      Contact a customer or prospect unreviewed. Sequences, review requests and follow-ups go out under a human name, and the first send is read by a human every time.

      Spend money. Ad budgets, bid changes and tool purchases stay behind an approval. An agent that can move spend needs a hard ceiling and an audit trail first.

      Handle personal data loosely. Customer lists, health information and financial details stay in systems the business controls, with the agent given the narrowest access that works.

      Decide positioning or pricing. An agent can research and recommend both. Choosing what the business is and what it charges is the owner's job.

      Change a live site without a record. Every edit to a page, list or account needs to be reversible, with a log of what changed and why.

    
    None of this makes an agent less useful. It makes the useful part safe to run weekly.

    How to evaluate an AI marketing agent

    Evaluate an AI marketing agent on eight questions: what it reads, what it produces, how many marketing jobs it covers, where the human sits, what you keep, what it reports, who built it, and what happens in month three. A vendor who cannot answer these in plain language is selling a tool with an agent's label on it.

    
      What does it read first? Ask for the input list. If it excludes the website, the analytics and the customer language, the output will be generic and stay that way.

      What does it actually ship? Ask for a real artefact from a real business: a page, a sequence, a report. Screenshots are not output.

      How many of the ten jobs does it cover? One lane done well is a legitimate purchase, as long as it is clear that a social scheduler with an AI writer is a tool.

      Where exactly does the human sit? Get the approval points named. If nothing needs approval the product is not safe; if everything does, it is a slower way of doing it yourself.

      What do you keep if you leave? Pages, schema, tracking and content should live on the business's own accounts. Anything that evaporates on cancellation was rented.

      What is in the monthly report? Enquiries, sources, cost per enquiry, what shipped and what to stop. Follower counts are not a report.

      Who built it, and do they do the work? Ask what the builder has shipped for a business your size. Flow AI's open skill library is one form of that answer.

      What happens in month three? The honest answer involves a plateau and a decision about the next department, not a straight line up.

    
    The free AI-readiness benchmark names the department to fix first.

    Where Flow AI fits in this category

    Flow AI is an AI marketing transformation practice: the strategy, the systems and the agents that run a marketing function, engineered end to end. It was built by a marketing engineer rather than assembled by a platform team, and it runs the eleven departments above as installable systems that stay on the business's own domain and accounts. A human reviews everything before it ships, which is a design rule rather than a plan setting.

    It starts with a free audit: a written plan on the business, produced before any money changes hands, naming the first department and why. The departments available today are on the sprints page.

The short version

    An AI marketing agent reads the business, plans the work, produces it across several channels and ships it under review. It is not a faster chatbot and not a cheaper agency. It is the first way a business with no marketing department can have marketing that runs every week without the owner starting it.

    Before an agent, small business marketing happened in the gaps, which is why it stopped every time the business got busy. After one, production runs on a system and the month ends with a report rather than an apology. With only 13% of marketers using agentic AI while 61% of New Zealand businesses already use AI somewhere, moving from tools to a system this year is being early on purpose.

    To see which of the ten marketing jobs to install first, request a free audit.

Q: Is ChatGPT an AI marketing agent?
A: No. ChatGPT is a general AI tool: it produces work when a person prompts it, and it stops when the person stops. An AI marketing agent holds a goal, decides the next task itself, works across several channels on a schedule, and reports what it did. A general tool is one of the things an agent uses, not a substitute for one.
Q: Does my small business need an AI marketing agent?
A: A business needs an agent when marketing has to run every week across more than one channel and nobody inside the business has the hours to run it. Below that, a general AI tool and one tightly scoped freelancer is cheaper. The clearest signal is a month where nothing shipped because the owner was busy serving customers.
Q: What is the difference between an AI marketing agent and marketing automation?
A: Marketing automation executes rules a human wrote: if a contact fills this form, send that email. An AI marketing agent decides what the work should be, produces it, then uses automation to deliver it. Automation is the delivery layer and it needs a person to design every branch; an agent supplies the plan and the content that fill those branches.
Q: Can an AI marketing agent replace a marketing agency?
A: It replaces the production hours, not the judgment or the relationship. An agent can research, write, build, schedule and report at a volume a small retainer cannot fund. It cannot sit in a room with a founder, negotiate a sponsorship, or take responsibility for a brand decision.
Q: Is an AI CMO the same thing as an AI marketing agent?
A: They overlap and the labels are used loosely. AI CMO usually describes the planning and prioritising half: what to work on, in what order, against which numbers. AI marketing agent describes the whole loop, planning plus production plus shipping plus reporting. A product sold as an AI CMO that produces no work is a planner, and should be judged as one.
Q: Is it safe to let an AI agent run marketing?
A: It is safe when three limits are set before anything runs: a named human approves anything published under the business name, the agent has no authority to spend money or contact customers unreviewed, and every action is logged so a decision can be traced and reversed. Without those limits the risk is not bad content, it is unreviewed claims and unhappy customers.

## AI marketing transformation for small business: the 90-day roadmap
URL: https://www.flowai.co.nz/blog/ai-marketing-transformation-small-business.html
Author: Amber Lan, Flow AI
Updated: 2026-10-02

Short answer: AI marketing transformation for a small business is the move from marketing done in spare hours to marketing run by systems, one job at a time. A practical 90-day path fixes positioning and measurement first, then search and content, then social and outbound, with a human approving everything that reaches a customer.

Why AI marketing transformation stalls before it starts

    AI marketing transformation stalls because most small businesses buy tools before deciding what the business claims, who it sells to and how success is counted. The tools then produce more of the wrong work, faster. A transformation that holds runs in phases: fix the inputs, install two departments, then compound.

    The pattern is visible in the adoption data. In Australia, the National AI Centre's adoption tracker for December 2025 to February 2026 found content generation and data analytics leading, each used by 54% of SME adopters. Marketing is where small businesses reach for AI first, and content is what they point it at.

    That is the wrong end of the department. Content sits downstream of positioning, the offer, and a decision about which customers matter. Point a content engine at a business that has not written down its own claim and it produces a month of fluent, generic pages.

    The reader here is the owner or marketing lead of a business with one to fifty staff in Australia or New Zealand. If the prior question is what AI marketing covers at all, the guide to AI marketing for small business maps the systems. This page is the order of operations.

    What is AI marketing transformation, and how long does it take?

    AI marketing transformation is the rebuild of a marketing department so AI does the production and a human keeps the judgment. For a small business it takes about 90 days: 30 days on positioning, brand facts and measurement, 30 days installing the first two departments, and 30 days making the output compound.

    AI marketing transformation is the process of moving a marketing department from human production to AI production under human review, one department at a time, so that positioning, search, content, social, outbound and measurement all run on a cadence the owner reviews rather than starts.

    Ninety days is not arbitrary. It is three monthly cycles, the shortest span in which a business can see whether the system survives a busy month. Most self-run marketing dies in month three, when a large job lands and the owner stops shipping.

    What 90 days does not buy is full coverage. Six departments running well takes six to nine months. The goal at day 90 is two departments shipping weekly, a third in setup, and a measurement loop that tells the owner which one to fund next.

    The problem: adoption is high, transformation is rare

    Australian and New Zealand businesses have adopted AI tools quickly and transformed almost nothing. Nine in ten New Zealand organisations use AI in some form, but only 4% say it has changed how their core operations run, and most small businesses are still learning by unguided experiment rather than by a plan.

    The gap between using AI and running on it is the whole problem. Datacom's 2026 AI Index found 91% of New Zealand organisations using some form of AI, while just 4% said AI had transformed their core operations and 81% remained in the exploratory or implementation stages. In Australia, Deloitte's February 2026 State of AI survey found only 28% of Australian respondents had moved 40% or more of their AI pilots into production.

    At the small end the numbers are lower again. The Australian Bureau of Statistics reported around 12% of Australian businesses using AI in 2024-25, with small and micro businesses at around 11%. The same release records something more useful for a roadmap: adoption among innovation-active small businesses ran at 19%, almost five times the rate of small businesses doing no innovation activity.

    Method, not tooling, is the differentiator. Xero's May 2026 research found 61% of Kiwi SMEs proactively using AI but 79% learning through self-guided experimentation, while MYOB's April 2026 data put 40% of Australian SMEs on AI and found them growing 2.8 times faster than the rest. The CMO Survey's 2026 topline report put AI at 24.17% of marketing activity, projected to reach 55.91% within three years, with content creation the top use at 73.9%.

    Phase 1, days 1 to 30: the foundation

    Phase one produces no published marketing. It produces the inputs: one page of positioning, a written set of brand facts, two numbers that count, and a baseline of what the business currently ranks for in search and what AI engines say about it when asked. Nothing installs until those exist.

    This is the phase businesses skip, and skipping it is why month two produces generic output. An AI system inherits whatever the business can articulate. If nobody has written down the claim, the proof and the prices, the system invents plausible substitutes and the owner spends two months editing them out.

    
      Positioning. One page: what the business does, who for, what it claims, what it will not claim, and the three proof points behind the claim. This becomes the source file every other department reads. Flow AI runs it as the positioning sprint.

      Measurement. Pick two numbers, usually qualified enquiries and cost per enquiry, and make sure they are tracked. Fix the analytics before the marketing, or phase three has nothing to judge. The analytics sprint covers the setup.

      Search and AI search. Baseline only. Record what the site ranks for, and what ChatGPT, Claude, Perplexity and Google's AI answers say when asked to recommend a business like yours. Most owners have never checked, and the answer is usually a competitor.

      Content. Inventory what exists and mark what earns traffic or enquiries. Retire the rest. A content engine pointed at forty dead pages will faithfully produce a forty-first.

      Social. Choose one channel where customers actually are and stop posting to the others. One channel weekly beats four monthly, and it halves the review load in phase two.

      Outbound. Clean the customer list and the CRM: deduplicate, fix the fields you would personalise on, record consent. Unglamorous, and the reason phase three either works or does not.

    
    By day 30 nothing has been published, which feels like failure and is not. What exists instead is a set of correct inputs.

    Phase 2, days 31 to 60: the first installs

    Phase two installs two departments and ships real work. For most small businesses those two are search and AI search first, then content, because search is where buyers and AI engines both look for a recommendation and content is what search needs to have something to find.

    Two is the limit. A business with no marketing department cannot absorb six new weekly review loops at once, and the failure mode is not bad output but abandoned output.

    
      Search and AI search. The first install. Fix the technical basics, publish the pages that answer what buyers type and ask, and add the structure AI engines need to quote the site. Flow AI runs this as the AI-search sprint. SparkToro measured 68.01% of Google searches ending without a click across January to April 2026, up from 60.45% in 2024, so being quoted in the answer now beats being tenth in the list.

      Content. The second install. One guide or comparison a week, written against the positioning file from phase one, each answering a question a buyer asks out loud. The content engine sprint covers the cadence and the review step.

      Positioning. Propagate. The phase-one claim goes on the home page, the service pages, the email signature and the proposal template, in the same words. Consistency is what lets AI engines resolve the business as an entity rather than a guess.

      Measurement. Turn on a weekly report that fits one screen: enquiries, source, cost, what shipped. Read it on the same day each week. A report nobody reads is a longer version of no report.

      Social. Repurpose rather than produce. Every guide becomes two or three posts on the one channel chosen in phase one. No new source material, no second review loop.

      Outbound. Hold. Do not send cold sequences off a list that has been clean for two weeks. Outbound amplifies whatever is true about the offer, including the parts that are not ready.

    
    By day 60 the business is publishing weekly, the search baseline has moved, and the owner has a report they read. That is the point at which most owners want to add four more departments, and should not.

    Phase 3, days 61 to 90: making it compound

    Phase three adds the departments that need the first two working, and turns the whole thing into a monthly loop. Outbound goes live because there is now something to point people at, social settles into a cadence, and measurement stops being a report and becomes a monthly decision about what to fund next.

    Compounding is a specific mechanic: each month's output makes the next month's cheaper. Published guides feed outbound. Outbound replies name objections that become the next guides. Search data names the questions worth answering. None of that works in month one because there is nothing to feed on.

    
      Outbound. The third install. Short, researched sequences to a defined list, each linking to a guide that already answers the recipient's likely objection. Flow AI runs it as the outbound sprint, and it is the department that most needs a human on the send button.

      Social. Move from repurposing to a cadence with a point of view: two posts a week on the one channel, one from the content lane and one from what the business learned that week.

      Content. Add the refresh loop. Every published page gets revisited once a quarter against what search and outbound revealed, because updating a page that already ranks is the cheapest traffic there is.

      Search and AI search. Track prompts, not just keywords. Ask the four major engines the ten questions a buyer would ask, monthly, by hand, and record whether the business is named. It takes about an hour.

      Measurement. Convert the weekly report into a monthly decision: which department earned more budget, which to install next, what to stop. Two numbers, one page, one decision.

      Positioning. Revisit the phase-one page with three months of evidence. Buyers will have shown, through what they clicked and replied to, which claim is the real one. Rewrite the file and let the other departments inherit it.

    

    The 90-day roadmap on one table

    The table maps each phase to what changes in the six marketing departments and the outcome that phase should reach. Read it as a sequence rather than a checklist: every row depends on the row above it having been done first.

    
      PhaseDaysWhat changes, by departmentOutcome

      
        1. Foundation1 to 30Positioning: write the one-page claim, proof and exclusions. Measurement: pick two numbers, fix the tracking. Search and AI search: baseline rankings and what AI engines say today. Content: inventory, retire what earns nothing. Social: choose one channel. Outbound: clean the list, record consent.Correct inputs in writing, nothing published yet

        2. First installs31 to 60Search and AI search: first install, technical fixes and answer pages. Content: second install, one guide a week under review. Positioning: propagate the claim everywhere. Measurement: weekly one-screen report. Social: repurpose only. Outbound: hold.Two departments shipping weekly under review

        3. Compounding61 to 90Outbound: third install, researched sequences to a defined list. Social: two posts a week with a point of view. Content: quarterly refresh loop. Search and AI search: monthly prompt tracking. Measurement: monthly funding decision. Positioning: rewrite against buyer evidence.Three departments running, the next install chosen from data

      
    
    The order of the installs is not fixed: a business whose customers all come from referral should install outbound before content. What is fixed is that phase one comes first, and that no more than two departments install at once.

    What stays human in an AI marketing department

    Four things stay human at every stage: what the business claims, what it charges, what it publishes about real customers, and what it sends to a named person. Everything else in a marketing department is production, and production is what AI does well under review.

    That split is not a compromise, it is the design. Business.govt.nz's guidance on implementing AI recommends designating an owner for AI use, setting policies on approved tools and data, starting with a task whose results are easy to review, and remembering that the business stays responsible for the final result. That is a marketing operating model, written by a government agency.

    
      The claim. No AI system should decide what a business promises. It can draft twelve versions and argue for one; a human picks.

      Price. Anything that quotes a number to a customer gets read by a person first.

      Customer stories. Case studies, testimonials and named results are verified with the customer before publication. An AI system will happily produce a plausible one.

      Anything addressed to a person. Outbound and reply drafts get a human read before sending. This is the control that keeps outbound from damaging a brand.

      The stop decision. Knowing when a channel is not working, and turning it off, is judgment. Systems are built to continue.

    
    Roughly two to four hours a week covers all of it for a business of five to fifty staff. That is the real cost of running an AI marketing department, and the line most vendors leave out. The guide to AI marketing cost in Australia and New Zealand prices the rest.

    Five mistakes that stall an AI marketing transformation

    The five failures are consistent across small businesses: starting with content instead of positioning, installing every department at once, running without measurement, treating AI output as finished work, and buying tools instead of building a cadence. Each one is a sequencing error rather than a technology problem.

    
      Starting with content. It is the most visible department and the most downstream. Content produced before positioning is fluent and forgettable, and MYOB's data shows this is exactly where most AU and NZ small businesses point AI first.

      Installing everything at once. Six departments means six review loops in a business that had none. The output does not get worse, it gets ignored, and by week six nothing is reviewed at all.

      Running without measurement. If the two numbers were not tracked in phase one, phase three has no basis for a decision, and the next install gets chosen by whatever the owner read that week.

      Treating output as finished. AI production is a first draft with the research already done. Businesses that publish it unread get caught once, usually on a factual claim about their own pricing.

      Buying tools instead of building a cadence. Four subscriptions is not a transformation. The asset is the weekly loop of produce, review, ship, measure, and it runs on almost any tool stack. Run the free AI-readiness benchmark first, to see which department is actually broken.

    

    Where Flow AI fits in the 90-day roadmap

    Flow AI is an AI marketing transformation practice: the strategy, the systems and the agents that run a marketing function, engineered end to end. It runs the roadmap above as fixed-scope installs of one marketing department at a time, starting with a written free audit naming which department to install first. The owner keeps the four human decisions; Flow does the production and the cadence.

    The free audit is phase one in writing: what the business claims, where marketing is losing, and which of the six departments to fund first. The departments available today are listed on the sprints page, and the methods behind them are published as an open skill library anyone can read or run.

    Flow AI is not the right fit for a business that wants a marketer in the room every day, or one that needs daily bid management on a large media budget. It fits a business of five to fifty staff that has been doing marketing in the gaps and wants it running weekly under review.

The short version

    AI marketing transformation for a small business is a sequencing problem, not a tooling problem. Thirty days on positioning and measurement, thirty on installing search and content, thirty on adding outbound and turning the output into a compounding loop, with four decisions kept human throughout.

    Before this, marketing happened in the gaps between customer work, and the AI in it produced volume nobody could tell apart from a competitor's. After it, two or three departments ship every week against a written claim, the owner reviews rather than produces, and the next install is chosen from a report instead of a hunch. That is the gap the data keeps pointing at: 91% of New Zealand organisations use AI and 4% say it has changed how they operate.

    To get phase one in writing for your business, including which department to install first and why, request a free audit.

Q: Where do I start with AI in marketing?
A: Start with positioning and measurement, not content. Write down what the business claims, who it sells to and which two numbers count, then pick the one department where the business already loses to competitors, usually search and AI search. Install that first, and keep the first month to one department only.
Q: How long does an AI marketing transformation take for a small business?
A: Ninety days is enough to get two marketing departments running on a weekly cadence with a human reviewing the output. Full coverage of positioning, search, content, social, outbound and measurement takes six to nine months. The 90-day mark matters because it is the point at which the system either survives a busy month or quietly stops.
Q: What does an AI transformation roadmap for a marketing department look like?
A: Three phases of 30 days. Days 1 to 30 fix positioning, brand facts and measurement so the AI has correct inputs. Days 31 to 60 install two departments, usually search and AI search plus content, and ship real work. Days 61 to 90 add social and outbound, then set the monthly review that keeps it running.
Q: Do I need to hire anyone to run AI marketing?
A: No, but somebody has to own it. Business.govt.nz advises designating an AI owner and setting policies on approved tools, data and review before rolling anything out. In a small business that owner is usually the founder or an office lead spending two to four hours a week on review and decisions, not a new full-time hire.
Q: What should AI never do in a marketing department?
A: AI should never decide what the business claims, approve a price, publish a customer story nobody verified, or send anything to a named person without a human reading it first. Business.govt.nz makes the same point about accountability: the business stays responsible for the final result, so the output has to be checked.

## AI marketing statistics for Australia and New Zealand, 2026
URL: https://www.flowai.co.nz/blog/ai-marketing-statistics-australia-new-zealand.html
Author: Amber Lan, Flow AI
Updated: 2026-09-10

Short answer: Around half of small and medium businesses in Australia and New Zealand now use AI in some form, but far fewer use it to run marketing work end to end. This page collects 62 figures on adoption, marketing use, AI search and time saved, each linked to its primary source and free to quote with attribution.

Last verified 10 September 2026. Every source below was opened and read before the figure was recorded.

    AI marketing statistics are easy to find and hard to trust. Roundups quote roundups, American survey results get relabelled as global, and the same unsourced percentage travels for two years until nobody can say who measured it. For a business owner in Australia or New Zealand trying to decide whether AI belongs in their marketing, that is worse than no data.

    This page collects the statistics that survive a check. Each one comes from the organisation that ran the survey or published the paper: the Australian Bureau of Statistics, the Reserve Bank of Australia, the Australian Small Business and Family Enterprise Ombudsman, MYOB, Xero, the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment, HubSpot, the Content Marketing Institute, ADMA, Salesforce, the U.S. Chamber of Commerce, Gartner, Bain, Semrush and a peer-reviewed KDD paper.

    Where a widely repeated number could not be confirmed on its original source, it is not here. That is the whole point of the page.

    How many small businesses use AI for marketing?

    In Australia, 40% of small and medium businesses use AI, according to MYOB's April 2026 Business Monitor, while the Australian Bureau of Statistics recorded AI use at about 11% of small and micro businesses in 2024-25. Marketing is the most common use: Salesforce ranks marketing campaign optimisation first among SMB AI use cases.

    The gap between 40% and 11% is not an error. The ABS asks a narrow question about the business as a whole in an official statistical survey; MYOB asks operators whether they use AI tools, which captures a marketer drafting a caption in ChatGPT. Both numbers are real, and a page that quotes only one of them is selling something.

    AI adoption statistics for Australia

    Australian AI adoption is rising quickly from a very low base, and it rises with business size. Official ABS data puts overall business AI use at 12% in 2024-25, against 1% in 2021-22. Industry surveys of operators report higher rates because they count lighter, tool-level use of AI.

    
      StatisticFigureSourceYear

      
        Australian businesses reporting use of AI12%ABS, Characteristics of Australian Business2024-25

        Small and micro businesses using AIAbout 11%ABS media release2024-25

        Medium businesses using AI22%, up from 3% in 2021-22ABS media release2024-25

        Large businesses using AI35%, up from 9% in 2021-22ABS media release2024-25

        Innovation-active small businesses using AI, against small businesses doing no innovation activity19% against 4%ABS media release2024-25

        Highest-adopting industry, information, media and telecommunications38%ABS, Characteristics of Australian Business2024-25

        Australian SMEs using AI40%MYOB Business Monitor2026

        Growth of AI-adopting SMEs against non-adopters2.8 times fasterMYOB Business Monitor2026

        SMEs not using AI and not intending to within 12 months46%MYOB Business Monitor2026

        Medium and large firms reporting AI adoption in some formTwo-thirdsRBA Bulletin, liaison survey of 105 firms2025

        Medium and large firms with no plans to adopt AISlightly less than 10%RBA Bulletin2025

        Employers with at least ten staff concerned about technology and AI replacing work done by people70%ASBFEO Small Business Pulse2025

      
    
    Two things stand out. Innovation activity predicts AI use more strongly than size does at the small end, which suggests adoption is a habit rather than a budget. And the RBA found returns so far are mixed, with few firms reporting material AI-driven productivity gains, so early adoption is not the same as early payoff.

    AI adoption statistics for New Zealand

    New Zealand small business AI adoption looks high when operators are asked directly and low when intent to invest is measured. Xero found 61% of New Zealand small and medium businesses proactively using AI in 2026, while the government's AI strategy records 68% of SMEs with no plans to evaluate or invest in the technology.

    
      StatisticFigureSourceYear

        SMEs who believe AI could be the most significant opportunity since the rise of the internet45%Xero2026

        New Zealand workers who had heard of AI, against those who could clearly explain what it is97% against 34%MBIE, New Zealand's AI Strategy, from Verian's 2024 worker survey2025

      
    
    The Xero segments are the most practical part of the New Zealand data. Explorers, at 44% of businesses, are using AI on individual tasks without changing how the work is organised, which is exactly the pattern that produces activity without results. What the other three groups ask for is training, vetted tools and worked examples, not more capability.

    AI marketing statistics: what marketers actually use it for

    Marketing is the department where AI use is most widespread and least mature. HubSpot found 86.4% of marketing teams using AI in at least a few areas in 2026, and ADMA found 77% of Australian marketers using AI tools at least weekly, but only 13% of those Australian marketers had received formal training.

    
      StatisticFigureSourceYear

    The Salesforce SMB survey covers 26 countries and includes Australia and New Zealand, and it puts marketing campaign optimisation first and content generation second among AI use cases. The U.S. Chamber figures are American, included because they are the longest clean time series anywhere on small business generative AI use, running 23% to 40% to 58% across three years.

    AI search and answer engine statistics

    Search is where AI changes marketing fastest. Gartner predicted traditional search engine volume would fall 25% by 2026, Bain measured 60% of searches ending without a click through to a website, and the KDD 2024 paper that named generative engine optimisation showed content changes can lift visibility in AI answers by up to 40%.

    
      StatisticFigureSourceYear

      
        Predicted fall in traditional search engine volume by 202625%Gartner press release2024

        Consumers relying on AI-written results for at least 40% of their searches80%Bain and Company2025

        Searches that end without the user clicking through to another website60%Bain and Company2025

        Reduction in organic web traffic Bain attributes to AI search15% to 25%Bain and Company2025

        Queries showing a Google AI Overview, January against July6.49% rising to 24.61%Semrush AI Overviews study, 10 million keywords2025

        Zero-click rate for the same keywords before and after an AI Overview appearedFell from 33.75% to 31.53%Semrush AI Overviews study2025

        Visibility gain from generative engine optimisationUp to 40%Aggarwal et al., GEO, KDD 20242024

        Improvement of the best GEO methods over baseline41% on position-adjusted word count and 28% on subjective impressionAggarwal et al., KDD 20242024

        Visibility gain for a source ranked fifth in search from adding quotations99.7%Aggarwal et al., KDD 20242024

        Visibility gain for a source ranked fifth in search from adding statistics97.9%Aggarwal et al., KDD 20242024

        Visibility improvement measured on Perplexity.ai, a live generative engineUp to 37%Aggarwal et al., KDD 20242024

      
    
    Read the GEO paper carefully, because it is the most misquoted source in this field. It reports that citations, quotations and statistics all raise visibility substantially, and that the gains are largest for pages ranked fifth rather than first, which is why a small business page can be lifted into an AI answer above a bigger competitor. It does not report a clean 41% for quotations and 33% for statistics, a pairing that circulates widely and does not appear in the paper. The AI search sprint is built on the findings that do.

    Cost and time statistics for AI marketing

    The most consistent measured benefit of AI in marketing is time, not money. MYOB found 54% of Australian SMEs using AI report saving time and 34% report improved productivity, and HubSpot found roughly a third of marketing teams saving 10 to 14 hours a week with another third saving 15 hours or more.

    
      StatisticFigureSourceYear

      
        Australian SMEs using AI who report saving time54%MYOB Business Monitor, more than 1,000 SMEs, April 20262026

        Australian SMEs using AI who report improved productivity34%MYOB Business Monitor2026

        Australian SME employers with no plans to offer AI training72%MYOB Business Monitor2026

        Marketing teams saving 10 to 14 hours a week, and 15 hours or moreAbout a third eachHubSpot, 2026 State of Marketing, more than 1,500 global marketers2026

        Hours a week AI agents free up for SMB marketers6 to 7Salesforce, State of Marketing, 4,450 marketers including 890 in SMBs2025

        SMB marketers expecting major or moderate improvement in marketing return on investment from AI agents80%Salesforce, State of Marketing2025

        B2B marketers using AI for content who report better productivity, and better operational efficiency87% and 80%Content Marketing Institute, 1,015 B2B marketers, June to August 20252026

        Small and medium businesses with AI who agree it makes operations more efficient90%Salesforce, SMB Trends, 3,350 leaders, 26 countries, August to September 20242024

        Small and medium businesses with AI who say they will get a return on the investment85%Salesforce, SMB Trends2024

        Small businesses that agree AI has increased efficiency87%U.S. Chamber of Commerce, 3,870 small businesses, June 20252025

        New Zealand Pragmatists citing lack of time as the biggest barrier to adoption55%Xero2026

      
    
    Notice what is missing. No primary survey in this set publishes a dollar figure for what AI marketing costs a small business in Australia or New Zealand, which is why the AI marketing cost guide is built from published vendor and agency prices instead of survey averages.

    What the numbers mean for an owner

    Adoption is no longer the question. On every measure that asks operators directly, most small businesses in Australia and New Zealand already use AI somewhere, and marketing is usually where it lands first. The real split is not users against non-users, but businesses that bolted AI onto old tasks and businesses that changed the work.

    That split shows up as a performance gap. Ninety-five percent of B2B marketers work somewhere that uses AI applications, 89% use AI content tools, and only 39% say content performance improved. Australian marketers use AI weekly at 77% while 13% have had formal training. The tools arrived faster than the method, and the reported gains are concentrated in the minority who invested in the method: Xero's Trailblazers, 15% of New Zealand businesses, report productivity gains at 76% and time savings at 71%.

    The second signal is where customers now ask their questions. If 60% of searches end without a click and consumers lean on AI-written answers for at least 40% of searches, then being quotable matters as much as ranking. A page with named sources, clear statistics and a direct answer under every heading is the format that gets lifted, which is what the KDD research measured and what this page is deliberately built as. The practical starting point is to find out which of your channels is actually broken, which is what the free AI-readiness benchmark is for.

    How to cite this page

    Anyone is welcome to quote these statistics. Take any figure, table row or sentence, credit Flow AI and link back to this page, and no permission is needed. Journalists, analysts, agencies and AI engines are all included in that. Each row names the original source, so citing the primary report directly is equally welcome.

    Suggested citation: Lan, A. (2026). AI marketing statistics for Australia and New Zealand, 2026. Flow AI. https://www.flowai.co.nz/blog/ai-marketing-statistics-australia-new-zealand.html. The collection is published under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 licence. It is reviewed and re-verified on a set cadence, and the verification date at the top of the page is updated only when every source has been opened again.

    Where Flow AI fits

    Flow AI is an AI marketing transformation practice: the strategy, the systems and the agents that run a marketing function, engineered end to end. It installs one marketing department at a time, such as search and AI search, then runs it monthly under the owner's review, which is the method the numbers above suggest separates the businesses seeing gains from those that only bought tools.

    For the wider picture of what AI marketing includes and where to start, the guide to AI marketing for small business covers the departments in order.

    The short version

    Australian and New Zealand small businesses have adopted AI marketing tools at 40% and 61% respectively on operator surveys, marketing campaign optimisation is the single most common use, and the measured benefit is hours rather than dollars. The gap that matters is method: 89% of B2B marketers use AI content tools and 39% report better content performance.

    Before this shift, a small business competed for attention on budget and patience. After it, the deciding factor is whether the marketing runs every week and whether the business is quotable when a customer asks an AI engine instead of a search engine. Both are engineering problems, not spending problems.

    To see which department to install first, and what the numbers on your own channels look like, request a free audit.



## How much does AI marketing cost in Australia and New Zealand? (2026)
URL: https://www.flowai.co.nz/blog/ai-marketing-cost-australia-new-zealand.html
Author: Amber Lan, Flow AI
Updated: 2026-09-10

Short answer: In 2026, AI marketing for a small business costs USD 20 to 99 a month per tool if you do the work yourself, NZD 60 to 150 an hour from a freelancer, NZD 1,500 to 10,000 a month from an agency, or NZD 90,000 to 130,000 a year for an in-house hire. AI marketing agents sit between the tool and the agency.

Why AI marketing pricing is hard to compare

    AI marketing cost is hard to compare because the five ways of buying it are priced on different units: software by the seat, freelancers by the hour, agencies by the monthly retainer, staff by the salary, and AI marketing agents by the install and the month. This guide puts all five on one table, in AUD and NZD, from published 2026 sources.

    The market does not make it easy. In a June 2026 audit of 140 Australian agencies, Digital Nomads HQ found that 78% publish no prices at all. New Zealand has fewer published guides again, and most of the ones that exist are written by agencies pricing their own work.

    The reader here is the owner or marketing lead of a business with one to fifty staff, in Australia or New Zealand, who wants marketing to run every week without buying a whole department. Every figure below links to the page it came from, with the currency named. Where a number could not be sourced, the cell says so rather than guessing.

    If the broader question is what AI marketing includes in the first place, the guide to AI marketing for small business covers the four systems and where to start. This page is only about the money.

    What does AI marketing cost in Australia and New Zealand?

    In 2026, AI marketing costs USD 20 to 99 a month per tool done yourself, AUD 80 to 200 or NZD 60 to 150 an hour from a freelancer, AUD 800 to 6,000 or NZD 1,500 to 10,000 a month from an agency, and AUD 105,000 to 130,000 or NZD 90,000 to 130,000 a year for an in-house hire.

    AI marketing agents and platforms sit between the tool and the agency. Most vendors bill in USD in both countries: Autohive lists USD 99 a month for its Starter plan and USD 499 for Team, and HubSpot Marketing Hub Professional starts at USD 800 a month plus a required USD 3,000 onboarding fee. No New Zealand vendor publishes an AI marketing agent price in NZD.

    Those ranges are wide because the options bundle different things. The rest of this guide takes them apart, one option at a time, so the comparison is between what each dollar buys rather than between headline numbers.

    What you are actually paying for

    Every marketing price is a bundle of five things: hours of production, judgment about what to say and to whom, the software that does the work, the setup that connects it to the business, and accountability for results each month. The five options below bundle those differently, which is why comparing headline prices alone misleads.

    
      Production hours. Writing, building, posting, researching prospects, fixing pages. This is the part AI has made cheap, and it is most of what an agency retainer or a junior salary used to buy.

      Judgment. Deciding what the business should claim, which customers to go after, and what to stop doing. Still human, still expensive, and rarely more than a few hours a month for a small business.

      Software. The tools that do the production. Cheap per seat, but an agency's tool stack is inside its fee and a freelancer's is often inside theirs. Do it yourself and it is a separate line.

      Setup. Connecting the tools to the website, the CRM, the ad accounts and the analytics. One-off, often invoiced separately, and the source of most surprise costs.

      Accountability. Who is responsible if nothing ships this month. A salary buys the most of this, a tool subscription buys none.

    
    The useful question is not "what does it cost" but "what does one month of shipped marketing cost, and who carries the risk if it does not ship". Read the table with that question in mind.

    AI marketing cost comparison: five options in AUD and NZD

    The table compares five ways to buy marketing in 2026: doing it yourself with AI tools, hiring a freelancer, using an AI marketing agent or platform, retaining an agency, and employing a marketer. Australian figures are in AUD and New Zealand figures in NZD; software vendors bill in USD in both countries, so those cells stay in USD.

    
      OptionAustraliaNew ZealandBest for

      
        Do it yourself with AI toolsUSD 20 to 99 a month per tool: HubSpot Marketing Hub Starter USD 20 a seat, Autohive Lite USD 20 to Starter USD 99, Jasper Pro USD 69 a seat. Plus the owner's hours.Same tools, same USD prices. AUD and NZD list prices not published by these vendors.Solo operators with time, one channel, and a low tolerance for fixed costs.

        Freelancer or consultantAUD 80 to 200 an hour, specialists AUD 250 and up. Cemoh's vetted consultants average AUD 813 a day, or AUD 107 an hour.NZD 60 to 150 an hour, or NZD 500 to 3,000 a month on retainer. Jelly Digital puts freelancers at NZD 50 to 120 an hour.One well-defined channel run by one specialist, with the owner coordinating.

        AI marketing agent or platformPlatforms: Autohive USD 99 to 499 a month; HubSpot Professional USD 800 a month plus USD 3,000 onboarding.         Marketing agency retainerMost businesses pay AUD 2,000 to 6,000 a month; full service AUD 3,000 to 8,000. Median small-business retainer AUD 3,400 to 4,800.NZD 1,000 to 10,000 a month.
