        In-house hireSEEK advertised average for marketing managers in marketing and communications: AUD 111,784. One specialist all in: AUD 105,000 to 130,000 a year.SEEK advertised average for marketing managers in marketing and communications: NZD 106,322. Coordinator NZD 55,000 to 70,000; manager NZD 90,000 to 130,000, plus about 20% overhead.Businesses past 20 staff where marketing needs a full-time owner inside the company.

      
    
    Three notes on reading the table. Agency and freelancer figures exclude media spend, which goes to Google or Meta on top. Australian agency prices are almost always quoted exclusive of 10% GST, and New Zealand quotes usually exclude 15% GST. Salary figures are what employers advertise, not what the role costs once superannuation or KiwiSaver, tools and management time are added.

    Option 1: do it yourself with AI tools

    Doing it yourself costs USD 20 to 99 a month per tool and as many owner hours as the marketing needs. HubSpot's Marketing Hub Starter is USD 20 a seat, Jasper Pro is USD 69 a seat, and Autohive runs from a free tier through USD 20 and USD 99 plans. The cash cost is small; the time cost is the whole business.

    The tools have become good enough that one person can draft a month of content, fix page titles and set up an email sequence in a weekend. What they cannot do is decide what to make, keep making it when the business gets busy, or tell the owner that the thing they built is not working. Those three jobs are the reason most self-run marketing stops by the third month.

    There is also a tool sprawl cost. Digital Nomads HQ budgets AUD 300 to 800 a month in tool costs for a single in-house specialist, and a solo owner who tries to cover search, content, social and email ends up with a similar stack. Four subscriptions at USD 20 to 99 each is a modest agency fee with none of the accountability.

    
      Works when: one channel matters, the owner enjoys the work, and revenue does not yet justify a fixed monthly fee.

      Fails when: the owner is the bottleneck for production, or nobody reviews the output before it ships under the company's name.

      Before spending anything: run the free AI-readiness benchmark to see which channel is actually broken.

    

    Option 2: a freelancer or AI marketing consultant

    A freelance marketer costs AUD 80 to 200 an hour in Australia and NZD 60 to 150 an hour in New Zealand, with retainers from NZD 500 to 3,000 a month. An AI marketing consultant, who advises rather than produces, charges more per hour: NZD 150 to 250 in New Zealand, and AUD 191 an hour for CMO-level consultants in Australia.

    The Australian figures come from two sources that agree. workspacein.com puts standard freelance roles at AUD 80 to 200 an hour, with copywriters at AUD 80 to 180 and specialists at AUD 250 and up. Cemoh's live rate guide, updated 9 September 2026, averages AUD 813 a day across 23 marketing roles, from AUD 456 a day for a social media coordinator to AUD 1,451 a day for a CMO consultant.

    In New Zealand, King Tide's July 2026 guide puts freelancers at NZD 60 to 150 an hour and consultants at NZD 150 to 250 an hour, or NZD 2,000 to 5,000 a month for ongoing advice. It also draws a floor: a business that cannot put NZD 1,000 to 1,500 a month into marketing should not hire anyone yet.

    A freelancer who uses AI does not usually charge less per hour. They deliver more per hour, which is a real saving if the scope is fixed and a smaller one if it is open-ended. The structural cost is coordination: marketing needs several lanes, and a business with three freelancers has hired itself a part-time job managing them.

    Option 3: an AI marketing agent or platform

    An AI marketing agent or platform costs USD 99 to 499 a month for self-serve products such as Autohive, USD 800 a month plus USD 3,000 onboarding for HubSpot Marketing Hub Professional, and AUD 800 to 2,000 a month where an Australian agency sells AI-led SEO to a small business. No vendor publishes an NZD price list.

    An AI marketing agent is software that plans, produces and ships marketing work across several channels under a business owner's review, priced by the install and the month rather than by the hour.

    The category is new enough that its pricing splits into three shapes. Self-serve platforms sell seats and credits: Autohive's published plans run Free, Lite at USD 20, Starter at USD 99 and Team at USD 499 a month. Suites sell tiers with onboarding attached: HubSpot's Professional tier starts at USD 800 a month on an annual commitment with a required one-time USD 3,000 onboarding fee, and Enterprise at USD 3,600 a month with USD 7,000 onboarding.

    The third shape is an agency that runs AI inside a retainer. Marketix Digital's AI SEO pricing guide puts small businesses at AUD 800 to 2,000 a month, mid-sized companies at AUD 2,000 to 6,000, and a one-off AI SEO audit at AUD 1,000 to 3,500. It also notes that about 20% of such a budget goes to tools, with the rest split between content and strategy.

    What the agent buys that a tool does not is the plan and the cadence: the work is scoped, scheduled and shipped without the owner having to start it each week. What it buys that an agency does not is a price set by the department installed rather than by the hours consumed. What it does not buy is a person in the room; the owner still reviews and decides. Flow AI's installable sprints are one example of this model, with search and AI search as the most common first department.

    Option 4: a marketing agency retainer

    A conventional agency retainer runs AUD 2,000 to 6,000 a month for most Australian businesses, with full service at AUD 3,000 to 8,000 and a median small-business retainer of AUD 3,400 to 4,800. In New Zealand the range is NZD 1,000 to 10,000 a month, with multi-channel work at NZD 1,500 to 4,000 and full service from NZD 4,000.

    Three Australian sources triangulate the same picture. Precision Digital's 2026 guide puts SEO retainers at AUD 1,500 to 5,000, Google Ads management at AUD 800 to 2,500 plus spend, and social media management at AUD 1,000 to 3,000 a month. Digital Nomads HQ's audit of 140 agencies found a median SEO price of AUD 1,470 a month and a typical Google Ads management range of AUD 1,200 to 3,500 plus spend. workspacein.com reports mid-market full-service engagements at AUD 8,500 to 14,500 a month.

    New Zealand is cheaper at the bottom and similar at the top. Jelly Digital prices a single channel at NZD 500 to 1,500 a month, SEO at NZD 750 to 3,000, social at NZD 500 to 2,000, and Google Ads management at NZD 300 to 1,500 flat or 10 to 20% of spend. King Tide sees NZD 1,000 to 2,000 for one channel, NZD 2,000 to 4,000 for a primary channel plus support, and NZD 5,000 and up for multi-channel.

    The structural issue with a small retainer is what it buys. At AUD 2,000 or NZD 1,500 a month, a business is buying a limited number of agency hours, and small accounts get the junior ones. The agencies now branding themselves as AI marketing agencies are addressing exactly this: the production hours drop, so the same retainer buys more output. The judgment hours, and the account management, cost what they always did.

    Option 5: an in-house hire

    An in-house marketer costs AUD 105,000 to 130,000 a year all in for one specialist in Australia, and NZD 90,000 to 130,000 in salary for a marketing manager in New Zealand plus about 20% in overhead. SEEK's advertised averages for marketing managers in the marketing and communications industry are AUD 111,784 and NZD 106,322 respectively.

    The advertised salary is the visible half. Digital Nomads HQ's all-in figure of AUD 105,000 to 130,000 is built from an AUD 85,000 to 100,000 salary, 12% superannuation and AUD 300 to 800 a month of tools, which lands at AUD 8,700 to 10,800 a month. workspacein.com puts mid-level in-house marketers at AUD 80,000 to 120,000 plus super and senior at AUD 130,000 to 180,000, and adds 30% for the fully loaded cost.

    New Zealand runs a step lower in salary. King Tide puts a marketing coordinator at NZD 55,000 to 70,000 and a marketing manager at NZD 90,000 to 130,000, with about 20% on top in tools, training, recruitment and overhead. SEEK's September 2026 data shows NZD 117,500 as the advertised average in Auckland Central, against AUD 125,000 in Sydney.

    A hire is the only option that puts a person in the room full time, and for a business past 20 staff that often matters more than the cash. The trade-off is that one person, however good, cannot cover search, content, social, outbound and reporting by hand. The best-run marketing hires in 2026 spend part of their week running AI systems, which is the point at which the agent and the hire stop being alternatives and start being a pairing.

    The hidden costs: data, setup and your own time

    Hidden marketing costs in Australia and New Zealand include setup fees of AUD 500 to 3,000, reporting fees of AUD 150 to 400 a month, tool subscriptions of AUD 300 to 800 a month, platform onboarding such as HubSpot's USD 3,000, GST on top of nearly every quote, and the owner's own hours preparing data and reviewing output, which no invoice records.

    
      Setup and onboarding. One-off setup fees of AUD 500 to 3,000 are common at Australian agencies; Digital Nomads HQ found ads setup fees of AUD 499 to 1,999 and onboarding from AUD 550. HubSpot's required onboarding is USD 3,000 for Professional and USD 7,000 for Enterprise.

      Reporting and tools. Some agencies bill reporting separately at AUD 150 to 400 a month. Whoever runs the work, tools cost AUD 300 to 800 a month for one specialist's stack.

      Media spend and its management fee. Ad budgets go to the platforms on top of every figure in this guide, and management is often charged at 10 to 20% of that spend rather than a flat fee.

      Tax. Australian agency prices are almost always exclusive of 10% GST. New Zealand quotes usually exclude 15% GST. USD software bills also move with the exchange rate.

      Your data. Every AI system is only as good as the customer list, the website analytics and the brand facts it is given. Cleaning a CRM, fixing tracking and writing down what the business actually claims is unpaid owner time, and it is the first month of almost every engagement.

      Your time. Doing it yourself costs the most hours, an agency the fewest, and an agent sits in between: a review session a week, plus decisions. Price that time at the owner's own hourly rate and the table above changes shape.

    
    The free pricing model on this site exists for exactly this reason: it adds the hidden lines to the headline price so the comparison is between totals.

    Verdict: the right option by business size

    For a solo operator, tools plus one freelancer is the cheapest working setup. For 5 to 20 staff, an AI marketing agent gives several channels a weekly cadence for less than one salary. For 20 to 50 staff, a marketing lead running an agent or an AI-led agency beats a conventional retainer on cost per shipped piece.

    Solo and under 5 staff

    Cash matters more than time until it does not. Start with USD 20 to 99 a month of tools on the one channel that brings customers, and buy a freelancer's hours for the piece that needs a specialist: NZD 60 to 150 or AUD 80 to 200 an hour, scoped tightly. The trigger to move up is the month the owner becomes the reason nothing shipped.

    5 to 20 staff

    This is where the agent model earns its place. The business needs search, content and follow-up running every week, cannot justify AUD 105,000 to 130,000 or NZD 90,000 to 130,000 a year for a hire, and would get junior hours from a small retainer. One department installed and run monthly, reviewed by the owner or an office lead, is the cheapest way to get several channels moving at once.

    20 to 50 staff

    Marketing now needs a full-time owner inside the company, so hire the lead. Then equip that person with an agent or an AI-led agency rather than a conventional retainer, because the production hours are the part worth automating. A lead at SEEK's advertised averages plus an agent costs less than a lead plus a full-service retainer of AUD 3,000 to 8,000 or NZD 4,000 to 10,000 a month, and ships more.

    Where Flow AI fits in this comparison

    Flow AI is an AI marketing transformation practice: the strategy, the systems and the agents that run a marketing function, engineered end to end. It works as a fixed-scope install of one marketing department, such as search and AI search or content, then a monthly run in which Flow produces the work and the owner reviews it. Current figures come with the free audit.

    The free audit is a written plan on the business, produced before any money changes hands, and it names which department to install first and why. It sits in the agent row of the table above: priced by the department and the month, not by the hour, with the owner keeping the decisions. The five departments available today are listed on the sprints page.

    Flow AI is not the right choice for a business that wants a person in the room every day, or for one with a large media budget that needs daily bid management. It is the right choice for a business of 5 to 50 staff that has been doing marketing in the gaps and wants it to run weekly under review.

The short version

    AI marketing in Australia and New Zealand costs anywhere from USD 20 a month to NZD or AUD 130,000 a year, and the number that matters is the cost of one month of marketing that actually ships. Tools are cheapest in cash and dearest in hours; a hire is the reverse; an AI marketing agent is priced in the middle and built for the 5 to 50 staff business.

    Before this decision, most small businesses were paying for marketing in the most expensive unit available to them, whether that was the owner's evenings or a retainer buying junior hours. After it, the production runs on a system priced by the department, the judgment stays with the owner, and the monthly figure is known before the month starts. With 78% of Australian agencies publishing no prices, having that figure in writing is itself a competitive advantage.

    To get the current install and monthly figures for one department, along with a written plan on the business, request a free audit.

Q: What does AI marketing cost in New Zealand?
A: In New Zealand in 2026, a freelance marketer charges NZD 60 to 150 an hour or NZD 500 to 3,000 a month on retainer, agencies charge NZD 1,000 to 10,000 a month depending on how many channels they run, and a marketing manager costs NZD 90,000 to 130,000 a year in salary plus about 20% in overhead. AI marketing platforms bill in USD, typically USD 20 to 499 a month, and no New Zealand vendor publishes an AI marketing agent price in NZD.
Q: Is an AI marketing agency cheaper than a normal agency?
A: At the small-business end, yes. Marketix Digital puts AI-led SEO retainers at AUD 800 to 2,000 a month for small businesses, against a median conventional small-business retainer of AUD 3,400 to 4,800 a month reported by workspacein.com. The saving comes from the production hours, not the strategy hours, so the gap narrows for mid-sized scopes where both models charge AUD 2,000 to 6,000 a month.
Q: How much does an AI marketing consultant or freelancer charge?
A: In Australia, Cemoh's network of vetted marketing consultants averages AUD 813 a day or AUD 107 an hour as of September 2026, with CMO-level consultants at AUD 191 an hour. In New Zealand, King Tide reports freelancers at NZD 60 to 150 an hour and consultants at NZD 150 to 250 an hour, or NZD 2,000 to 5,000 a month for ongoing advice. A consultant who uses AI tools does not usually charge less per hour; they deliver more per hour.
Q: Is it cheaper to hire a marketer or use an AI marketing agent?
A: An AI marketing agent is cheaper on cash. One in-house specialist in Australia costs AUD 105,000 to 130,000 a year all in, and a New Zealand marketing manager NZD 90,000 to 130,000 plus overhead, which is AUD 8,700 to 10,800 a month before the person does anything. An agent runs several channels for a fraction of that, but it still needs an owner or lead spending a few hours a week on review and decisions.
Q: What hidden costs come with AI marketing?
A: Expect setup fees of AUD 500 to 3,000, reporting fees of AUD 150 to 400 a month at some agencies, tool subscriptions of AUD 300 to 800 a month, GST on top of almost every quoted price, and platform onboarding such as HubSpot's required USD 3,000 fee for Marketing Hub Professional. The largest hidden cost is the owner's time cleaning up customer data and reviewing output, which no invoice shows.

## AI marketing for small business in NZ: the complete guide.
URL: https://www.flowai.co.nz/blog/ai-marketing-for-small-business-nz.html
Author: Amber Lan, Flow AI
Updated: 2026-08-20

Short answer: AI marketing for a New Zealand small business covers four systems: SEO so Google finds you, answer engine optimisation so ChatGPT and AI search quote you, a content engine that publishes every week, and outbound follow-up that never forgets. Most businesses start with one system, prove it, then add the next.

Why AI changes the marketing math for NZ small businesses

    The old math was brutal. A small business could not justify a full-time marketer, so the owner did the marketing personally, in the gaps between actual work. Content went out when there was time, which meant rarely. SEO was something the website person mentioned once. Leads got followed up when someone remembered. The result was a business that was good at its job and invisible to everyone who had not already heard of it.

    AI changes which parts of that need a human. Adoption reflects it: in the U.S. Chamber of Commerce's 2025 Empowering Small Business report, the share of small businesses using generative AI jumped from 40% to 58% in a single year. The pattern in New Zealand looks the same from where I sit: the owners I talk to already use ChatGPT for one-off tasks. The gap is between using AI occasionally and having it run a system.

    Here is the distinction that matters, and the one most AI marketing content glosses over. AI removes repetitive work. It does not remove judgment. Drafting fifty product descriptions is repetitive work. Deciding what your business should claim, and to whom, is judgment. A system that automates the first and leaves you the second makes one person as productive as a small team. A system that pretends to automate both produces the generic sludge you already recognise in your inbox.

    The four things AI marketing actually covers

    Strip away the vendor noise and AI marketing for a small business is four systems. Each one can stand alone. Together they cover the whole funnel.

    1. SEO: being found on Google

    Still the foundation. Most NZ buying journeys start with a search, and the basics have not changed: a technically healthy site, pages that answer what people actually type, and business information that is consistent everywhere it appears. What AI changes is the cost of the work. Auditing, fixing metadata, writing location and service pages, and maintaining structured data used to be billable hours; now they are largely system output that a human reviews.

    Concretely, for a NZ service business that means: every service you offer gets its own page written the way customers search ("gutter cleaning north shore" rather than "our services"), your Google Business Profile stays complete and current, and the technical layer that most owners never see, from page titles to schema markup, is generated and checked by the system instead of waiting for a web developer's next free week.

    

    2. AEO and GEO: being cited by ChatGPT and AI search

    The new layer, and the one almost no NZ small business has touched. When someone asks ChatGPT, Perplexity, or Google's AI Overviews to recommend a business that does what you do, the assistant answers with names. Getting into that answer is called answer engine optimization, and it is engineering rather than magic: let the AI crawlers in, describe your business in structured data, publish content that can be quoted in isolation, and keep your facts consistent across the web. I run an open-source toolkit for exactly this, and this website is its live demonstration.

    The reason to move on this now is simple: the space is nearly empty. Very few NZ businesses have made themselves legible to AI assistants, which means the ones that do are competing against absence. In every other marketing channel you fight incumbents with budgets. In this one, for the moment, you mostly fight nobody.

    

    3. A content engine: publishing without a content team

    Consistency beats brilliance in small-business content, and consistency is exactly what a solo operator cannot sustain by hand. A content engine fixes the math: one source document goes in, and a month of platform-shaped posts comes out, each checked against codified brand-voice rules before anything ships. The owner's job collapses from writing everything to approving what a system drafted. I have written up how the one I run in production works, including why the quality gate matters more than the generation.

    What goes in as the source matters more than owners expect. A recorded voice memo about a job that went sideways, a customer question you answered by email, a before-and-after from last week: these are the raw material of content people actually read, because they contain things only you know. The engine's job is to shape them per platform; your job is to keep noticing them.

    

    4. Outbound automation: follow-up that never forgets

    Most small businesses do not lose deals to competitors. They lose them to silence: the quote that never got a follow-up, the enquiry that sat over a busy weekend. Outbound automation covers prospect research, personalised first contact inside safe sending limits, and follow-up sequences that stop the moment a human replies. The hard rule that keeps it trustworthy: automation opens doors, a person walks through them.

    For a small B2B business this typically means a short, honest first email to a well-researched list, a polite follow-up or two, and instant handover to you the moment anyone answers. No fake personalisation, no pressure sequences. The win is coverage: every lead and lapsed customer hears from you, which is more than most competitors manage.

    

    What a week looks like when the systems run

    Theory aside, here is roughly how a week runs once the four systems are live, based on how I operate the same stack in production.

    Monday, about an hour. Review the content packet the engine drafted from last week's source material. Approve most of it, rewrite the two pieces where the judgment call matters, schedule the lot. Skim the weekend's enquiries and check the follow-up system caught them all.

    Midweek, in the gaps. Answer the replies outbound generated, because a human always takes over the moment a buyer engages. Capture one piece of raw material for next week's content: a customer question, a job story, a number worth sharing.

    Friday, half an hour. Read the one-page report: what shipped, what moved, which channel produced this week's conversations. Decide one adjustment for next week. That is the whole management overhead.

    The point of the walkthrough is the shape of the owner's time. Almost none of it is production. Nearly all of it is judgment, which is the part only you can do, and the part that was always the actual value of marketing.

    How to choose your first system

    If you only build one thing this quarter, pick it by where your next customer actually comes from.

    
      Local service business (trades, clinics, home services): start with SEO plus AI-search visibility. Your buyers search with intent and location; being the answer wins the job before anyone else quotes.

      B2B with a defined buyer (consultancies, software, wholesale): start with outbound. A small, well-researched list with reliable follow-up beats months of content while your pipeline is empty.

      Expertise business (advisors, agencies, specialists): start with the content engine. Your buying decision is a trust decision, and consistent published judgment is how strangers learn to trust you.

      Already getting traffic that does not convert: start with analytics and follow-up before spending anything on more visibility. Fix the leak before paying for more water.

    

    What this costs against an agency, a freelancer, or a hire

    The honest answer is that every option can work, and each has a structural trade-off. Prices for agencies and freelancers vary widely in NZ, so get current quotes rather than trusting anyone's summary of the market, including mine. What I can compare is the structure of what you pay for.

    
      OptionWhat you pay forStructural trade-off

      
        AgencyA team's hours across your account, usually on a monthly retainer with a minimum term.Breadth of skills, but your budget buys hours, and small retainers get junior hours. The work usually stops when the invoice does.

        FreelancerOne specialist's time, per project or per hour.Strong in their lane, but marketing needs several lanes, and coordinating freelancers becomes your job.

        In-house hireA salary, plus tools, plus management time.Full attention on your business, at the highest fixed cost, and one person still cannot cover strategy, content, SEO, and outbound by hand.

        Fractional marketerSenior judgment, a day or two a week.Excellent strategy, but execution still needs hands or budget on top.

        AI systems + one engineerSystems that do the production, one accountable person doing the judgment. Flow AI's version is public: NZ$997 one-time for one system, or NZ$1,000/month for the full engine.Depth of a team's output at one person's price. The trade-off is trust: the model only works if the operator shows receipts, which is why mine are public on GitHub.

      
    
    

    A practical starting checklist

    You do not need all four systems on day one. This is the order that compounds.

    Week 1: find out where you stand

    
      Ask ChatGPT and Google to recommend a business that does what you do, in your town. Note who comes up. That is your real competition for the new front page.

      Run a basic health check on your own site: does it load fast, does every page have a clear title and description, does it say plainly what you do and where?

      If you want a structured version of this step, my free AI-readiness benchmark takes two minutes and needs no email.

    
    Weeks 2 to 4: fix the basics

    
      Make your business information identical everywhere: site, Google Business Profile, directories, social bios.

      Let the AI crawlers in via robots.txt and add structured data that says who you are, what you sell, and where you serve.

      Publish honest answers to the questions buyers actually ask, one page per real question.

    
    Month 2 and on: build the cadence

    
      Stand up a content rhythm you can sustain forever, even if that is one good piece a week. A system helps precisely here.

      Wire up follow-up: every enquiry gets a response path that does not depend on your memory.

      Measure. One page of numbers a month tells you which channel pays. Without it you are guessing.

    

    Common mistakes NZ small businesses make with AI marketing

    Buying tools without a system. A ChatGPT subscription is not a marketing function. Tools produce output; a system decides what to produce, checks the quality, and ships it on schedule. The tool spend is wasted without the surrounding discipline.

    Ignoring AI search entirely. Optimising only for Google in 2026 is optimising for part of the front page. The assistants answer with names either way; the only question is whether yours is one of them.

    Publishing unreviewed AI output. Readers recognise generated text faster every month, and nothing burns trust quicker. Every line should pass a human or a codified quality gate before it carries your name.

    Doing everything at once. Four systems launched simultaneously by one busy owner means four systems abandoned by June. Sequence them. The checklist above is the order I use with clients.

Q: What is AI marketing for a small business?
A: AI marketing means using AI systems to run the repetitive parts of marketing: drafting content, keeping SEO and AI-search visibility healthy, researching and contacting prospects, and reporting. The owner keeps the judgment calls; the systems do the production. Done well, one person can run what used to need a team.
Q: How much does AI marketing cost for a small NZ business?
A: It ranges from roughly the cost of a few software subscriptions if you run tools yourself, up to agency-level retainers. Flow AI publishes its pricing as a reference point: a NZ$997 one-time starter sprint, or NZ$1,000 per month for the full marketing engine, cancel anytime.
Q: Do I still need SEO if I am doing AEO?
A: Yes. Answer engine optimization builds on SEO rather than replacing it. AI assistants read the same web Google crawls, and many draw on search indexes directly. A site that is technically healthy, fast, and clearly structured is the starting condition for both. AEO adds the layer that makes content quotable and machine-readable.
Q: Can one person really run all of this?
A: Yes, if the systems are built first. One person cannot hand-write a month of content and research fifty prospects a week. One person can absolutely review what systems produce and make the judgment calls. That is the entire design principle: machines do production, the human does strategy and quality control.
